### Executive Summary & Thermodynamic Derivations

The Hall–Héroult process has remained the dominant technology for primary aluminium production since 1886—operating at bath temperatures of approximately $960\text{--}1000\,^\circ\text{C}$ and consuming an industry-average energy of roughly $13\text{--}14\,\text{kWh/kg Al}$ (as stated in the question's premises)—because of an interlocking set of thermodynamic, materials-science, and magnetohydrodynamic constraints. Specifically:
1. **Thermodynamic Voltage Depolarization:** Using a consumable carbon anode lowers the reversible decomposition potential of alumina ($\text{Al}_2\text{O}_3$) by roughly $1.02\,\text{V}$ at $960\,^\circ\text{C}$ compared to pure oxygen evolution, substituting lower-cost chemical energy from petroleum coke for expensive electrical energy.
2. **Cryolite Solvation Uniqueness:** Molten sodium hexafluoroaluminate ($\text{Na}_3\text{AlF}_6$) is one of the very few ionic melts capable of dissolving appreciable quantities of oxide ions ($2\text{--}8\,\text{wt}\%\ \text{Al}_2\text{O}_3$) while remaining electrochemically more stable than $\text{Al}_2\text{O}_3$ and maintaining a liquid density ($\approx 2.1\,\text{g/cm}^3$) lower than that of liquid aluminium ($\approx 2.3\,\text{g/cm}^3$), enabling natural gravity separation at the cathode.
3. **Self-Healing Frozen Sidewall Ledge:** Because molten fluorides corrode virtually all known refractory oxides and metals at $960\,^\circ\text{C}$, the cell relies on deliberate heat rejection through its walls to freeze a solid crust of cryolite bath against the carbon/silicon carbide lining. That thermal-equilibrium ledge requires significant superheat and ohmic dissipation to remain stable.

To displace the Hall–Héroult process at commercial scale rather than merely in pilot plants, **inert oxygen-evolving anodes** must simultaneously overcome a $\sim 1.0\,\text{V}$ thermodynamic voltage penalty through a reduced anode–cathode distance (ACD) coupled with a Dimensionally Stable Wettable Cathode ($\text{TiB}_2$), while maintaining an anode corrosion rate low enough (typically estimated below $1\text{--}2\,\text{cm/year}$) to prevent iron, nickel, or copper contamination of smelter-grade aluminium. Conversely, the **aluminium chloride ($\text{AlCl}_3$) route**—which operates at lower temperatures ($\approx 700\,^\circ\text{C}$) and achieved lower cell energy consumption (estimated around $9\text{--}10\,\text{kWh/kg Al}$ in historical industrial trials)—must overcome the prohibitive capital and environmental cost of anhydrous carbochlorination of alumina, severe trace-moisture HCl corrosion, and toxic organochlorine (hexachlorobenzene/dioxin) byproduct generation in the upstream chemical plant.

### 1. Physical and Economic Constraints Sustaining the Hall–Héroult Process

#### 1.1 Aqueous Impossibility and Carbothermic Reduction Limits
Aluminium cannot be electrodeposited from aqueous solutions because the standard reduction potential of $\text{Al}^{3+}/\text{Al}$ ($-1.66\,\text{V}$ vs. SHE) lies far below that of hydrogen evolution ($0.00\,\text{V}$ vs. SHE at $\text{pH}=0$; $-0.83\,\text{V}$ at $\text{pH}=14$). Any attempt to electrolyze an aqueous aluminium salt reduces water to $\text{H}_2$ gas long before $\text{Al}^{3+}$ can be plated.

Similarly, direct carbothermic reduction of alumina in a blast furnace ($\text{Al}_2\text{O}_3 + 3\text{C} \rightarrow 2\text{Al} + 3\text{CO}$) requires temperatures exceeding $2000\,^\circ\text{C}$ for the Gibbs free energy change ($\Delta G$) to become negative, as reflected on an Ellingham diagram. At $>2000\,^\circ\text{C}$, two parasitic mechanisms render carbothermic smelting commercially unviable:
* **Carbide and Oxycarbide Formation:** Intermediate reactions form solid or dissolved $\text{Al}_4\text{C}_3$ and $\text{Al}_4\text{O}_4\text{C}$, trapping the reduced metal in refractory slags.
* **Suboxide Volatilization:** Alumina reacts with molten aluminium and carbon to produce volatile aluminium suboxide gas ($\text{Al}_2\text{O}_{(g)}$) and aluminium vapor ($\text{Al}_{(g)}$), causing severe yield losses and furnace choking upon condensation in cooler zones.

Consequently, industrial production is forced into molten-salt electrolysis at temperatures above the melting point of aluminium ($660.3\,^\circ\text{C}$) so the product can be tapped as a continuous liquid phase.

#### 1.2 The Uniqueness of the Cryolite ($\text{Na}_3\text{AlF}_6$) Solvent Window
Pure $\text{Al}_2\text{O}_3$ has a melting point of $2072\,^\circ\text{C}$, making neat oxide electrolysis impossible in practical containment vessels. Cryolite ($\text{Na}_3\text{AlF}_6$, melting point $\approx 1010\,^\circ\text{C}$) is uniquely suited as a solvent for four coupled physical reasons:
1. **Oxide Solubility via Oxyfluoride Complexation:** Most molten halide salts (such as $\text{NaCl}$ or $\text{KCl}$) have negligible solubility for $\text{Al}_2\text{O}_3$ ($<0.01\,\text{wt}\%$). Molten cryolite dissociates into $\text{Na}^+$, $\text{AlF}_6^{3-}$, $\text{AlF}_4^-$, and $\text{F}^-$ ions. When $\text{Al}_2\text{O}_3$ is added, the oxide ion ($\text{O}^{2-}$) bridges aluminium fluoride complexes to form soluble oxyfluoride anions such as $\text{Al}_2\text{OF}_6^{2-}$ and $\text{Al}_2\text{O}_2\text{F}_4^{2-}$, dissolving up to $\sim 10\,\text{wt}\%\ \text{Al}_2\text{O}_3$ near the eutectic temperature.
2. **Melting Point Depression into the $960\text{--}1000\,^\circ\text{C}$ Window:** By adding dissolved $\text{Al}_2\text{O}_3$ ($2\text{--}5\,\text{wt}\%$), excess aluminium fluoride ($\text{AlF}_3$, $10\text{--}12\,\text{wt}\%$), and calcium fluoride ($\text{CaF}_2$, $4\text{--}6\,\text{wt}\%$), the liquidus temperature of the bath is depressed to $\approx 940\text{--}950\,^\circ\text{C}$. Operating with $10\text{--}20\,^\circ\text{C}$ of superheat fixes the operating temperature strictly around $960\,^\circ\text{C}$. Lowering the temperature further by adding more $\text{AlF}_3$ or $\text{LiF}$ sharply reduces $\text{Al}_2\text{O}_3$ solubility and ionic conductivity, triggering anode effects and alumina sludging on the cathode.
3. **Electrochemical Stability Window:** The decomposition potential of $\text{NaF}$, $\text{CaF}_2$, and $\text{AlF}_3$ is substantially higher than that of dissolved $\text{Al}_2\text{O}_3$. As long as oxide ions are present at the anode surface, oxygen-bearing complexes are discharged preferentially over $\text{F}^-$, preventing perfluorocarbon ($\text{CF}_4$, $\text{C}_2\text{F}_6$) evolution under normal alumina feeding.
4. **Density Inversion Constraints:** At $960\,^\circ\text{C}$, liquid aluminium has a density of $\approx 2.30\,\text{g/cm}^3$, whereas the modified cryolite bath has a density of $\approx 2.08\text{--}2.12\,\text{g/cm}^3$. This small buoyancy differential ($\Delta\rho \approx 0.2\,\text{g/cm}^3$) is essential so that molten aluminium settles to the bottom of the cell, shielded from re-oxidation by anode gases. Additives that substantially lower the bath melting point often alter bath density or reduce alumina solubility enough to cause undissolved alumina ($\rho \approx 3.9\,\text{g/cm}^3$) to sink beneath the metal pad and form an electrically insulating bottom sludge.

#### 1.3 Thermodynamic Advantage of the Consumable Carbon Anode
From first principles, the stoichiometric Faraday requirement to reduce $\text{Al}^{3+}$ ($n = 3$ electrons per atom, atomic weight $M = 26.9815\,\text{g/mol}$, Faraday constant $F = 96,485\,\text{C/mol}$) is:
$$Q_{\text{Faraday}} = \frac{3 F}{M_{\text{Al}} \times 3600\,\text{C/(A}\cdot\text{h)}} = \frac{3 \times 96,485}{26.9815 \times 3600} \approx 2.980\,\text{Ah/g Al} = 2980\,\text{Ah/kg Al}$$

At $T = 960\,^\circ\text{C}$ ($1233\,\text{K}$), compare the two possible cell reactions:

1. **Inert Anode Reaction (Oxygen Evolution):**
   $$\frac{1}{2}\text{Al}_2\text{O}_{3(\text{diss})} \rightarrow \text{Al}_{(l)} + \frac{3}{4}\text{O}_{2(g)}$$
   From standard thermodynamic tables for alumina and dissolved cryolite solutions at $1233\,\text{K}$, the Gibbs free energy change $\Delta G^\circ_{1233}$ is approximately $+635\,\text{kJ/mol Al}$ (for $3\,\text{mol } e^-$). The reversible decomposition voltage $E^\circ_{\text{rev}}$ is:
   $$E^\circ_{\text{inert}} = \frac{\Delta G^\circ}{3F} = \frac{635,000\,\text{J}}{3 \times 96,485\,\text{C}} \approx 2.19\,\text{V}$$

2. **Carbon Anode Reaction ($\text{CO}_2$ Evolution):**
   $$\frac{1}{2}\text{Al}_2\text{O}_{3(\text{diss})} + \frac{3}{4}\text{C}_{(s)} \rightarrow \text{Al}_{(l)} + \frac{3}{4}\text{CO}_{2(g)}$$
   Because the oxidation of carbon to $\text{CO}_2$ ($C + \text{O}_2 \rightarrow \text{CO}_2$, $\Delta G^\circ_{1233} \approx -396\,\text{kJ/mol }\text{CO}_2$) is strongly exergonic, $\frac{3}{4}\,\text{mol}$ of carbon oxidation contributes $\frac{3}{4}(-396\,\text{kJ}) \approx -297\,\text{kJ/mol Al}$. Thus:
   $$\Delta G^\circ_{\text{carbon}} \approx 635 - 297 = +338\,\text{kJ/mol Al}$$
   $$E^\circ_{\text{carbon}} = \frac{338,000\,\text{J}}{3 \times 96,485\,\text{C}} \approx 1.17\,\text{V}$$
   *(Accounting for non-unit activity of dissolved $\text{Al}_2\text{O}_3$ below saturation, the actual operational reversible potential in a Hall–Héroult cell is $\approx 1.20\text{--}1.22\,\text{V}$.)*

**Economic Implication of Carbon Depolarization:**
The consumable carbon anode acts as a chemical fuel cell at the anode interface, depolarizing the cell by $\Delta E = 2.19 - 1.17 = 1.02\,\text{V}$. At an industrial current efficiency ($\eta_I$) of $94\%$ (driven by the back-reaction $2\text{Al}_{(l)} + 3\text{CO}_{2(g)} \rightarrow \text{Al}_2\text{O}_{3} + 3\text{CO}_{(g)}$), the actual specific charge required per kilogram of aluminium is:
$$Q_{\text{actual}} = \frac{2.980\,\text{kAh/kg Al}}{0.94} \approx 3.17\,\text{kAh/kg Al}$$
A $1.02\,\text{V}$ reduction in reversible cell potential directly saves:
$$\Delta W_{\text{elec}} = 3.17\,\text{kAh/kg Al} \times 1.02\,\text{V} \approx 3.23\,\text{kWh/kg Al}$$
Historically and in most electricity markets today, supplying $\sim 0.40\text{--}0.45\,\text{kg}$ of calcined petroleum coke and coal-tar pitch per kg of $\text{Al}$ (which has a theoretical stoichiometric consumption of $\frac{3/4 \times 12.01}{26.98} = 0.334\,\text{kg C/kg Al}$, elevated to $\sim 0.42\,\text{kg/kg}$ by $\text{CO}$ back-reaction and air/$\text{CO}_2$ burn) has been cheaper than purchasing an extra $3.23\,\text{kWh/kg Al}$ of electrical energy plus the capital cost of additional rectifier capacity.

#### 1.4 Origin of the $13\text{--}14\,\text{kWh/kg Al}$ Energy Floor: MHD Stability and the Frozen Ledge
Since the actual charge requirement at $94\%$ current efficiency is $3.17\,\text{kAh/kg Al}$, the specific electrical energy consumption ($W$, in $\text{kWh/kg Al}$) is a linear function of total cell voltage ($V_{\text{cell}}$):
$$W = Q_{\text{actual}} \times V_{\text{cell}} \approx 3.17 \times V_{\text{cell}}$$
To operate at $13.0\text{--}14.0\,\text{kWh/kg Al}$ (as referenced in the prompt), the total cell voltage must lie between $4.10\,\text{V}$ and $4.42\,\text{V}$. A typical voltage breakdown for a modern prebake cell ($\approx 4.20\,\text{V}$) illustrates why this voltage cannot easily be compressed in a traditional cell:
* **Reversible Decomposition Voltage ($E_{\text{rev}}$):** $\approx 1.20\,\text{V}$
* **Anodic Overpotential ($\eta_a$, C–O discharge kinetics):** $\approx 0.50\,\text{V}$
* **Gas-Bubble-Induced Voltage Drop ($\Delta V_{\text{bubble}}$):** $\approx 0.20\text{--}0.30\,\text{V}$ ($\text{CO}_2$ bubbles flatten under the horizontal carbon anode block, blinding $30\text{--}50\%$ of the active surface)
* **Electrolyte Ohmic Drop across the Anode–Cathode Distance ($\Delta V_{\text{bath}}$):** $\approx 1.40\text{--}1.60\,\text{V}$
* **External Busbar, Anode Assembly, and Cathode Lining Drops ($\Delta V_{\text{ext}}$):** $\approx 0.70\text{--}0.85\,\text{V}$

Why can the electrolyte ohmic drop ($\Delta V_{\text{bath}} = j \cdot d_{\text{ACD}} / \kappa$, where $j \approx 0.8\text{--}1.0\,\text{A/cm}^2$ is current density, $\kappa \approx 2.2\,\text{S/cm}$ is bath conductivity, and $d_{\text{ACD}} \approx 3.5\text{--}4.5\,\text{cm}$ is the anode–cathode distance) not simply be eliminated by reducing $d_{\text{ACD}}$ to $1\,\text{cm}$? Two coupled physical mechanisms prevent this:

1. **Carbon-Non-Wetting and Magnetohydrodynamic (MHD) Interfacial Waves:**
   Molten aluminium does not readily wet the carbon cathode lining; therefore, a deep liquid metal pad ($15\text{--}25\,\text{cm}$ thick) must be maintained over the carbon blocks to ensure uniform current collection. In modern cells carrying $300\text{--}600\,\text{kA}$, huge horizontal and vertical currents interact with the self-generated magnetic fields ($\mathbf{J} \times \mathbf{B}$ Lorentz forces) across the small density difference ($\Delta\rho \approx 0.2\,\text{g/cm}^3$) between the metal pad and the cryolite bath. This excites gravito-electromagnetic interfacial waves (sloshing and doming of the liquid aluminium pad). If $d_{\text{ACD}}$ is reduced below $\approx 3.0\text{--}3.5\,\text{cm}$, wave crests touch the underside of the carbon anode, causing direct short-circuiting and rapid re-oxidation of liquid $\text{Al}$ by $\text{CO}_2$ bubbles, collapsing current efficiency.

2. **Thermal Balance for the Self-Healing Frozen Sidewall Ledge:**
   Only around $2.0\text{--}2.1\,\text{V}$ of the $4.20\,\text{V}$ cell voltage goes into the endothermic enthalpy of reaction and sensible heat to bring reactants to $960\,^\circ\text{C}$ ($\approx 6.3\text{--}6.6\,\text{kWh/kg Al}$). The remaining $\sim 2.1\,\text{V}$ ($\sim 6.5\text{--}7.0\,\text{kWh/kg Al}$) is dissipated as Joule heat. This massive heat rejection is not merely waste: it is required to maintain a steep thermal gradient across the cell sidewalls so that a solid ledge of frozen cryolite ($5\text{--}15\,\text{cm}$ thick) remains frozen against the inner wall. If ohmic heating is cut without completely redesigning cell insulation, the bath cools and freezes over; conversely, if insulation is increased to allow low-voltage operation, any transient power excursion or anode effect melts the frozen sidewall ledge, exposing the silicon carbide/carbon wall to rapid chemical dissolution by molten cryolite and causing catastrophic tap-out failure.

### 2. Hurdles for Inert-Anode Technology to Achieve Industrial Displacement

An inert-anode Hall–Héroult cell replaces the consumable carbon anode with a non-consumable, oxygen-evolving electrode ($\frac{1}{2}\text{Al}_2\text{O}_3 \rightarrow \text{Al} + \frac{3}{4}\text{O}_2$). While pilot demonstrations (such as the Elysis joint venture between Alcoa and Rio Tinto) have produced commercial-grade metal at pilot/demonstration scale, displacing carbon anodes across the global smelter fleet requires overcoming four fundamental barriers:

#### 2.1 Overcoming the $\sim 1.02\,\text{V}$ Thermodynamic Penalty and the $\sim 0.8\,\text{V}$ Enthalpy Deficit
As derived in Section 1.3, eliminating carbon raises the reversible decomposition potential from $\approx 1.17\,\text{V}$ to $\approx 2.19\,\text{V}$ ($+1.02\,\text{V}$). Worse still, in terms of thermal enthalpy ($\Delta H^\circ$ at $960\,^\circ\text{C}$):
* The thermoneutral voltage ($E_{\text{tn}} = \Delta H / 3F$) for the carbon reaction (including warming reactants from $25\,^\circ\text{C}$ to $960\,^\circ\text{C}$) is $\approx 2.0\text{--}2.1\,\text{V}$.
* For the inert-anode oxygen-evolving reaction, because the exothermic enthalpy of carbon combustion is removed, the thermoneutral voltage jumps to $E_{\text{tn,inert}} \approx 2.85\text{--}2.95\,\text{V}$.

Partially offsetting this, the anodic overpotential ($\eta_a$) for $\text{O}_2$ evolution on catalytic metal/oxide surfaces ($\approx 0.15\text{--}0.25\,\text{V}$) is lower than the sluggish C–O bond formation overpotential on carbon ($\approx 0.50\,\text{V}$), saving $\approx 0.30\,\text{V}$. Nevertheless, at an identical anode–cathode distance ($d_{\text{ACD}}$), an inert-anode cell requires roughly $0.7\text{--}0.8\,\text{V}$ higher total cell voltage—translating to an energy penalty of $+2.2\text{ to }+2.5\,\text{kWh/kg Al}$ (pushing consumption to $15.5\text{--}16.5\,\text{kWh/kg Al}$).

**What Must Be Overcome:**
To break even on electrical energy ($\approx 13\text{--}14\,\text{kWh/kg Al}$), an inert-anode cell must cut the electrolyte ohmic drop ($\Delta V_{\text{bath}}$) by at least $0.7\text{--}0.8\,\text{V}$, which requires shrinking $d_{\text{ACD}}$ from $\sim 4.0\,\text{cm}$ down to $\sim 1.5\text{--}2.0\,\text{cm}$ or adopting vertical interdigitated electrode geometries. However, shrinking $d_{\text{ACD}}$ in a conventional cell with a deep liquid aluminium pad causes MHD wave short-circuiting. Therefore, full energy competitiveness requires pairing the inert anode with a **drained, wettable cathode** (typically titanium diboride, $\text{TiB}_2$, or $\text{TiB}_2$–carbon composites). $\text{TiB}_2$ is wetted by molten aluminium, allowing the cell to operate with a thin, drained film of liquid $\text{Al}$ ($1\text{--}3\,\text{mm}$) flowing into a collection sump, eliminating the deep metal pad and its MHD wave instabilities. Yet $\text{TiB}_2$ cathodes face their own durability limits: slow dissolution into liquid aluminium (saturated at $\sim 100\text{--}200\,\text{ppm}$ Ti and B), grain-boundary penetration by liquid $\text{Al}$ and $\text{Na}$, and thermal-shock cracking during cell startup.

#### 2.2 Materials Corrosion vs. Smelter-Grade Metal Purity
Molten cryolite containing dissolved $\text{Al}_2\text{O}_3$ at $960\,^\circ\text{C}$ under nascent atomic/molecular oxygen evolution at $1.0\,\text{A/cm}^2$ is one of the most corrosive environments in industrial chemistry. Three candidate classes of inert anodes have been investigated:
1. **Ceramics** ($\text{SnO}_2\text{–Sb}_2\text{O}_3\text{–CuO}$, nickel ferrite $\text{NiFe}_2\text{O}_4$): High chemical resistance to oxygen, but brittle (susceptible to catastrophic thermal shock when inserted into a $960\,^\circ\text{C}$ bath) and poor electrical conductivity.
2. **Metals/Alloys** ($\text{Cu–Ni–Fe}$, $\text{Ni–Fe–Cu–Al}$): Excellent electrical conductivity and fracture toughness, relying on an *in-situ* passivating surface layer of $\text{NiFe}_2\text{O}_4$. However, if alumina concentration drops locally or current density fluctuates, the passivating scale spalls or dissolves, causing rapid catastrophic dissolution of the underlying metal.
3. **Cermets** ($\text{NiFe}_2\text{O}_4\text{–NiO}$ dispersed with $\sim 15\text{--}20\,\text{wt}\%\ \text{Cu–Ag}$ or $\text{Cu–Ni}$ metallic phase): Designed to combine ceramic corrosion resistance with metallic conductivity and toughness.

**The Purity Constraint Derivation:**
Any oxide or metal from the inert anode ($\text{FeO}$, $\text{NiO}$, $\text{CuO}$, $\text{SnO}_2$) that dissolves into the cryolite bath is thermodynamically much less stable than $\text{Al}_2\text{O}_3$ ($E^\circ$ of $\text{Fe}^{3+}$, $\text{Ni}^{2+}$, $\text{Cu}^{2+}$ are $>1.0\,\text{V}$ more positive than $\text{Al}^{3+}/\text{Al}$). Consequently, nearly $100\%$ of dissolved anode cations are immediately co-deposited into the liquid aluminium cathode.
Standard smelter-grade primary aluminium (such as P1020A) strictly limits impurities to $<0.20\,\text{wt}\%\ \text{Fe}$ and $<0.10\,\text{wt}\%\ \text{Si}$, with trace limits on $\text{Ni}$, $\text{Cu}$, and $\text{Sn}$ (often $<0.01\text{--}0.03\,\text{wt}\%$ each).
Consider a flat-plate anode operating at $j = 0.8\,\text{A/cm}^2$ and $94\%$ current efficiency, producing:
$$\dot{m}_{\text{Al}} = \frac{0.8\,\text{A/cm}^2}{3.17\,\text{Ah/g Al}} \times 24\,\text{h/day} \times 365\,\text{days/yr} \approx 2210\,\text{g Al}/(\text{cm}^2\cdot\text{yr})$$
If an anode of density $\rho_{\text{anode}} \approx 6.0\,\text{g/cm}^3$ corrodes at just $1.0\,\text{cm/yr}$, it releases $6.0\,\text{g}/(\text{cm}^2\cdot\text{yr})$ of heavy metals ($\text{Fe, Ni, Cu}$) into the $2210\,\text{g/cm}^2$ of aluminium produced beneath it:
$$\text{Impurity fraction} = \frac{6.0}{2210} \approx 0.27\,\text{wt}\% \ (2700\,\text{ppm})$$
Thus, even a $1\,\text{cm/yr}$ recession rate already exceeds P1020A impurity limits! To achieve $<0.05\text{--}0.10\,\text{wt}\%$ total anode-derived contamination, the anode recession rate must be kept below $\sim 0.2\text{--}0.4\,\text{cm/yr}$, which require maintaining the bath strictly near alumina saturation at all times.

#### 2.3 Lower-Temperature Bath Trade-Offs
To slow anode dissolution down to $<0.3\,\text{cm/yr}$, inert-anode designs typically lower the operating temperature from $960\,^\circ\text{C}$ to $800\text{--}900\,^\circ\text{C}$ using high-$\text{AlF}_3$ acidic cryolite or $\text{KF–AlF}_3$ electrolytes. However, lowering bath temperature creates a severe mass-transport bottleneck:
* $\text{Al}_2\text{O}_3$ solubility drops from $\sim 8\text{--}10\,\text{wt}\%$ at $960\,^\circ\text{C}$ to only $\sim 2\text{--}4\,\text{wt}\%$ at $800\text{--}850\,^\circ\text{C}$, and dissolution kinetics slow down by an order of magnitude.
* The operating window becomes razor-thin: feed slightly too much $\text{Al}_2\text{O}_3$, and undissolved alumina sinks to form an insulating cathode sludge; feed slightly too little $\text{Al}_2\text{O}_3$, and the anode is starved of $\text{O}^{2-}$ ions, causing the protective oxide film on the inert anode to dissolve into the fluoride melt within minutes (catastrophic fluoridation corrosion).

#### 2.4 Brownfield Retrofit vs. Greenfield CAPEX Economics
Existing smelters have billions of dollars of sunk capital in prebake carbon anode plants (calcining, pitch mixing, vibro-compacting, Ring Reidhammer baking furnaces, and anode rodding shops) alongside potlines engineered precisely for horizontal carbon anodes and $960\,^\circ\text{C}$ heat balances. Because an inert-anode cell operates with a different thermal balance ($E_{\text{tn}} \approx 2.9\,\text{V}$ vs. $2.05\,\text{V}$), different bath chemistry, and often vertical/slotted electrode geometries, it frequently cannot be dropped into existing pots as a simple plug-and-play replacement without rebuilding the pot shell, busbars, and alumina point-feeders. Unless carbon pricing ($>\$100\text{--}150/\text{t }\text{CO}_2$) or green-aluminium price premiums offset both the higher electricity consumption (if not paired with $\text{TiB}_2$ cathodes) and the greenfield potroom capital cost, carbon anodes remain economically entrenched.

### 3. Hurdles for the Chloride-Based ($\text{AlCl}_3$) Route to Achieve Industrial Displacement

The chloride electrolysis route—most famously developed and operated by **Alcoa** at a demonstration/commercial scale ($15,000\text{--}30,000\,\text{t/yr}$ capacity in Palestine, Texas, between 1976 and 1982)—avoids cryolite entirely by electrolyzing anhydrous aluminium chloride ($\text{AlCl}_3$) dissolved ($3\text{--}10\,\text{wt}\%$) in a molten alkali-chloride melt (typically equimolar $\text{NaCl–KCl}$ or $\text{NaCl–LiCl}$) at $\approx 700\,^\circ\text{C}$:
$$\text{AlCl}_{3(\text{diss})} \rightarrow \text{Al}_{(l)} + \frac{3}{2}\text{Cl}_{2(g)}$$

#### 3.1 Why the Chloride Electrolytic Cell Is Physically Superior
Inside the electrolysis pot itself, the Alcoa chloride process solved nearly all the physical limitations of the Hall–Héroult cell:
1. **Bipolar Graphite Electrodes:** Because $\text{Cl}_2$ gas does not oxidize graphite at $700\,^\circ\text{C}$ (unlike $\text{O}_2$, which burns carbon to $\text{CO}_2$), graphite acts as a truly **inert anode** for chlorine evolution! Alcoa stacked 10 to 30 horizontal/inclined graphite plates in series inside a single sealed refractory vessel. Each intermediate plate operated as a bipolar electrode (chlorine evolving on the bottom face, liquid aluminium depositing on the top face and draining to a bottom sump).
2. **Short ACD and Gas-Lift Circulation:** With no deep metal pool on the intermediate plates, MHD sloshing was eliminated. The anode–cathode gap was reduced to $\approx 1.0\text{--}1.5\,\text{cm}$, and rising $\text{Cl}_2$ bubbles pumped the electrolyte naturally through internal channels.
3. **Low Specific Energy Consumption:** Although the reversible potential of $\text{AlCl}_3$ at $700\,^\circ\text{C}$ is $\approx 2.0\,\text{V}$, the small ACD ($1.3\,\text{cm}$), high conductivity of $\text{LiCl–NaCl}$ melts, and low chlorine overpotential on graphite ($\approx 0.1\,\text{V}$) allowed each bipolar stage to run at $\approx 2.7\text{--}3.0\,\text{V}$, achieving an electrical energy consumption of **$9.0\text{--}9.5\,\text{kWh/kg Al}$**—roughly $30\%$ lower than Hall–Héroult.

#### 3.2 Why the Chloride Route Failed to Displace Hall–Héroult (and What It Must Overcome)
Despite the triumph of the electrolysis cell, Alcoa permanently shut down the Palestine plant in the early 1980s because the **upstream chemical conversion of $\text{Al}_2\text{O}_3$ to anhydrous $\text{AlCl}_3$** proved economically and environmentally intractable. To displace Hall–Héroult, a chloride process must overcome four fundamental barriers:

1. **Thermodynamic Impossibility of Aqueous Dehydration:**
   Unlike $\text{NaCl}$ or $\text{CaCl}_2$, hydrated aluminium chloride ($\text{AlCl}_3\cdot 6\text{H}_2\text{O}$, easily made by leaching bauxite or kaolin clay with aqueous $\text{HCl}$) **cannot be thermally dehydrated** by heating. Because $\text{Al}^{3+}$ has an extremely high charge-to-radius ratio (high polarizing power), heating the hexahydrate hydrolyzes the coordinated water molecules:
   $$2(\text{AlCl}_3\cdot 6\text{H}_2\text{O}) \xrightarrow{\Delta} \text{Al}_2\text{O}_{3(s)} + 6\text{HCl}_{(g)} + 9\text{H}_2\text{O}_{(g)}$$
   Instead of anhydrous $\text{AlCl}_3$, calcination simply reverts back to alumina and hydrochloric acid gas!

2. **Energy, Carbon, and CAPEX Penalty of Carbochlorination:**
   Because thermal dehydration fails, anhydrous $\text{AlCl}_3$ must be synthesized from dry Smelter-Grade Alumina (or calcined clay) via high-temperature **carbochlorination** ($700\text{--}900\,^\circ\text{C}$ in a fluidized bed reactor):
   $$\text{Al}_2\text{O}_{3(s)} + \frac{3}{2}\text{C}_{(s)} + 3\text{Cl}_{2(g)} \rightarrow 2\text{AlCl}_{3(g)} + \frac{3}{2}\text{CO}_{2(g)}$$
   Notice the thermodynamic irony:
   * **Carbon Consumption Remains:** The carbon anode eliminated from the electrolytic cell is simply shifted upstream into the carbochlorination reactor! Exactly the same stoichiometric amount of carbon ($\frac{3}{4}\,\text{mol C/mol Al}$) is oxidized to $\text{CO}_2$ and $\text{CO}$ to strip oxygen from $\text{Al}_2\text{O}_3$.
   * **Double Plant CAPEX:** The smelter must first pay the full cost of the Bayer process to produce pure $\text{Al}_2\text{O}_3$ (or pay for elaborate fractional distillation to remove $\text{FeCl}_3$, $\text{SiCl}_4$, and $\text{TiCl}_4$ if chlorinating raw bauxite/kaolin), and *then* build a massive chemical plant to react $\text{Al}_2\text{O}_3$, carbon, and recycled $\text{Cl}_2$, condense sublime $\text{AlCl}_3$ solid (which sublimes at $180\,^\circ\text{C}$ without melting at atmospheric pressure), and feed it hermetically into the cells. The capital and operating costs of this chemical plant more than wiped out the $4\,\text{kWh/kg Al}$ electricity savings in the electrolysis cell.

3. **Trace Moisture, Oxide Sludge, and Graphite Intercalation/Spalling:**
   Anhydrous $\text{AlCl}_3$ is fiercely hygroscopic. If even trace moisture ($\text{H}_2\text{O}$) or residual $\text{Al}_2\text{O}_3$ enters the $700\,^\circ\text{C}$ chloride cell, it reacts to form corrosive $\text{HCl}$ gas and dissolved oxychloride ions ($\text{AlOCl}$). Worse, oxygen species discharge at the graphite bipolar anodes before chlorine, burning the graphite plates to $\text{CO}_2$, roughening the precisely machined $1.3\,\text{cm}$ inter-electrode gap, and causing alkali-metal intercalation swelling and spalling of the graphite plates.

4. **Toxic Chlorinated Hydrocarbons (Hexachlorobenzene and Dioxins):**
   In the fluidized-bed carbochlorinator at $700\text{--}850\,^\circ\text{C}$, reacting petroleum coke or coked alumina with $\text{Cl}_2$ gas in the presence of catalytic metal chlorides inevitably synthesizes persistent, carcinogenic organochlorines—specifically hexachlorobenzene ($\text{C}_6\text{Cl}_6$), polychlorinated biphenyls (PCBs), and polychlorinated dibenzo-p-dioxins/furans (PCDD/Fs). Managing, scrubbing, and incinerating these hazardous chemical wastes at a million-tonne-per-year smelter scale posed a regulatory and financial barrier that ultimately killed industrial adoption.

**Summary of Displacement Requirements:**
* For **inert anodes** to displace Hall–Héroult at industrial scale, they must pair a cermet/metallic anode capable of surviving $3\text{--}5\text{ years}$ at a recession rate $<0.3\,\text{cm/yr}$ (to keep $\text{Fe/Ni/Cu} < 0.1\,\text{wt}\%$ in the aluminium) with a dimensionally stable wettable $\text{TiB}_2$ cathode that suppresses MHD waves, enabling a $\le 2\,\text{cm}$ ACD that recovers the $1.02\,\text{V}$ thermodynamic voltage penalty.
* For the **chloride route** to displace Hall–Héroult, a breakthrough non-carbothermic, dioxin-free chemical pathway to convert $\text{Al}_2\text{O}_3$ or $\text{AlCl}_3\cdot 6\text{H}_2\text{O}$ into anhydrous $\text{AlCl}_3$ at low cost and without trace oxide/moisture contamination would have to be invented; otherwise, the upstream carbochlorination plant negates both the energy and carbon advantages of the chloride electrolysis cell.

### 1. Thermodynamic and Physicochemical Foundations of Hall–Héroult Dominance

The Hall–Héroult process has produced primary aluminium since 1886 by dissolving alumina ($\text{Al}_2\text{O}_3$) in a molten cryolite ($\text{Na}_3\text{AlF}_6$) bath and electrolyzing it with consumable carbon anodes:

$$\text{Al}_2\text{O}_3\ (\text{dissolved}) + \frac{3}{2}\text{C}\ (\text{s}) \longrightarrow 2\text{Al}\ (\text{l}) + \frac{3}{2}\text{CO}_2\ (\text{g})$$

The persistence of this configuration stems from a unique convergence of thermodynamic, electrochemical, and materials properties.

```
+-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------+
|                                HALL–HÉROULT CELL ARCHITECTURE                           |
|                                                                                         |
|                           Carbon Anodes (+) [CO2 evolution]                             |
|                           [===]      [===]      [===]                                   |
|   +-------------------------|----------|----------|---------------------------------+   |
|   | Solidified Ledge ("Freeze")        v          v                                 |   |
|   | (Na3AlF6-Al2O3 self-lining)  Molten Cryolite Bath (~960 °C, rho ~ 2.1 g/cm3)    |   |
|   |                             ----------------------------------                  |   |
|   |                             Liquid Aluminium Pad (rho ~ 2.3 g/cm3)              |   |
|   |                             ==================================                  |   |
|   |                             Carbon Cathode Block (-)                            |   |
|   +---------------------------------------------------------------------------------+   |
|   | Refractory / Steel Pot Shell                                                    |   |
+---+---------------------------------------------------------------------------------+---+
```

#### A. The Thermodynamic Carbon Credit
Pure electrochemical decomposition of alumina without a consumable reducing agent evolves molecular oxygen:

$$\text{Al}_2\text{O}_3\ (\text{s}) \longrightarrow 2\text{Al}\ (\text{l}) + \frac{3}{2}\text{O}_2\ (\text{g})$$

At an operating temperature of $960\ ^\circ\text{C}$ ($1233\ \text{K}$), this reaction has a standard Gibbs free energy change ($\Delta G^\circ$) of approximately $+1282\text{ kJ/mol}$, corresponding to a reversible decomposition potential ($E_\text{rev}^\circ = -\Delta G^\circ / nF$, where $n = 6$ electrons per mole of $\text{Al}_2\text{O}_3$) of:

$$E_\text{rev, } \text{O}_2^\circ = -\frac{1{,}282{,}000\text{ J/mol}}{6 \times 96{,}485\text{ C/mol}} \approx -2.214\text{ V}$$

In the Hall–Héroult cell, coupling the oxidation of carbon to carbon dioxide ($\text{C} + \text{O}_2 \rightarrow \text{CO}_2$) offsets the free energy requirement by $\Delta G^\circ \approx -396\text{ kJ/mol }\text{O}_2$. The net reaction free energy falls to approximately $+688\text{ kJ/mol }\text{Al}_2\text{O}_3$, lowering the theoretical reversible cell potential to:

$$E_\text{rev, C}^\circ = -\frac{688{,}000\text{ J/mol}}{6 \times 96{,}485\text{ C/mol}} \approx -1.188\text{ V}$$

Consuming carbon pays a thermodynamic dividend of $\Delta E \approx 1.026\text{ V}$ (Grjotheim & Kvande, 1993). In modern prebake reduction cells operating at total cell voltages of $4.1\text{–}4.3\text{ V}$, this offset accounts for nearly one-quarter of the total electrical energy input.

#### B. The Cryolite Electrolyte Window
Alumina melts at $2072\ ^\circ\text{C}$, a temperature that defies containment in industrial electrochemical reactors. Molten cryolite ($\text{Na}_3\text{AlF}_6$, eutectic with added $\text{AlF}_3$, $\text{CaF}_2$, and $\text{LiF}$) dissolves $2\text{–}6\text{ wt}\%\ \text{Al}_2\text{O}_3$ at $950\text{–}980\ ^\circ\text{C}$ while fulfilling several simultaneous criteria:
1. **Electrochemical stability window:** The standard reduction potential of sodium ions on an aluminium cathode is close to that of aluminium complexes, but aluminium deposition remains thermodynamically favored by roughly $0.15\text{–}0.25\text{ V}$ in commercial baths with excess $\text{AlF}_3$ (acidic baths), preventing runaway co-deposition of sodium (Thonstad et al., 2001).
2. **Ionic conductivity:** Molten cryolite exhibits a high specific electrical conductivity ($\kappa \approx 2.2\text{–}2.8\text{ S/cm}$ at $960\ ^\circ\text{C}$), primarily via fast-moving $\text{Na}^+$ ions, minimizing ohmic bath resistance across the anode–cathode distance (ACD).
3. **Density stratification:** At $960\ ^\circ\text{C}$, the density of the molten fluoride bath is approximately $2.08\text{–}2.12\text{ g/cm}^3$, whereas the density of liquid aluminium is approximately $2.28\text{–}2.30\text{ g/cm}^3$ (Thonstad et al., 2001). Liquid aluminium naturally pools at the bottom of the cell, where it serves as the liquid cathode while avoiding physical contact with evolving anode gases ($\text{CO}_2$/$\text{CO}$).

#### C. The Frozen Ledge Self-Passivation Mechanism
Molten fluoride salts dissolve almost all known structural refractories and metals. The Hall–Héroult cell avoids direct wall corrosion through a thermal dynamic equilibrium: heat loss through the steel pot shell causes bath material to crystallize along the interior perimeter, forming a protective solid crust ("freeze" or "ledge") of cryolite and alumina. This frozen boundary isolates the carbon and silicon carbide sidewalls from both molten bath and liquid metal, solving what would otherwise be an intractable materials degradation problem.

---

### 2. Breakdown of the 13–14 kWh/kg Specific Energy Consumption

The specific electrical energy consumption ($w$, in $\text{kWh/kg}$) of an electrolytic cell is given by Faraday's law:

$$w = \frac{E_\text{cell} \cdot n \cdot F}{3600 \cdot M_\text{Al} \cdot \eta_\text{CE}} \times 10^{-3} = \frac{2.9806 \cdot E_\text{cell}}{\eta_\text{CE}}$$

where:
* $n = 3$ electrons per aluminium atom,
* $F = 96{,}485.3\text{ C/mol}$,
* $M_\text{Al} = 26.9815\text{ g/mol}$,
* $E_\text{cell}$ is the operational cell voltage ($\text{V}$),
* $\eta_\text{CE}$ is the cathodic current efficiency (fractional).

At typical modern performance metrics of $E_\text{cell} \approx 4.15\text{ V}$ and $\eta_\text{CE} \approx 0.945$ ($94.5\%$):

$$w = \frac{2.9806 \times 4.15}{0.945} \approx 13.09\text{ kWh/kg Al}$$

#### Voltage Overpotentials and Ohmic Losses
While theoretical decomposition requires only $1.19\text{ V}$, industrial cell voltages range from $4.0\text{ to }4.3\text{ V}$ due to irreversible thermodynamic and transport resistances:

```
Total Cell Voltage: ~4.15 V
├── Reversible potential (E_rev):                ~1.20 V  (28.9%)
├── Anode overpotential (reaction + diffusion):   ~0.45 V  (10.8%)
├── Cathode overpotential:                        ~0.05 V  ( 1.2%)
├── Ohmic bath drop (IR_bath, ACD ~3.5-4.5 cm):   ~1.40 V  (33.7%)
├── Gas bubble layer resistance:                  ~0.25 V  ( 6.0%)
└── External electrical busbar / contacts:        ~0.80 V  (19.3%)
```

1. **Ohmic bath drop ($I R_\text{bath}$):** The physical anode–cathode distance (ACD) must be maintained at $3.5\text{–}4.5\text{ cm}$ to prevent back-reaction:
   $$2\text{Al}\ (\text{dissolved}) + 3\text{CO}_2\ (\text{g}) \longrightarrow \text{Al}_2\text{O}_3\ (\text{bath}) + 3\text{CO}\ (\text{g})$$
   Hydrodynamic waves in the liquid aluminium pad—driven by Lorentz forces ($\mathbf{J} \times \mathbf{B}$) from high currents ($300\text{–}600\text{ kA}$) intersecting stray magnetic fields—dictate this minimum ACD. Narrowing the gap triggers cell shorting and accelerates pad re-oxidation, collapsing current efficiency.
2. **Thermal self-sustenance:** The $2.8\text{–}3.0\text{ V}$ of overvoltage and resistance is not purely wasted; the resulting Joule heating ($I^2 R$) supplies the thermal energy needed to maintain the bath at $960\ ^\circ\text{C}$ and sustain the protective frozen ledge against continuous ambient heat loss.

### 3. Economic and Industrial Lock-In

The long-standing dominance of Hall–Héroult rests on industrial and economic factors as much as chemical ones:

| Economic Driver | Mechanism of Lock-In |
| :--- | :--- |
| **Capital Intensity & Asset Lifespans** | Modern greenfield smelters require $\$4{,}000\text{–}\$5{,}500$ of capital investment per annual tonne of capacity. Potlines operate continuously for $40\text{–}60$ years; individual reduction pots undergo relining only every $5\text{–}8$ years. Abandoning this infrastructure presents high write-off costs. |
| **Byproduct Utilization** | Anodes are manufactured from calcined petroleum coke (CPC) and coal-tar pitch (CTP)—low-value residual byproducts of crude oil refining and metallurgical coke production. Even with consumption rates of $0.40\text{–}0.45\text{ kg carbon per kg Al}$, carbon remains an affordable reducing agent. |
| **Economies of Scale** | Cell amperage has scaled from early $10\text{–}20\text{ kA}$ pots to modern $500\text{–}600\text{ kA}$ systems (e.g., AP60). Magnetohydrodynamic (MHD) modeling, point-feed alumina hoppers, and automated dry scrubbing systems capturing fluorides for recycling back into the bath have preserved competitiveness against alternative routes. |

### 4. Inert-Anode Electrolysis: Constraints and Hurdles

Inert anodes (e.g., Alcoa and Rio Tinto's ELYSIS joint venture) replace consumable carbon with a non-reactive cermet, ceramic, or metallic substrate, evolving oxygen rather than carbon dioxide:

$$\text{Al}_2\text{O}_3\ (\text{dissolved}) \longrightarrow 2\text{Al}\ (\text{l}) + \frac{3}{2}\text{O}_2\ (\text{g})$$

```
+------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------+
|                          INERT ANODE CHALLENGE: VOLTAGE PENALTY                          |
|                                                                                          |
|  Hall-Héroult (Carbon):  E_rev ~ 1.20 V   + Overpotentials (~2.95 V) = Total ~ 4.15 V    |
|                          [==== 1.20 V ====][============ 2.95 V ============]            |
|                                                                                          |
|  Inert Anode (Oxygen):   E_rev ~ 2.21 V   + Overpotentials (~1.80-2.20 V) = Total ~ 4.0-4.4 V |
|                          [======== 2.21 V ========][======== 1.80-2.20 V ========]       |
+------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------+
```

To achieve industrial displacement, inert-anode technology must address four specific technical and economic barriers:

#### A. The Thermodynamic Voltage Penalty
Because oxygen evolution lacks carbon's chemical assistance, the reversible potential increases by $+1.026\text{ V}$ ($E_\text{rev} \approx 2.21\text{ V}$). To avoid using more electricity than modern carbon-anode smelters ($>13\text{ kWh/kg}$), an inert-anode cell must eliminate roughly $1.0\text{ V}$ of internal ohmic and kinetic losses elsewhere in the cell:
* **Wettable deoxygenated cathodes:** Anodes must be paired with titanium diboride ($\text{TiB}_2$)-coated or solid $\text{TiB}_2$ composite cathodes that liquid aluminium wets. Liquid metal then spreads as a thin draining film rather than an oscillating electromagnetic pad, dampening Lorentz waves and permitting the ACD to contract from $\sim 4.0\text{ cm}$ to $<2.0\text{ cm}$ without short-circuiting (Pawlek, 2014).
* **Lower bath temperature:** Reducing bath temperatures toward $750\text{–}850\ ^\circ\text{C}$ (e.g., via low-melting potassium/sodium fluoride baths) reduces overpotentials and substrate corrosion, but suppresses alumina solubility and dissolution kinetics, increasing the risk of insoluble alumina sludging at the cathode.

#### B. Chemical Solubility and Metal Contamination
Anodes operate under extreme conditions: temperatures near $900\ ^\circ\text{C}$, high oxygen partial pressures ($P_{\text{O}_2} \approx 1\text{ atm}$), and direct contact with molten oxyfluoride electrolytes.
* Common candidate materials (nickel-iron-copper cermets, doped tin dioxides $\text{SnO}_2$, nickel ferrite spinels $\text{NiFe}_2\text{O}_4$) exhibit small but finite equilibrium solubilities in cryolite (Kvande, 1999).
* Dissolved transition metal ions ($\text{Fe}^{n+}$, $\text{Ni}^{2+}$, $\text{Cu}^{2+}$, $\text{Sn}^{4+}$) transport via convection and diffusion to the cathode, where they reduce preferentially over aluminium because their standard reduction potentials are more positive.
* Commercial electrical-conductor grades and aerospace alloys impose strict contamination limits on iron ($\text{Fe} < 0.10\text{–}0.15\text{ wt}\%$) and trace transition metals ($\text{Ni}, \text{Sn} < 0.02\text{ wt}\%$). Anode degradation must stay below milligrams per square centimeter per year to meet these purity specifications without requiring post-electrolysis chemical refining.

#### C. Electrical Conductivity, Thermal Shock, and Substrate Joining
Refractory oxide spinels exhibit electrical conductivities two to three orders of magnitude lower than industrial graphite at $900\ ^\circ\text{C}$. To avoid internal resistance losses, anodes require complex cermet architectures with metallic cores or internal copper conductors. Transitioning between a high-conductivity metal core, an intermediate refractory ceramic cermet, and the surface passivation layer produces thermal expansion mismatches ($\Delta \alpha$) that risk mechanical spalling during thermal cycling and crust breaking.

#### D. The Economic Trade-Off
Inert anodes eliminate direct Scope 1 carbon dioxide emissions ($1.5\text{–}1.8\text{ t }\text{CO}_2\text{/t Al}$) and consumable carbon-anode baking plants. However, if net cell voltage remains even $0.2\text{–}0.4\text{ V}$ higher than in carbon cells, the process requires an additional $0.6\text{–}1.2\text{ kWh}$ of electricity per kilogram of aluminium. In regions with power costs above $\$40\text{–}\$50/\text{MWh}$, this operating expense increase outweighs the cost savings from carbon anode consumption unless supported by carbon pricing policies or premiums for low-carbon metal.

### 5. Chloride-Based Electrolysis: The Alcoa Smelting Process Case Study

In the 1970s and 1980s, Alcoa developed and piloted the Alcoa Smelting Process (ASP) at industrial scale at its Palestine, Texas facility (producing up to $15{,}000\text{ tonnes/year}$). The process relies on carbothermic chlorination of Bayer-grade alumina followed by molten chloride electrolysis:

$$\text{Al}_2\text{O}_3\ (\text{s}) + 3\text{C}\ (\text{s}) + 3\text{Cl}_2\ (\text{g}) \longrightarrow 2\text{AlCl}_3\ (\text{g}) + 3\text{CO}\ (\text{g})\quad (700\text{–}900\ ^\circ\text{C})$$

$$\text{AlCl}_3\ (\text{dissolved in }\text{NaCl}\text{–}\text{LiCl}) \longrightarrow \text{Al}\ (\text{l}) + \frac{3}{2}\text{Cl}_2\ (\text{g})\quad (700\text{–}750\ ^\circ\text{C})$$

```
+------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------+
|                             ALCOA SMELTING PROCESS (ASP) FLOW                            |
|                                                                                          |
|        Alumina (Al2O3) + Coke (C) + Chlorine Recycled (Cl2)                              |
|                              |                                                           |
|                              v                                                           |
|               [ Carbochlorination Reactor ] ----> Waste Cl-hydrocarbons, CO              |
|                              |                                                           |
|                              v Anhydrous AlCl3 Vapor (sublimes ~180 °C)                  |
|               [ Fractional Condensation / Purification ]                                 |
|                              |                                                           |
|                              v Pure Anhydrous AlCl3 Feed                                 |
|               [ Bipolar Molten Chloride Cell (700 °C) ]                                  |
|                 NaCl-LiCl-AlCl3 Electrolyte / Graphite Anodes                            |
|                 * Consumes ~9.5 kWh/kg Al                                                |
|                              |                                                           |
|                   +----------+----------+                                                |
|                   |                     |                                                |
|                   v                     v                                                |
|            Liquid Aluminium       Chlorine Gas (Cl2) ------------------------------------+
|                                   (Corrosive closed loop recycle)                        |
+------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------+
```

#### A. Demonstrated Advantages of Chloride Electrolysis
1. **Low operating temperature:** The $\text{NaCl}\text{–}\text{LiCl}\text{–}\text{AlCl}_3$ molten salt electrolyte operates at $700\text{–}730\ ^\circ\text{C}$, below the solubility threshold for substantial aluminium re-dissolution.
2. **Dimensionally stable, bipolar graphite electrodes:** Chlorine gas does not consume graphite anodes under anhydrous conditions ($\text{C} + 2\text{Cl}_2 \rightarrow \text{CCl}_4$ is thermodynamically unfavorable at $700\ ^\circ\text{C}$). Electrodes can be configured in compact, multi-compartment bipolar stacks.
3. **Reduced power consumption:** The short inter-electrode spacing and high electrical conductivity of alkali chloride baths lowered demonstrated power consumption to $9.5\text{–}10.0\text{ kWh/kg Al}$, approximately $30\%$ below Hall–Héroult cells of that era (Peace, 1982).

#### B. Failure Modes and Industrial Disqualification
Despite its electrochemical efficiency, Alcoa decommissioned the Palestine plant in the 1980s because of severe operational and materials bottlenecks elsewhere in the flowsheet:

* **Corrosive carbochlorination and moisture sensitivity:** Anhydrous aluminium chloride ($\text{AlCl}_3$) sublimes at $180\ ^\circ\text{C}$ and hydrolyzes on contact with moisture:
  $$\text{AlCl}_3 + 3\text{H}_2\text{O} \longrightarrow \text{Al(OH)}_3 + 3\text{HCl}$$
  Trace water generates hydrochloric acid ($\text{HCl}$) and aluminium oxychlorides ($\text{AlOCl}$). These species corroded reactor linings, eroded graphite electrodes, and caused cell polarization failures.
* **Chlorine containment and loop integrity:** Electrolysis releases dry chlorine gas ($\text{Cl}_2$) that must be scrubbed, liquefied, vaporized, and recycled to the carbochlorination reactors. Maintaining high-volume chlorine loops at $700\ ^\circ\text{C}$ without fugitive emissions presented safety, regulatory, and mechanical challenges (Dell, 1988).
* **Byproduct organochlorines:** High-temperature chlorination of carbonaceous petroleum coke generated trace volatile chlorocarbons, including hexachlorobenzene, tetrachloromethane, and polychlorinated dibenzo-p-dioxins and dibenzofurans. The capital and compliance costs of containing and scrubbing these hazardous compounds proved prohibitive.
* **Capital expenditure imbalance:** Power savings in the cell house were offset by the cost of building an adjacent chemical synthesis, condensation, and sublimation plant to handle hazardous solids, gases, and molten salts.

## Short answer

**The Hall–Héroult process survives because every part of it is the cheapest solution to a hard constraint, and the constraints are thermodynamic, not managerial.** Alumina is so stable that only electrolysis can reduce it at practical rates; molten cryolite is the only solvent that dissolves alumina, conducts, melts near 960 °C and lets the metal pool below it; and the carbon anode is simultaneously the electrode, the reductant and the cheapest consumable in the plant. The 13–14 kWh/kg (global average just under 14 kWh/kg in 2024, per the International Aluminium Institute) sits roughly twice above the thermodynamic minimum of ~6.3 kWh/kg because about half the energy is lost as ohmic heat, back-reaction and keeping the bath molten — and because electricity, not the anode or the alumina, is the dominant cost, smelters have been built where power is cheap and then run for 30–50 years, locking the process in. **An inert anode must prove it can survive years in 960 °C cryolite without dissolving into the metal and be cheap enough to beat the carbon-anode system; the chloride route must solve the supply of anhydrous, ultra-pure AlCl₃ and chlorine corrosion at scale** — the two problems that killed Alcoa's chloride pilot after ~15 years and >$25 million of R&D. ELYSIS's 450 kA inert-anode cell (November 2025, Alma, Québec) is the first demonstration at commercial amperage; the multi-year durability question is still open.

## 1. The physical constraints that fix the process

**Alumina is exceptionally stable.** The reduction 2Al₂O₃ → 4Al + 3O₂ has a very large positive free energy, so carbon alone cannot reduce it at any practical temperature (carbothermic routes need ~2000 °C and make aluminium sub-oxides and carbides instead of metal). Electrolysis is not a choice; it is the only reduction chemistry that works. The reaction enthalpy alone is 29.2 GJ/t Al (8.1 kWh/kg), and the electrochemical minimum is ~6.3 kWh/kg (IEA ETSAP, 2012).

**Cryolite is the only practical solvent.** Molten Na₃AlF₆ with AlF₃/CaF₂/LiF additions must simultaneously (a) dissolve alumina (up to ~8%), (b) conduct electricity, (c) melt at a workable temperature (pure cryolite 1010 °C; the industrial bath ~950–960 °C), (d) be less dense than aluminium so the metal pools on the cathode below the bath, and (e) not react with the product. No other known melt does all five. The 960–1000 °C operating temperature is therefore set by the bath liquidus, not by the operators' preference.

**The carbon anode is a reductant, not just an electrode.** The anode reaction is 2Al₂O₃ + 3C → 4Al + 3CO₂: carbon consumes the oxygen liberated at the anode, and its oxidation supplies part of the energy. That is why the anode is consumed — theoretical minimum 0.334 t C per t Al (IEA ETSAP), actual net consumption ~0.4 t/t — and why it produces ~1.5 t CO₂ per t Al plus perfluorocarbons (CF₄, C₂F₆) during anode effects. The anode is also cheap (petroleum coke + pitch binder), conductive and self-renewing by replacement. Any substitute must be an electrode, survive the melt, and replace the energetic contribution of carbon oxidation.

**The 13–14 kWh/kg.** The cell runs at ~4.0–4.5 V and 300,000–500,000 A, versus a thermodynamic decomposition voltage of ~1.2 V. The gap is ohmic heating in the bath, anode and cathode; current efficiency of 93–96% (the rest is lost to re-oxidation of dissolved aluminium — the back-reaction); and heat loss through the cell walls, which is itself necessary to maintain the frozen bath ledge that protects the steel shell. Best large-scale pilot cells reach 12.5 kWh/kg; the IAI global average was just under 14 kWh/kg in 2024 (14.21 kWh/kg in the 2018 IAI data). Half the input energy leaves as waste heat.

## 2. The economic constraints that lock it in

- **Sunk capital at enormous scale.** World primary output is ~70 million tonnes a year (69.0 Mt in 2022, China ~59%). A modern smelter costs several billion dollars and runs 30–50 years; a replacement technology must justify scrapping that, not merely matching the running cost.
- **Electricity dominates the cash cost.** At 13–14 kWh/kg, power is the largest single cost, so smelters are sited where hydro or cheap coal power exists (30% hydro, ~55% coal globally in 2021). A new process that saves 2 kWh/kg is worth less than a smelter that buys power 2 ¢/kWh cheaper.
- **The feedstock chain is settled.** Bauxite → Bayer alumina (99.6% pure) is cheap, and alumina is the only feed the process wants. Secondary (recycled) aluminium needs <5% of the energy, but it cannot supply primary-grade metal for all uses, so it caps demand growth rather than displacing the process.
- **Metal quality.** Most uses require 99.7%+ purity with tight limits on Fe, Si, Na and Cu. The carbon-anode process meets this routinely; any replacement must prove it does too, at full scale, for years.
- **It is the only commercial process.** As a 1984 US patent background states, the Bayer–Hall–Héroult process "is the only commercial process for producing aluminum metal" — every alternative has stayed at pilot scale.

## 3. Inert anodes: what must be overcome

An inert anode evolves oxygen instead of CO₂, so it eliminates direct process emissions, anode changes and the associated labour, and its constant geometry should allow a tighter anode–cathode distance and slightly lower energy. The furthest-advanced programme is **ELYSIS** (Alcoa + Rio Tinto): a 100 kA inert-anode cell produced metal in November 2021 at its Saguenay R&D centre; a **450 kA cell — the first at commercial amperage — started up in November 2025** at the end of an existing potline at Rio Tinto's Alma smelter; and a 10-pot demonstration plant (100 kA, up to 2,500 t/y) at Arvida is targeted for first production in 2027 (US$285 million). What it still has to prove:

1. **Durability without contamination.** The anode must survive years at ~960 °C in cryolite while evolving oxygen, without corroding or dissolving. The leading materials are nickel–iron spinel (NiFe₂O₄) cermets; any dissolution puts Fe/Ni/Cu into the metal and breaks the purity specification. The 450 kA demonstration "does not yet answer the multi-year durability, current-efficiency, and metal-purity questions that determine commercial viability."
2. **Cell redesign, not a drop-in.** With no anode consumption, the heat balance changes (no carbon-oxidation heat, no anode effects), alumina feeding and bath chemistry control must be re-tuned, and the frozen ledge must be maintained by other means. The cell has to be redesigned around the inert anode.
3. **Cost.** Cermet anodes are far more expensive to fabricate (sintering) than carbon anodes; the saving is the avoided anode plant, rodding shop and change-outs. That trade has to be positive per tonne of metal over the anode's life.
4. **A modest energy prize.** The thermodynamic floor (6.3 kWh/kg) does not move. The gain is a few kWh/kg at most, from a stable anode–cathode distance and higher current efficiency — real, but not the order-of-magnitude step that would force a fleet replacement on its own. The driver is carbon elimination, not energy.

## 4. The chloride route: what must be overcome

The chloride process electrolyses AlCl₃ dissolved in a molten alkali-chloride bath at ~700 °C, with graphite electrodes that are inert in that chemistry and chlorine recycled to the chlorinator. Alcoa announced it in 1973, spent ~15 years and >$25 million on R&D, and built a 15,000 t/y pilot plant in Anderson County. Its demonstrated advantages were real: ~9–9.6 kWh/kg including the chlorination step (versus 13.4 kWh/kg for Hall–Héroult), a lower temperature, a more compact cell, higher metal purity, and a single-cell voltage of ~2.7 V (reversible 1.8 V). It is "no longer known to be in operation." The constraints that killed it, and that any revival must solve:

1. **Anhydrous, ultra-pure AlCl₃ at scale.** AlCl₃ is made by carbochlorinating alumina at 700–900 °C. The step is itself energy-hungry, still consumes carbon and still produces CO₂, and demands a feed that is very pure and completely water-free — "production and handling of the very pure and water-free aluminum trichloride" was, in the patent literature's words, the difficult problem that "could not be solved satisfactorily." Bayer alumina typically contains ~0.5% Na₂O, which chlorinates to NaAlCl₄ (melting point ~150 °C), a liquid that causes extensive corrosive damage at chlorination temperatures and wastes chlorine.
2. **Corrosion.** AlCl₃ and Cl₂ are highly corrosive to cell materials, piping and gas handling; the cell needed a steel enclosure lined with silicon oxynitride refractory. Construction materials that survive for years at 700 °C in chloride service are the bottleneck.
3. **The chlorine loop and its side reactions.** Evolved Cl₂ must be fully recycled to the chlorinator; impurities trigger side reactions, and chlorinated alkanes (PAHs) and biphenyls (PCBs) have been reported, along with phosgene and other toxic gases during chlorination. Moisture causes further unwanted reactions. A leak is a toxic-release event, not a process upset.
4. **Economics of a more complex plant.** The chloride plant is really three plants (chlorinator + purifier + electrolysis + Cl₂ recycle) against one potline. Its energy advantage (~30%) was never enough to offset the capital and maintenance cost — and Hall–Héroult kept improving (larger cells, better current efficiency, lower energy), narrowing the gap. SINTEF, which is reassessing the route, notes it "has not been able to compete with the Hall-Héroult process, and little information is available on industrial experience with the method."

## 5. The bottom line

The Hall–Héroult process dominates because its constraints are met by the cheapest available materials (carbon, cryolite, alumina, electricity where it is cheap) and because the capital stock is enormous. An inert anode displaces it only if it proves multi-year survival in cryolite without contaminating the metal, at a cost below the carbon-anode system — ELYSIS is the first programme to test that at commercial amperage, and the answer will come from the Alma cell and the 2027 Arvida plant. A chloride route displaces it only if someone solves anhydrous AlCl₃ supply and chlorine corrosion cheaply enough to beat a process that has had 140 years of optimisation; Alcoa tried for 15 years and could not. Neither route lacks a pilot plant; both lack a demonstrated answer to their one binding constraint.

### Physical and Economic Lock-In of Hall–Héroult and the Hurdles for Alternative Routes

The Hall–Héroult process has maintained its monopoly over primary aluminium production because carbon consumption thermodynamically subsidises the cell voltage by over 1.0 V, cryolite uniquely dissolves alumina while forming an insulating frozen side-ledge, and electricity represents $650–$1,120 per tonne of metal (roughly 30–40% of cash operating costs), making any process that increases net cell voltage or capital expenditure commercially non-viable. Displacing it requires overcoming specific thermodynamic and chemical bottlenecks: inert anodes must overcome a +1.03 V theoretical penalty by reducing anode-cathode distance (ACD) via drained wetted cathodes, while chloride routes must solve the toxic, highly corrosive carbochlorination of alumina rather than the electrolysis itself.

---

### 1. Correction of Energy Economics and the Thermodynamic Carbon Subsidy

A foundational economic lock-in of the Hall–Héroult process is that power consumption is the single largest variable cost component, but previous assessments misstate this by three orders of magnitude. 

* **Recomputation of Smelting Power Costs:** At the established consumption of 13.0–14.0 kWh kg⁻¹ ($13{,}000–14{,}000\text{ kWh t}^{-1}$) and industrial electricity tariffs of $\$0.05–\$0.08\text{ kWh}^{-1}$:
  $$\text{Minimum Power Cost} = 13{,}000\text{ kWh t}^{-1} \times \$0.05\text{ kWh}^{-1} = \$650\text{ t}^{-1}\text{ Al}$$
  $$\text{Maximum Power Cost} = 14{,}000\text{ kWh t}^{-1} \times \$0.08\text{ kWh}^{-1} = \$1{,}120\text{ t}^{-1}\text{ Al}$$
  Against benchmark Western primary aluminium cash operating costs of $\$1{,}800–\$2{,}400\text{ t}^{-1}$, electrical energy constitutes 30–40% of smelting costs.
* **The Thermodynamic Carbon Subsidy:** The consumable carbon anode acts as a continuous chemical fuel that depolarises the anode reaction. At 960 °C (1233 K):
  * **Carbon anode:** $0.5\text{ Al}_2\text{O}_3 + 0.75\text{ C} \rightarrow \text{Al} + 0.75\text{ CO}_2$, $\Delta G^\circ \approx 342\text{ kJ (mol Al)}^{-1}$, yielding a reversible potential of $E^\circ_{\text{rev}} = \frac{\Delta G^\circ}{nF} = \frac{342{,}000}{3 \times 96{,}485} \approx 1.18\text{ V}$.
  * **Inert anode:** $0.5\text{ Al}_2\text{O}_3 \rightarrow \text{Al} + 0.75\text{ O}_2$, $\Delta G^\circ \approx 640\text{ kJ (mol Al)}^{-1}$, yielding $E^\circ_{\text{rev}} = \frac{640{,}000}{3 \times 96{,}485} \approx 2.21\text{ V}$.
* **The Constraint:** Switching to an inert anode automatically imposes a thermodynamic penalty of $\Delta E^\circ = 2.21\text{ V} - 1.18\text{ V} = +1.03\text{ V}$ (Grjotheim & Kvande, 1993, *Introduction to Aluminium Electrolysis*, Aluminium-Verlag). Unless cell resistance is drastically cut elsewhere, operating voltage climbs from ~4.2 V to >5.2 V, increasing electricity consumption to 16.0–17.5 kWh kg⁻¹ and adding $\$150–\$250\text{ t}^{-1}$ in power costs alone.

---

### 2. Physical Constraints of the Cryolite Bath and Cell Enclosure

The operating envelope of 960–1000 °C is dictated by liquidus equilibria and mass transfer in the $\text{Na}_3\text{AlF}_6\text{–AlF}_3\text{–CaF}_2$ electrolyte:

* **Alumina Solubility vs. Operating Temperature:** Cryolite melts at 1011 °C; industrial additions of excess $\text{AlF}_3$ (typically 10–12 wt%) and $\text{CaF}_2$ (4–6 wt%) suppress the bath liquidus to 940–960 °C. The cell must operate at a superheat of 8–12 °C (950–970 °C) because $\text{Al}_2\text{O}_3$ solubility drops sharply below 950 °C (falling below 3–4 wt%), which triggers diffusion starvation, severe concentration overpotentials, and catastrophic anode effects (perfluorocarbon emissions, $\text{CF}_4/\text{C}_2\text{F}_6$).
* **Self-Passivation via Frozen Side-Ledges:** Molten cryolite dissolves nearly all oxide refractories. The process survives because the heat balance creates a dynamic crust and side-ledge of frozen cryolite along the walls, protecting the carbon sidewalls and shell. This thermal equilibrium requires continuous internal Joule dissipation ($I^2R$), tying cell geometry, current density (0.8–1.0 A cm⁻²), and heat loss together.

---

### 3. Barriers Inert-Anode and Chloride Routes Must Clear at Industrial Scale

For an alternative route to displace modern Hall–Héroult potlines (such as AP60 technology operating at >95% current efficiency), it must clear specific physical, material, and chemical engineering hurdles:

#### A. Inert-Anode Routes (e.g., ELYSIS, Cermet/Metallic Anodes)
1. **The ACD-Reduction Requirement:** Because of the +1.03 V thermodynamic penalty, inert anodes cannot run in conventional horizontal cells with a 4.0–4.5 cm anode-cathode distance (ACD). To match 13 kWh kg⁻¹, the ACD must be lowered to <2.0 cm. In a standard cell, magnetohydrodynamic (MHD) waves in the liquid aluminium pad cause short-circuits at this distance. Industrial adoption therefore requires drained, wettable titanium diboride ($\text{TiB}_2$) composite cathodes to maintain a thin, stable aluminium film.
2. **Corrosion and Metal Contamination:** Cermets (e.g., $\text{NiFe}_2\text{O}_4\text{–NiO–Cu}$) and metallic substrates slowly dissolve in fluoride baths. Even an anode wear rate of 1 mm yr⁻¹ contaminates the metal pad with Fe, Ni, and Cu exceeding P1020 purity limits (>0.10% Fe, >0.03% Si), rendering the product unacceptable for high-value aerospace or extrusion alloys without costly downstream refining (Kvande, 1999, *JOM*, 51(5), 27–29).
3. **Heat Deficit:** Eliminating exothermic carbon oxidation leaves a thermal shortfall that requires either increased external insulation or higher current densities, complicating retrofits into existing prebake potlines.

#### B. Chloride-Based Routes (e.g., Alcoa Smelting Process, ASP)
Electrolysis of anhydrous $\text{AlCl}_3$ in an $\text{NaCl–LiCl}$ melt at ~700 °C was proven at a 15,000 t yr⁻¹ demonstration plant (Anderson County, Texas, 1976–1985) and reduced electrical consumption to ~9.5 kWh kg⁻¹ with non-consumable bipolar graphite anodes. The process failed to scale industrially due to three upstream and containment barriers:
1. **Upstream Carbochlorination Bottleneck:** Bauxite/alumina cannot be directly dissolved in chloride melts. It must first be converted via carbochlorination ($\text{Al}_2\text{O}_3 + 3\text{ C} + 3\text{ Cl}_2 \rightarrow 2\text{ AlCl}_3 + 3\text{ CO}$) at 700–900 °C. This unit operation requires complex fluidized beds, produces traces of chlorinated biphenyls and polychlorinated dibenzodioxins, and generates trace phosgene ($\text{COCl}_2$).
2. **Moisture Sensitivity and Sludge:** Anhydrous $\text{AlCl}_3$ hydrolyses violently with moisture ($\text{AlCl}_3 + 3\text{ H}_2\text{O} \rightarrow \text{Al(OH)}_3 + 3\text{ HCl}$). Trace moisture ingress creates insoluble oxychlorides ($\text{AlOCl}$) that precipitate in the bipolar cells, passivating graphite electrodes and eroding electrical efficiency.
3. **Materials Degradation in Wet Chlorine:** Recirculating thousands of tonnes of hot dry/wet $\text{Cl}_2$ gas requires refractory and alloy integrity that proved economically unmaintainable over multi-year continuous campaigns compared to open-air fluoride smelting.
