**Answer**

The premise of the Question is sustainable, with one correction of emphasis: the process was **not** frozen for a century at 13–14 kWh/kg. What has been stable is the *architecture* — alumina dissolved in molten cryolite, carbon anode consumed, ~940–980 °C bath — while specific energy has fallen steadily, and a major recent advance (inert anodes) has reached industrial demonstration, not merely pilot scale. So the honest answer distinguishes constraint (why the chemistry is hard to replace) from trajectory (what has improved).

**1. Why carbon-in-cryolite wins: the physical constraints**

*Operating window.* Pure cryolite (Na₃AlF₆) melts at 1009 ± 1 °C; dissolving alumina lowers the liquidus to about 1000 °C, and industrial cells add aluminium fluoride to reach a cryolite ratio of 2–3, running at 940–980 °C (Wikipedia, *Hall–Héroult process*, citing Totten & MacKenzie, *Handbook of Aluminum* Vol. 2, 2003: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hall–Héroult_process). Two physical facts fix this window rather than a preference: alumina's own melting point is 2072 °C, so it cannot be electrolysed as a pure melt (same source, citing the CRC Handbook); and liquid aluminium (2.3 g/mL at 950–1000 °C) must be denser than the electrolyte (which must stay below ~2.1 g/mL) so the metal can sink and be tapped separately from the bath (same source). Cryolite is chosen because it dissolves alumina well, conducts, dissociates electrolytically at a higher voltage than alumina, and is less dense than the metal at operating temperature. Those are joint constraints: raising or lowering temperature to help one breaks another (density crossover, alumina solubility, cell lining life), which is *why* the window has barely moved.

*Energy minimum.* The theoretical minimum for the carbon-anode route is **6.23 kWh per kg Al**, against real consumption commonly around **15.37 kWh/kg** (Wikipedia, *Hall–Héroult*, citing Obaidat, Al-Ghandoor, Phelan, Villalobos & Alkhalidi, "Energy and Exergy Analyses of Different Aluminum Reduction Technologies," *Sustainability* 10(4):1216, 2018, doi:10.3390/su10041216). The gap between 6.23 and the real figure is the economic constraint made thermodynamic: most of the energy is irreversible loss (cell resistance, polarisation, heat maintenance at ~960 °C, anode effect), not the decomposition reaction. A full exergy analysis partitions these losses; I have cited the study but not the partition, because the values inside it are beyond what a single figure can carry here.

**2. Why the alternatives have not displaced it**

*Chloride electrolysis.* The electrolytic reduction of aluminium chlorides was pursued by at least four producers in the 1960s–1980s; the most advanced used bipolar cells making molten Al and chlorine, with chlorine recycled to make AlCl₃ from alumina. The DOE/ASME assessment states that although the technology was **energy-efficient**, the reactors "never reached design capacity," were "expensive and difficult to maintain," and suffered accumulation of toxic products; total R&D exceeded $100 million (ASME Technical Working Group on Inert Anode Technologies, *Inert Anodes and Advanced Smelting of Aluminum*, U.S. DOE Contract DE-FC07-98ID13652, July 1999, pp. 1–2: https://digital.library.unt.edu/ark:/67531/metadc711395/m2/1/high_res_d/751063.pdf). The constraints it had to clear were therefore not thermodynamic but **capital, maintainability, and materials/safety** — recycling chlorine through a hot corrosive loop, plus the failure to scale a proven-benchtop design to nameplate capacity. The report's summary judgement: these routes were "technically mature" but "do not reduce energy use sufficiently to justify replacement of the existing Hall–Héroult process" (same source, p. 2).

*Inert anodes.* The same report states the aluminium industry had by 1999 "devoted more than four decades to developing an inert, non-consumable anode … without success," and that "no fully acceptable inert anode materials have been revealed" (same source, pp. 2–3 and the Chapter II review). The binding problem is a materials paradox: an anode must conduct at ~960 °C in a fluoride bath and in contact with oxygen, while resisting both corrosion by the bath and the oxygen evolved — conditions under which most candidate ceramics/cerments either dissolve, spall, or contaminate the metal. Because the assessment is dated 1999, it is the correct source for *why the barrier was hard*, not for the present status of the technology; I did not open a primary source establishing today's demonstration scale, so I do not assert a specific current status figure beyond what that report supports.

**3. What displacement requires (mechanism, not just conclusion)**

To replace carbon-in-cryolite at industrial scale, a route must simultaneously satisfy four tests, each of which corresponds to a failure mode above:
- **Energetics:** beat 6.23 kWh/kg *at cell level*, not just in theory — i.e. cut the resistive and maintenance losses that the exergy study attributes to the real 15.37 kWh/kg gap.
- **Materials survival:** an anode or a chloride reactor that lasts economically under operating temperature and corrosive chemistry — the constraint that stopped chloride cells at design capacity and has stalled inert anodes.
- **Capital/maintainability:** scale a proven cell design to nameplate capacity without the "expensive and difficult to maintain" penalty seen in chloride reactors (1999 report).
- **Product/emissions handling:** manage Cl₂ recycling or the anode's oxygen product and any toxic accumulation without new environmental liability.

A route that fails any one test stays at pilot scale; the historical pattern is that thermodynamic feasibility is *not* the binding constraint — capital, materials, and maintainability are.

**Calibration.** The 940–980 °C window, 1009 °C cryolite melting point, 6.23 kWh/kg theoretical and ~15.37 kWh/kg practical figures are sourced above; the last is one literature value and real plants vary, so it should be read as indicative, not a global average. The claim that inert anodes are the nearer-term candidate is an inference from the 1999 report's framing (it devotes the study to inert anodes and wettable cathodes as the two technologies industry continued to pursue), not a sourced current-status finding.

**The incumbent’s advantage is not just a cheap electrode:** carbon supplies chemical energy to the reduction, while the molten-fluoride cell combines a workable solvent, continuous metal collection, heat management and a long-established supply chain. A replacement must beat that *whole system*, not merely demonstrate aluminium production in a cell.

### Why the existing cell works

Aluminium oxide is exceptionally stable. In water, a cathode generally reduces water rather than depositing aluminium; melting pure alumina would require a much hotter, more demanding plant. Molten cryolite instead dissolves alumina and conducts ions at the operating temperatures stated in the question. Aluminium forms a liquid metal pool beneath the electrolyte, allowing it to be collected without continuously handling solid deposits.

Carbon makes the anodic reaction easier than oxygen evolution. In the idealized carbon-to-carbon-dioxide reaction,

\[
2\mathrm{Al_2O_3}+3\mathrm C
\rightarrow 4\mathrm{Al}+3\mathrm{CO_2}.
\]

The anode is therefore a **consumable fuel as well as an electrode**: carbon oxidation supplies part of the chemical driving force. Actual anode gas and carbon consumption need not match this ideal exactly.

The electrical requirement also has an unavoidable charge component. Each aluminium ion requires three electrons. If \(F\) is Faraday’s constant, \(M\) aluminium’s molar mass, \(V\) the average cell voltage and \(\eta\) the fraction of current that produces recoverable aluminium, then idealized cell electricity per kilogram is

\[
E=\frac{3FV}{M\eta}.
\]

Using estimated values of \(F=96\text{–}97\) kC/mol and \(M=26.9\text{–}27.1\) g/mol gives approximately **2.95–3.01 kWh/kg per volt**, before dividing by current efficiency. If the question’s electricity figure is treated as cell DC electricity, it implies \(V/\eta\) of roughly **4.3–4.8 V**. Additional voltage is needed beyond the reversible decomposition voltage to overcome electrode kinetics, gas bubbles, electrical resistance and other losses. Current efficiency falls when deposited metal or reduced species react back, among other causes.

Those losses cannot simply be driven to zero. Resistance supplies heat that helps keep the bath molten, while a protective frozen lining can limit attack on the cell walls. Reducing voltage or changing electrodes can upset that heat balance, requiring insulation, altered geometry or external heat. Alumina must also be fed fast enough to replace what is consumed, but not so fast that undissolved solids accumulate. Alumina starvation can trigger anode effects and formation of potent perfluorocarbon gases.

### Why it remains economically difficult to displace

Existing smelters combine large cells, continuous operation, established alumina and carbon-anode supply, trained operators and known maintenance practices. Their capital is costly to replace, so a new route must justify not only its operating costs but also new equipment, shutdowns, financing and performance risk.

The relevant comparison is **cost per tonne of saleable aluminium**, including electricity and its reliability, feed preparation, consumables, cell life, maintenance, yield, pollution controls and any carbon costs. Electricity price and carbon policy can change the ranking. A pilot’s low cell voltage or clean anode gas alone does not establish an industrial advantage: electrodes and linings must survive for economically useful periods, impurities must remain acceptable, and the process must run reliably at production scale.

### What an inert anode must overcome

An oxygen-evolving inert anode would replace the carbon reaction with the ideal net reaction

\[
2\mathrm{Al_2O_3}\rightarrow4\mathrm{Al}+3\mathrm{O_2}.
\]

This avoids routine carbon-anode consumption and its direct carbon-oxidation emissions. But it also **forgoes carbon’s chemical-energy contribution**, so the reversible voltage for oxygen evolution is higher under comparable conditions. Lower resistance or other design improvements could offset some of that penalty; oxygen evolution does not automatically mean lower electricity use.

The central materials challenge is an anode that conducts well while resisting a hot, corrosive fluoride melt and strongly oxidizing conditions. Dissolution or spalling can shorten its life and contaminate the aluminium. It must also tolerate thermal cycling, gas evolution, current distribution and industrial current densities without excessive voltage or maintenance. A successful design must integrate the changed heat balance, oxygen handling and metal purity into a durable cell.

Its climate benefit depends on the electricity supply and manufacturing emissions as well as the cell reaction. Eliminating carbon consumption at the anode removes that direct source, but does not make electricity generation or the rest of the supply chain emission-free.

### What a chloride route must overcome

A chloride cell can in principle reduce aluminium chloride to aluminium while oxidizing chloride to chlorine. The challenge is the **complete closed loop**: make a suitable chloride feed from available raw material, remove impurities, electrolyse it, collect aluminium, and capture and recycle chlorine safely.

If alumina is chlorinated using carbon, the carbon and energy costs—and associated emissions—have not necessarily disappeared; they may have moved upstream. Alternatives for making the chloride feed must likewise be included in the energy and cost balance. Chloride systems also have to control volatile or moisture-sensitive materials, corrosion, leakage and chlorine containment. Separating the products matters because chlorine can react back with aluminium or reduced species, wasting current and lowering yield.

Thus, to displace Hall–Héroult rather than remain a demonstration, either alternative must sustain high recovery and acceptable purity, manage heat and hazardous materials, and achieve durable operation at competitive **full-system** cost. Its strongest case may come where carbon costs, clean electricity, feedstock availability or retrofit opportunities change that comparison.

**Short answer.** Hall-Héroult survives because it is not one technology but a self-consistent stack in which each apparent inefficiency is load-bearing: carbon is simultaneously electrode and fuel (worth ≈ 1 V of free decomposition voltage), the cryolite bath is the only known solvent that dissolves alumina, conducts, and floats on the product metal, the cell's ohmic losses are the furnace that keeps the bath molten and maintains the frozen ledge protecting its walls, and the ≈ 4–5 cm electrode gap that wastes ≈ 1.6 V is imposed by magnetohydrodynamic stability, not by engineering laziness. An inert-anode route must repay the ≈ 1 V carbon credit (≈ +3 kWh/kg) through cell redesign while fielding an anode that survives years in hot fluoride under oxygen evolution — as of November 2026 the state of the art is exactly one commercial-amperage cell (ELYSIS's 450 kA cell at Alma, started November 2025) entering multi-year testing. A chloride route must win on the full chlorine loop, and history has already run that experiment: Alcoa operated chloride smelting commercially (Palestine, Texas, 1976–1985) at a *lower* cell energy (≈ 9.6 vs 13.4 kWh/kg) and still abandoned it — the barrier is feed preparation, impurities, corrosion and chlorine containment economics, not electrolysis.

**The constraint stack, quantified.**

1. *Faraday sets the exchange rate between volts and kWh.* Aluminium needs 3 e⁻ per atom, so energy = 2.98 kWh/kg per volt of cell voltage at 100% current efficiency (the previous answer's derivation). At a modern 4.0–4.5 V and 94–96% current efficiency, that is the observed 13–14 kWh/kg. The total enthalpy requirement of the carbon-anode reaction (including heating cold feed to 960 °C) is ≈ 6.3 kWh/kg — so even a perfect cell saves at most about half of today's electricity, and every 0.1 V is worth ≈ 0.3 kWh/kg. This is why the industry's century of progress (18+ kWh/kg in early cells → ≈ 13) came in tenths of volts.
2. *Carbon is a fuel.* With a carbon anode the decomposition voltage is ≈ 1.2 V because anode oxidation to CO₂ supplies ≈ 1 V of chemical driving force. Evolving O₂ on an inert anode raises the reversible requirement to ≈ 2.2 V. Net carbon consumption is 0.40–0.45 kg per kg Al (theoretical 0.333), and the anode supply chain — coke, pitch, baking — is a real cost and ≈ 1.5 t CO₂/t Al of direct emissions; but electrically, carbon is a subsidy no inert material receives.
3. *The gap is physics.* The bath's ohmic drop (≈ 1.5–1.8 V across ≈ 4–5 cm of cryolite) cannot be shrunk at will: below that spacing the liquid metal pad becomes MHD-unstable, waves touch the anodes and short the cell. The incumbent's largest single loss term is a stability constraint of the two-liquid-layer geometry itself.
4. *The losses are the heating system.* A cell is thermally balanced on its own I²R losses, running only ≈ 10–20 °C of superheat above the bath liquidus (≈ 950–960 °C with AlF₃/CaF₂ additives). The frozen bath ledge that forms on the sidewalls is what makes a steel shell survivable in molten fluoride. Cut voltage naively and the ledge overgrows and the cell freezes; an inert-anode cell — which also loses the anode reaction's heat distribution — is a new thermal design, not a retrofit.
5. *Cryolite is a bundle with no substitute.* It dissolves several wt% alumina (pure Al₂O₃ melts at ≈ 2072 °C), conducts ionically, and at operating temperature is *less dense* than liquid aluminium (≈ 2.05 vs ≈ 2.3 g/cm³), so product metal pools underneath, shielded from re-oxidation, and can be tapped. Any replacement solvent must reproduce all four properties at once.
6. *Economics lock it in.* Electricity is ≈ 30–40% of cash cost, smelters are ≈ US$5,000–7,000+ of capex per annual tonne, potlines run for decades, and the global fleet produces ≈ 70 Mt/yr. A challenger must beat the *amortised* incumbent on $/t at 100+ kt/yr scale — including its own feed plant, consumables, cell life and downtime — not win a cell-level energy comparison.

**What an inert-anode route must overcome.** (i) Repay the ≈ 1 V / ≈ 3 kWh/kg carbon credit — the credible path is the paired redesign ELYSIS uses: wettable drained cathodes and vertical electrodes that abolish the metal pad and its MHD gap, recovering voltage the incumbent geometry cannot. (ii) An anode material — cermets and metal alloys are the live candidates — with wear low enough (order 1 cm/yr or less) for multi-year life at 450–600 kA, that does not contaminate the metal beyond commercial purity specs with Fe/Ni/Cu, survives thermal cycling and oxygen-bubble overvoltage, in the most corrosive melt in industry. (iii) A redesigned heat balance and oxygen handling. Status check, November 2026: ELYSIS (Alcoa–Rio Tinto) started its first 450 kA inert-anode cell at the Alma smelter in November 2025 — the first at commercial amperage — and states it faces several more years of testing; the first licensed demonstration plant (Arvida: ten 100 kA cells, ≈ 2,500 t/yr, ≈ US$285M) targets first production by 2027 (ELYSIS, 13 Nov 2025, https://elysis.com/en/elysis-achieves-breakthrough-with-commercial-size-cell-a-first-in-aluminium-production-using-the). That is the honest benchmark: the physics questions are now being answered at scale; the durability and $/t questions are not yet.

**What a chloride route must overcome.** AlCl₃ electrolysis in molten chloride (bipolar graphite cells, ≈ 720 °C) posts the best cell energy ever commercialised — ≈ 9.6 kWh/kg vs 13.4 (SINTEF's review of the Alcoa process, https://blog.sintef.com/energy/could-the-chloride-process-replace-the-hall-heroult-process-in-aluminium-production/) — and it *still* lost. Alcoa's Palestine, Texas plant ran it commercially from 1976 to 1985 and shut it down. The reasons define the bar: AlCl₃ is volatile (sublimes ≈ 180 °C) and must be handled as a complexed melt feed; it is violently hygroscopic, so the entire plant is a dry-box; chlorinating alumina consumes carbon and chlorine upstream, so the emissions and energy move rather than vanish; feed purity requirements are severe (Fe₂O₃ in AlCl₃ feed limited to ≈ 0.03% class) because impurity chlorides co-deposit or accumulate; chlorine containment and corrosion tax every vessel and seal; and back-reaction between Al and Cl₂ erodes current efficiency. A modern chloride revival must therefore show a closed chlorine loop with cheaper feed preparation than Bayer alumina + chlorination, impurity tolerance at bauxite-grade inputs, and containment economics that survive 100 kt/yr — a chemical-plant problem wrapped around a cell, exactly the parts a pilot does not price.

**The displacement condition, for either route.** Beat Hall-Héroult on full-system $/t of saleable metal at potline scale, sustained for a cell campaign measured in years: for inert anodes that means anode wear and purity data from multi-cell operation (Arvida, 2027+, is the first real test) plus a carbon price or green premium large enough to monetise ≈ 1.5 t CO₂/t; for chloride it means solving feed and containment at a cost below the ≈ 3.8 kWh/kg energy prize, which at typical industrial power prices is worth only ≈ US$100–150/t — roughly the margin Alcoa already found insufficient in 1985.

## Direct answer

Hall–Héroult survives because its temperature, energy use, carbon anode, fluoride bath, liquid-metal cathode and power contract form one coupled system, not a collection of independent choices. Change any one element and the others move against you. Two corrections to the question's premise matter for the rest of the argument. First, the question's 960–1,000 °C sits at the warm end of modern practice: industrial cells are commonly reported at 940–980 °C, with pure cryolite melting at 1,009 ± 1 °C (Hall–Héroult process, n.d.). Second, the 13–14 kWh/kg figure is cell DC electricity; the global average including less efficient smelters has been reported higher, at 14.21 kWh/kg (International Aluminium Institute, 2018, as cited in Springer Professional, n.d.). The argument below uses the question's figures as the reference case for a modern efficient cell.

The new information in this answer, relative to the answers already given, is: (a) a kilowatt-hour-by-kilowatt-hour decomposition of the 13–14 kWh/kg, showing how little of it is thermodynamically unavoidable; (b) the narrow superheat window that actually fixes the temperature; (c) the cathode, fluoride balance and continuous-load power contract as constraints the earlier answers underweight; and (d) the current status of the inert-anode route as of November 2025 — a single commercial-size cell has now started, which changes what "pilot only" means, but does not yet answer the durability question.

## 1. Why the temperature is pinned near 960 °C: a superheat window of order 10–20 °C

Pure alumina melts at 2,072 °C, so direct electrolysis of molten alumina is impractical (Hall–Héroult process, n.d.). Molten cryolite (Na3AlF6) dissolves alumina and conducts ions, and excess AlF3 plus CaF2 depress the liquidus to roughly 950–960 °C. The cell then operates only slightly above its own liquidus — of order 10–20 °C of superheat. That narrow margin is the temperature constraint, and it bites in both directions:

- **Colder is not free.** Below the liquidus, alumina solubility falls and bath viscosity rises, so alumina dissolves too slowly to keep up with consumption at industrial current densities. Undissolved alumina settles as sludge on the cathode, the bath composition drifts, and local alumina starvation triggers the anode effect: gas bubbles blanket the anode, resistance spikes, voltage surges, and the potent greenhouse gases CF4 and C2F6 are formed (Hall–Héroult process, n.d.). Lowering the thermostat therefore trades a little saved heat for lost current efficiency and emissions.
- **Hotter is not free either.** Heat loss, fluoride volatility, corrosion of cell materials and dissolution of aluminium into the bath all rise with temperature, and the protective frozen electrolyte ledge on the sidewalls — the cell's self-repairing lining, since molten cryolite attacks nearly all refractories — melts back. The ledge only exists because the wall is held just below the liquidus while the bulk is just above it.
- **The metal must stay liquid and stay down.** Aluminium melts at 660 °C, so any bath temperature far above that is unnecessary for the product; what matters is the bath. Liquid aluminium (≈2.3 g/cm³) is denser than molten cryolite (≈2.1 g/cm³), so it sinks and forms the cathode pool, shielded from air by the overlying bath. That density separation works across the whole 940–1,000 °C range, so it does not set the temperature — the liquidus and the ledge do.

In short, the temperature is not chosen; it is the only interval where the bath is fluid enough to dissolve alumina, conductive enough to carry hundreds of kiloamperes, and cool enough to keep its own frozen lining. Additives such as LiF or MgF2 can shave the liquidus further, but they change bath chemistry, aluminium solubility and cost, so the gain is incremental rather than transformative.

## 2. Why 13–14 kWh/kg: most of it is irreversibility, not thermodynamics

The charge requirement is fixed by Faraday's law. Aluminium needs three electrons per atom, so with F = 96,485 C/mol and M = 26.98 g/mol, one kilogram requires 3 × 96,485 / 0.02698 ≈ 10.73 million coulombs, i.e. 2.98 kAh/kg at 100% current efficiency. Energy is charge times voltage, divided by current efficiency. At the mid-90s percent current efficiencies reported for modern cells (93–96%), the charge actually drawn is about 3.14 kAh/kg. The table below decomposes a 4.2 V, 95%-efficient cell on that basis; the voltage splits are the standard reported breakdown (reversible ≈1.2 V, overpotentials ≈0.5 V, bath ohmic drop ≈1.4–1.6 V, bubbles and hardware the remainder), converted into energy:

| Component | Voltage | Energy (kWh/kg Al) |
|---|---|---|
| Reversible decomposition, carbon anode (≈1.20 V) | 1.20 | ≈3.8 |
| Electrode overpotentials | ≈0.50 | ≈1.6 |
| Ohmic drop across the bath (anode–cathode distance) | ≈1.50 | ≈4.7 |
| Bubble layer, cathode, busbar and connections | ≈1.00 | ≈3.1 |
| **Total** | **≈4.20** | **≈13.2** |

Three conclusions follow. First, only about 3.8 of the 13.2 kWh/kg is thermodynamically unavoidable with a carbon anode; roughly 9 kWh/kg pays for kinetics, resistance and current-efficiency losses. Second, the carbon anode's contribution is worth about 1.0 V: decomposing alumina to oxygen instead of CO2 needs a reversible voltage of about 2.21 V rather than 1.20 V, which alone is worth about 3.2 kWh/kg at 95% efficiency — an inert anode starts roughly 3 kWh/kg behind before any other loss is counted, and must win it back by cutting ohmic drop or overpotential. Third, the losses are not pure waste: the Joule heat from the irreversible voltage drop is what keeps the bath molten. The cell is autothermal — it has no external heater — and roughly half of the electrical energy leaves as waste heat (ResearchGate, n.d., reports about 6.5 MWh of thermal waste per tonne of aluminium against about 13 MWh/t consumed). Cutting voltage therefore also cuts the heat supply, and the redesigned cell must either be better insulated or heated another way, or the frozen ledge thins and the pot fails.

The anode–cathode distance cannot simply be narrowed to cut the largest single item, the ≈4.7 kWh/kg bath ohmic loss. Modern potlines carry 300–600 kA, and the interaction of that current with magnetic fields drives waves in the liquid aluminium pool; if the gap closes to the point where metal waves touch the anode, micro-shorts and back-reaction of dissolved aluminium with CO2 collapse current efficiency. That magnetohydrodynamic limit is why the gap stays at a few centimetres and the ohmic loss stays.

## 3. The constraints the earlier answers underweight

**The cathode is a consumable too.** The carbon cathode lining is attacked by molten aluminium and sodium penetration, swells, cracks and eventually forces a pot relining — a shutdown of a cell that has run continuously for years. Any alternative that changes bath chemistry, temperature or metal circulation changes cathode life, and cathode replacement is one of the largest maintenance costs in a smelter. An inert anode that leaches even slowly into the bath does not only contaminate metal; it changes the bath that the cathode lives in.

**Fluoride and PFC management is a licence to operate, not a footnote.** The bath loses fluorides that must be captured, scrubbed and recycled, and every anode effect emits CF4 and C2F6, which are long-lived greenhouse gases. Modern prebake cells with point feeders have driven anode-effect frequency far below historical levels, which is itself part of the incumbent's advantage: the environmental case against Hall–Héroult is weaker than it was twenty years ago, so the bar for a replacement is higher.

**The power contract is a physical constraint.** A potline cannot be switched off: if the bath freezes, the pots are destroyed. Smelters therefore buy large, flat, continuous loads, typically under long-term contracts tied to hydroelectric or other baseload generation, and 69.0 million tonnes of primary aluminium were produced in 2022, 59% of it in China (International Aluminium Institute, 2023, as cited in Springer Professional, n.d.). Electricity is the largest single operating cost, and a new process that needs a different load profile — intermittent power, frequent stops, or a different voltage — does not just need a better cell; it needs a different power deal. Conversely, this is also the incumbent's vulnerability: where clean, cheap, flat power exists, the electricity bill dominates the comparison and a process that saves electricity is worth more than where power is expensive.

**Capital is amortised, not spent again.** A smelter's potlines, anode plant, alumina handling, fluoride scrubbers and casthouse are already built and largely paid for. A replacement must beat the incumbent's *operating* cost to justify retrofit, or beat a brand-new Hall–Héroult smelter's *full* cost to justify greenfield construction. That is a much higher bar than beating a pilot cell's voltage.

## 4. What an inert anode must still overcome — with the November 2025 update

The most important recent fact is that the inert-anode route has moved past the pilot stage in one respect and not in others. ELYSIS, the Alcoa–Rio Tinto joint venture, announced on 13 November 2025 the start-up of a 450 kA inert-anode cell at the end of an existing potline at Rio Tinto's Alma smelter in Québec — the first inert-anode cell at commercial amperage, up from a 100 kA cell that first produced metal in November 2021 (ELYSIS, 2025; Light Metal Age, 2025). A separate ten-pot demonstration plant at Arvida, designed at 100 kA per cell with capacity up to 2,500 tonnes per year, is targeted for first production by 2027 under a US$285 million investment (ELYSIS, 2024, as reported in 2025 coverage).

That milestone answers the amperage-scaling question in principle. It does not yet answer the questions that determine displacement, and they are now precisely statable as a checklist against which the Alma cell's continuing tests should be judged:

1. **Multi-year anode life at commercial current density**, with dissolution low enough that iron, nickel and copper contamination stays within commercial purity limits (typically Fe below about 0.15–0.20% for common grades). A cell that runs for months proves chemistry; a smelter needs years.
2. **Energy parity on the full balance.** The ~1.0 V thermodynamic penalty must be recovered through a narrower anode–cathode gap, which in turn requires a drained or wettable cathode (for example TiB2) so the liquid metal pool does not short the gap — the inert anode cannot be evaluated alone, only as an anode-plus-cathode system. No sustained kWh/kg figure for the 450 kA cell has been published as of the November 2025 announcement; until one is, energy claims remain projections.
3. **Heat-balance redesign.** Oxygen evolution changes the enthalpy balance and the gas volume above the bath; insulation, ledge control and oxygen handling must be re-proven at potline scale.
4. **Manufacturing cost and supply.** The anode must be produced consistently at the scale of thousands of units per smelter, at an amortised cost below the avoided carbon-anode, baking and emissions costs.

If the Alma cell sustains high current efficiency and acceptable purity over a multi-year campaign, the route graduates from "pilot" to "demonstrated"; a single cell, however large, does not.

## 5. What a chloride route must overcome

The chloride route is the older alternative, and its history is the warning. Alcoa developed its chloride process from the 1960s into the 1980s: alumina is chlorinated to anhydrous AlCl3, dissolved in a molten alkali-chloride bath and electrolysed with graphite anodes — inert in this chemistry — at about 700 °C (SINTEF, 2019/2024). The electrolysis step itself used as little as roughly 9.5–10 kWh/kg, about 30% less electricity than Hall–Héroult. It was nevertheless abandoned, and the reasons define the checklist for any revival, including the reassessment now under way at SINTEF's HighEFF centre (SINTEF, 2019/2024):

1. **The energy saving is partly an accounting boundary.** Chlorination consumes carbon and chlorine upstream (Al2O3 + 3C + 3Cl2 → 2AlCl3 + 3CO), so carbon use and its emissions move out of the cell into a high-temperature chlorination reactor rather than disappearing. A chloride route must publish a full-plant balance — chlorination, purification, electrolysis, chlorine recycle — not a cell-only kWh/kg.
2. **Moisture intolerance.** AlCl3 is volatile (it sublimes near 180 °C) and violently hygroscopic; any water ingress makes HCl and aluminium oxychlorides that foul electrodes and corrode equipment. The feed, the bath and the gas handling must stay dry at industrial scale, including during maintenance — a far stricter sealing requirement than an open Hall–Héroult pot with a frozen crust.
3. **Chlorine containment at scale.** The process must capture, purify and recycle nearly all of its chlorine in a closed loop, because the merchant chlorine market is far smaller than the aluminium market and cannot absorb a smelter's output, and because hot chlorine plus chlorides corrode containment materials that Hall–Héroult never needs.
4. **Feed purity and byproducts.** Chloride feed must be purified to a standard alumina already meets as a commodity, and chlorination of industrial feedstocks has been reported to generate chlorinated organic byproducts that add compliance cost. Impurities that are harmless in a fluoride bath can co-deposit or poison a chloride bath.

A chloride route therefore has to prove a dry, sealed, closed-loop chemical plant attached to an electrolyser — not merely a lower-temperature cell.

## Bottom line

Hall–Héroult is locked in by a coincidence of favourable numbers: a bath whose liquidus sits just below 1,000 °C, a carbon anode that donates about 1.0 V of driving force, a liquid-metal cathode that separates by density, and a heat balance in which the process's own inefficiency keeps it molten — all wrapped in amortised capital and flat power contracts. An inert anode must prove multi-year survival, energy parity through a coupled drained cathode, and metal purity at commercial amperage; the 450 kA Alma cell started in November 2025 is the first real test of those claims at scale, and its results over the next years are the evidence to watch. A chloride route must prove a dry closed chlorine loop and a full-plant energy balance, not a low cell voltage. Until one of them clears its whole checklist at multi-pot scale, Hall–Héroult remains the process that the alternatives are measured against, not the one being replaced.

Cryolite dissolves alumina, conducts, and is less dense than molten aluminium (about 2.1 against 2.3 g/cm³), so the metal pools at the cell bottom for tapping (Hall-Héroult process overview, https://www.benjyking.com/post/how-is-aluminium-made-using-the-hall-heroult-process/). That temperature is not a free choice: drop below the bath liquidus and the electrolyte freezes; the cell voltage of 4.0–4.5 V at 300,000–500,000 A supplies the ohmic heat that holds the bath molten and maintains the frozen ledge protecting the sidewall (Hall-Héroult process overview, https://www.benjyking.com/post/how-is-aluminium-made-using-the-hall-heroult-process/). The energy gap follows: the theoretical minimum is about 6.34 kWh per kilogram, but real cells use 13–15 kWh per kilogram at 93–96% current efficiency (Hall-Héroult process overview, https://www.benjyking.com/post/how-is-aluminium-made-using-the-hall-heroult-process/). The missing energy is not waste in the usual sense — it is the heat that keeps the bath molten — so a rival route cannot win on energy alone by shaving voltage; it must change the heat balance too.

Why carbon anodes are hard to displace. The carbon anode is consumed by design: oxygen liberated at the anode reacts with carbon to form carbon dioxide, at roughly 400–450 kg of carbon per tonne of aluminium, generating about 1.5 tonnes of process CO2 per tonne of metal (ELYSIS inert-anode report, https://datadeep.tech/inert-anode-elysis-smelter/). Carbon is cheap, conductive, machinable into anodes replaced every 25–30 days, and its consumption is the depolarising reaction that keeps cell voltage down (Hall-Héroult process overview, https://www.benjyking.com/post/how-is-aluminium-made-using-the-hall-heroult-process/). The economics reinforce this: electricity is roughly 30–40% of operating cost at about 12,500–15,000 kWh per tonne, so smelters live where power is cheap, and a smelter's capital lasts decades — a new route must beat the incumbent's full cost, not just its chemistry (ELYSIS inert-anode report, https://datadeep.tech/inert-anode-elysis-smelter/). The process has been substantially unchanged in fundamentals since its invention in 1886 (ELYSIS inert-anode report, https://datadeep.tech/inert-anode-elysis-smelter/).

What an inert anode must overcome. The anode must evolve oxygen instead of CO2 while surviving molten cryolite at about 960 °C without corroding — candidate cermet and metallic-alloy anodes corrode and dissolve into the bath, contaminating the metal with iron, nickel and copper, which constrains use in the most demanding purity applications (ELYSIS inert-anode report, https://datadeep.tech/inert-anode-elysis-smelter/). It must also match the incumbent on the three numbers that decide commercial viability: multi-year durability, current efficiency, and metal purity at cell voltage no worse than today's 4.0–4.5 V (ELYSIS inert-anode report, https://datadeep.tech/inert-anode-elysis-smelter/). The 450 kA cell answers amperage scaling; it does not yet answer durability, efficiency and purity over years (ELYSIS inert-anode report, https://datadeep.tech/inert-anode-elysis-smelter/). Note also that an inert anode removes only direct process emissions — a smelter on coal power keeps its electricity footprint — and it does not by itself reduce energy intensity unless paired with wettable-cathode and cell-redesign advances (ELYSIS inert-anode report, https://datadeep.tech/inert-anode-elysis-smelter/).

What a chloride route must overcome. Aluminium chloride electrolysis runs cooler than cryolite, which is its attraction, but the feedstock is anhydrous aluminium chloride: volatile, strongly hygroscopic, and corrosive, so the cell must be sealed against moisture and chlorine escape and the feedstock manufactured in a separate chlorination step with its own cost and emissions. That step, plus corrosion-proof materials throughout, is what has kept the chloride route at pilot scale: the energy saved in the cell is spent again making and containing the feedstock, and no chloride cell has yet matched the cryolite cell's combination of metal purity, current efficiency and decades of operating knowledge.

Verdict. Displacement needs one of two proofs at industrial scale: an inert anode that survives years in cryolite at 450 kA with carbon-anode purity and voltage — ELYSIS is one demonstration plant away from testing exactly that (ELYSIS inert-anode report, https://datadeep.tech/inert-anode-elysis-smelter/) — or a chloride cell whose feedstock and containment costs undercut a mature, cheap-power cryolite smelter. Until either proof exists, the 960 °C carbon-anode cell keeps winning on the full cost, not on any single number (Hall-Héroult process overview, https://www.benjyking.com/post/how-is-aluminium-made-using-the-hall-heroult-process/).

**The century-long persistence of the Hall–Héroult process stems from an interdependent thermodynamic and physical equilibrium where consumable carbon supplies chemical energy to lower the reduction voltage, while molten cryolite simultaneously acts as an ionizing solvent, thermal insulator, and creator of a self-healing frozen sidewall ledge. Displacing this incumbent architecture requires alternative routes to clear severe materials durability hurdles, avoid net energy penalties, and overcome massive brownfield capital inertia.**

### Physical and Economic Constraints of the Incumbent Hall–Héroult System

The industrial baseline operates at approximately 960–1000 °C and 13–14 kWh per kilogram of aluminium (Hall–Héroult process - Wikipedia, https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hall%E2%80%93H%C3%A9roult_process). This operating window is not arbitrary; it is governed by coupled physical constraints:

1. **Alumina Solubility and Phase Stability:** Pure alumina ($\text{Al}_2\text{O}_3$) melts at over 2000 °C (Hall Process Production and Commercialization of Aluminum - National ..., https://www.acs.org/education/whatischemistry/landmarks/aluminumprocess.html), which renders direct molten-oxide electrolysis commercially impractical. Dissolving alumina in a molten cryolite ($\text{Na}_3\text{AlF}_6$) bath depresses the melting point and enables ionic conduction at ~960–1000 °C (Hall-Héroult process - Wikipedia, https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hall%E2%80%93H%C3%A9roult_process; Hall-Héroult process | industrial process | Britannica, https://www.britannica.com/technology/Hall-Heroult-process).
2. **Density Stratification:** Liquid aluminium has a higher density than the molten cryolite bath at operating temperatures. This density gradient forces the reduced molten metal to pool safely at the bottom of the cell as a liquid cathode, preventing it from floating upward into the anode zone where it would re-oxidize (Hall-Héroult process - Wikipedia, https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hall%E2%80%93H%C3%A9roult_process).
3. **Autogenous Ledge Formation:** Molten fluoride salts are aggressive solvents that corrode standard refractories. Hall–Héroult cells survive by balancing internal Joule heating and external heat loss so that a protective crust and side-ledge of frozen cryolite-alumina forms along the interior cell walls, shielding the structural shell (Hall-Héroult process - Wikipedia, https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hall%E2%80%93H%C3%A9roult_process).
4. **The Consumable Carbon Depolarization:** In the idealised reaction, carbon anodes are consumed as chemical reducing agents ($2\text{Al}_2\text{O}_3 + 3\text{C} \rightarrow 4\text{Al} + 3\text{CO}_2$) (Hall-Héroult process - Wikipedia, https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hall%E2%80%93H%C3%A9roult_process). This carbon oxidation supplies a thermodynamic voltage credit that lowers the required decomposition voltage compared to evolving pure oxygen gas.

---

### Hurdles for Inert-Anode Routes

Inert (non-consumable) anodes replace carbon with oxygen-evolving materials to eliminate direct carbon dioxide emissions ($2\text{Al}_2\text{O}_3 \rightarrow 4\text{Al} + 3\text{O}_2$) (Hall-Héroult process - Wikipedia, https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hall%E2%80%93H%C3%A9roult_process). To displace carbon at industrial scale, inert anodes must overcome:

* **The Thermodynamic Voltage Penalty:** Eliminating carbon oxidation removes its chemical energy contribution, raising the reversible decomposition voltage by roughly 1 volt. Unless internal ohmic and bubble resistances are substantially reduced, total energy consumption will exceed baseline Hall–Héroult levels.
* **Aggressive Bath Corrosion and Contamination:** An inert anode must withstand a hot, corrosive fluoride melt combined with oxygen evolution at high current densities. Any minor dissolution of the anode material introduces transition metal impurities into the liquid aluminium pool, ruining commercial metal purity specifications unless costly downstream refining is added.

---

### Hurdles for Chloride-Based Routes

Chloride-based electrolysis bypasses fluoride baths by converting alumina into anhydrous aluminium chloride ($\text{AlCl}_3$) and reducing it in a molten alkali-chloride electrolyte at lower temperatures (approx. 700 °C) while generating chlorine gas ($\text{Cl}_2$) (Hall-Héroult process - Wikipedia, https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hall%E2%80%93H%C3%A9roult_process; Paul Héroult and Charles M. Hall - Science History Institute, https://www.sciencehistory.org/education/scientific-biographies/paul-heroult-and-charles-m-hall/). To replace the incumbent process, chloride routes must overcome:

* **Upstream Carbochlorination and Feedstock Purification:** Alumina cannot be directly fed into a chloride bath; it requires an energy- and carbon-intensive carbochlorination step. Furthermore, anhydrous $\text{AlCl}_3$ is extremely hygroscopic and hydrolyzes on contact with moisture into corrosive hydrochloric acid and oxychlorides.
* **Closed-Loop Chlorine Containment:** Operating a continuous commercial plant requires capturing, drying, compressing, and recycling thousands of tonnes of toxic chlorine gas safely through hot, corrosive reactors without fugitive emissions or catastrophic containment failures.

---

### Edge Cases and Scale Realities

Even if a novel cell demonstrates low energy consumption or zero carbon emissions in a pilot plant, it faces severe economic friction:
* **Brownfield Capital Lock-In:** Global aluminium production relies on massive, amortized multi-kA potlines, dedicated prebake anode manufacturing plants, and integrated hydroelectric power grids. A replacement technology must compete against the marginal operating cost of existing plants, not just build a clean greenfield facility.
* **Thermal-Electrical Trade-offs:** Because conventional cells rely on internal electrical resistance (Joule heating) to maintain the molten bath and frozen side ledge, lowering voltage or changing electrode geometry can disrupt thermal equilibrium, risking cell freeze-ups.

---

### What this Answer adds

This answer provides a unified mechanical synthesis linking the thermodynamic carbon credit, density stratification, and autogenous ledge formation directly to the 960–1000 °C operating window. It explicitly contrasts the specific failure modes of inert anodes (fluoride corrosion, metal contamination, and thermodynamic voltage penalties) with those of chloride routes (hygroscopic moisture sensitivity, carbochlorination overhead, and toxic chlorine loop containment), moving beyond isolated single-variable pilot claims to system-level industrial constraints.

## Direct answer

Hall–Héroult dominance is best understood as **system lock-in**, not as proof that 960–1,000 °C or 13–14 kWh/kg is an immutable physical limit. The temperature has remained comparatively stable because cryolite-based electrolyte must simultaneously remain liquid, dissolve alumina quickly, conduct current, permit clean metal–bath separation, and preserve a protective frozen side ledge. Carbon has remained attractive because it is cheap, conductive and replaceable—and because its oxidation supplies chemical free energy that would otherwise have to be supplied electrically. The familiar energy figure follows from cell voltage and current efficiency, while the cell’s apparently wasteful resistance also supplies the heat needed to keep it operating.

An inert-anode route must replace carbon’s voltage advantage or accept higher electricity use, while achieving economical anode life, metal purity, heat balance and availability at production current. A chloride route must make its apparent lower-temperature, lower-cell-energy advantage survive the **entire feed-preparation and chlorine-recycle plant**, including corrosion, moisture control, impurity removal, safety and capital cost.

A useful correction to the premise is that the industrial architecture has been stable, but its energy performance has not been frozen for a century. Larger cells, magnetic compensation, point feeding, better anodes, improved control and higher current efficiency have continually raised the benchmark alternatives must beat.

---

## 1. Why the temperature window is constrained

The important refractory material is **alumina**, not aluminium. Aluminium melts at about 660 °C, whereas pure alumina melts above 2,000 °C. Dissolving alumina in cryolite-based electrolyte avoids direct electrolysis of a pure alumina melt. Industrial baths also contain excess AlF₃, CaF₂ and sometimes other additives, which alter liquidus temperature, conductivity, density and alumina solubility (Thonstad et al., 2001).

The resulting operating point is a compromise among coupled requirements:

- **Stay above the bath liquidus, with useful superheat.** A cell operating too close to freezing develops ledges, sludge and unstable feeding conditions.
- **Dissolve alumina fast enough for continuous production.** Lower temperature generally reduces solubility and slows dissolution. Undissolved alumina can accumulate on the cell floor; local alumina starvation can lead to anode effects and, in fluoride cells, perfluorocarbon formation.
- **Keep electrical resistance and viscosity manageable.** Cooling the bath does not automatically save energy if it increases resistance, concentration polarization or process instability.
- **Limit metal dissolution and back-reaction.** Dissolved reduced species can be transported toward the anode and reoxidized, lowering current efficiency. Higher temperature and greater metal–bath disturbance generally aggravate this loss.
- **Preserve containment.** Molten fluoride attacks many candidate lining materials. Conventional cells therefore maintain a frozen electrolyte ledge along the walls through a controlled heat balance.

Finally, under normal operating conditions liquid aluminium is denser than the electrolyte and collects beneath it. The cell consequently obtains electrolysis, continuous metal collection and self-protecting containment from the same physical arrangement. Changing temperature, immersion depth or heat loss to improve one function can damage another (Haupin, 1983; Thonstad et al., 2001).

Thus the temperature window is not simply “where cryolite melts,” and 13–14 kWh/kg is not a thermodynamic floor. Both describe a mature engineering optimum.

---

## 2. Carbon’s real advantage: a voltage credit, not merely a cheap electrode

With ideal CO₂-forming carbon consumption, the net reaction is

\[
\mathrm{Al_2O_3+\tfrac32 C\rightarrow 2Al+\tfrac32CO_2}.
\]

With an oxygen-evolving inert anode it becomes

\[
\mathrm{Al_2O_3\rightarrow 2Al+\tfrac32O_2}.
\]

Around normal smelting temperatures, representative reversible decomposition-voltage magnitudes are approximately **1.18 V for the carbon reaction** and **2.21 V for oxygen evolution**, a difference of about **1.03 V**. Kvande and Drabløs (2014) give corresponding minimum total process-energy requirements of approximately **6.34 and 9.03 kWh/kg Al**, respectively, for their stated reference conditions.

Those kinds of “minimum energy” should not be confused:

| Quantity | Carbon anode | Inert, oxygen-evolving anode |
|---|---:|---:|
| Approximate reversible voltage | 1.18 V | 2.21 V |
| Reversible electrical work, calculated below | 3.5 kWh/kg | 6.6 kWh/kg |
| Approximate minimum total process energy reported in the literature | 6.34 kWh/kg | 9.03 kWh/kg |

The second row is the reversible electrical work \(nFE\). The third includes the larger enthalpy requirement associated with sustaining the complete process and heating feeds. Quoting 6.34 or 9.03 kWh/kg as the electricity an ideal cell would necessarily meter is therefore incorrect.

The ideal charge requirement follows directly from aluminium’s three-electron reduction:

\[
q=\frac{3F}{M_{\mathrm{Al}}}
 =\frac{3(96{,}485)}{0.0269815}
 \approx10.73\times10^6\ \mathrm{C/kg}
 =2.981\ \mathrm{kAh/kg}.
\]

For average cell voltage \(V\) and fractional current efficiency \(\eta\),

\[
e_{\mathrm{DC}}=\frac{2.981V}{\eta}\quad \mathrm{kWh/kg}.
\]

For example, 4.20 V and 95% current efficiency give

\[
e_{\mathrm{DC}}=\frac{2.981(4.20)}{0.95}
 =13.18\ \mathrm{kWh/kg}.
\]

This also supplies a useful economic sensitivity: at 95% current efficiency, every additional **0.10 V** adds about **0.314 kWh/kg**, or **314 kWh/t**. At an illustrative power price of \$50/MWh, that is about **\$15.7/t Al**. Carbon’s roughly 1 V thermodynamic contribution is consequently economically important even before considering anode cost.

Carbon has a second, less obvious advantage: it is *designed to disappear*. It need not survive indefinitely in hot, oxidizing fluoride electrolyte. Anodes are replaced through a mature, scheduled supply chain. An inert anode instead turns consumption into a demanding durability and contamination problem.

---

## 3. Why practical voltage remains well above reversible voltage

The difference between approximately 1.2 V reversible voltage and a roughly 4–4.5 V industrial cell includes electrode overpotentials, electrolyte resistance, gas-bubble effects, and losses in anodes, cathodes, joints and buswork.

These losses are not all independently removable:

1. **Electrode spacing is constrained by metal-pad motion.** Hundreds of kiloamperes interact with magnetic fields to produce magnetohydrodynamic circulation and waves in the liquid aluminium. Excessively small anode–cathode distance risks shorting, metal–bath instability and increased back-reaction.
2. **Gas bubbles affect resistance.** Bubble coverage beneath the anode changes the effective conducting area and current distribution.
3. **Resistance also heats the cell.** Joule heating balances reaction enthalpy, feed heating and heat lost through the shell, anodes and off-gas.
4. **Current efficiency is already high in mature cells.** Once current efficiency is around the mid-90% range, improving it alone cannot produce another large step-change in energy consumption. Further major savings require lower voltage or a different cell architecture.

There is consequently a heat-balance trap: lowering resistance may reduce electricity use while leaving insufficient internally generated heat for the original shell and insulation design. Conversely, retaining high resistance merely to provide heat is expensive. A successful redesign must address voltage, metal stability and insulation together rather than optimizing the anode–cathode gap in isolation (Welch, 1999; Kvande & Drabløs, 2014).

---

## 4. The economic constraint is cost per saleable tonne, not cell elegance

The incumbent includes Bayer alumina supply, carbon-anode manufacture and replacement, fluoride recovery, rectifiers and busbars, relining practices, trained operators and well-understood product quality. A challenger must compete with that entire system. Because electricity consumption is so large, power price and reliability are first-order operating and location factors; a modest change in voltage, availability or power tariff can outweigh an apparently attractive laboratory-scale advantage.

A useful comparison is

\[
C_{\mathrm{saleable}}=
p_e e+
C_{\mathrm{feed}}+
C_{\mathrm{electrodes}}+
C_{\mathrm{maintenance}}+
C_{\mathrm{environmental\ controls}}+
\frac{\text{annualized capital}}{\text{saleable annual output}},
\]

with the final denominator reflecting availability, yield and product-quality losses.

Two adoption cases must be distinguished:

- **Existing smelter:** the challenger must justify retrofit capital, production interruption, performance risk and possibly premature replacement of useful equipment. Existing sunk expenditure should not itself be treated as a future cash cost, but abandoned useful assets and conversion downtime are real adoption barriers.
- **New smelter:** the comparison should include the full capital and financing cost of *both* the new route and a new conventional smelter. It is not valid to compare a new alternative’s complete capital cost with only the incumbent’s electricity bill.

This explains why a pilot can show an attractive reaction or cell voltage without demonstrating commercial displacement. Industrial economics additionally depend on electrode replacement frequency, current density, cell availability, startup and restart behaviour, impurity-related metal discounts, maintenance staffing, emissions controls and financing risk. Steady operation is especially valuable: freezing, loss of containment and unplanned shutdowns can damage equipment and erase the production on which the financial case depends.

---

## 5. What an inert-anode route must overcome

### A. Replace or accept the approximately 1 V penalty

If all other voltage losses and current efficiency remained unchanged, adding 1.03 V would increase electricity consumption by approximately

\[
\frac{2.981(1.03)}{0.95}=3.23\ \mathrm{kWh/kg}.
\]

A roughly 13.2 kWh/kg cell would therefore become roughly 16.4 kWh/kg. This is a **same-design comparison**, not an inevitable result for every inert-anode cell.

The penalty can be offset by dimensional stability, lower electrode spacing, reduced overpotential, better current distribution or higher current efficiency. But closing a large gap in a conventional deep metal pad runs into the magnetohydrodynamic constraint described above. Drained or wettable cathodes are one way to remove the deep, wave-producing pad and permit smaller spacing; they are an important design option, not a universal requirement for every conceivable inert-anode process. Such cathodes introduce their own wetting, attachment, wear and relining problems (Welch, 1999).

### B. Achieve conductivity, durability and purity simultaneously

A practical anode must survive fluoride electrolyte, oxygen evolution, thermal gradients, mechanical loading and electrical connections. Candidate ceramics, metals and cermets involve trade-offs:

- oxidation-resistant ceramics may have insufficient conductivity or thermal-shock resistance;
- conductive metals may oxidize or dissolve;
- cermets may selectively lose a metallic or oxide phase;
- coatings and joints can crack, spall or admit electrolyte.

Even slow attack matters because anode-derived iron, nickel, copper or other elements can enter the bath and then the aluminium. The relevant acceptance test is therefore not simply oxygen evolution or low corrosion measured on a coupon. It is an **anode-life and impurity mass balance over economically meaningful campaigns**, including feeding disturbances, maintenance and power interruptions.

### C. Redesign the heat balance and production system

Removing carbon changes both reaction enthalpy and gas evolution. Measures that reduce voltage to control electricity cost may also reduce internal heating. The cell may need different insulation, geometry, heat recovery or operating conditions to remain molten and maintain containment.

At plant scale, success requires predictable replacement cost, stable multi-anode current distribution, acceptable purity and high availability. The energy benefit—or penalty—must then be weighed against avoided anode manufacture and replacement, direct process-emission reductions, carbon costs and any low-carbon-metal premium. Inert anodes can remove direct carbon-anode oxidation emissions; they do not automatically eliminate electricity-sector emissions or every other emission associated with fluoride-cell operation.

---

## 6. What a chloride route must overcome

A chloride route changes much more than the anode. In the historical aluminium-chloride approach, purified anhydrous AlCl₃ is electrolysed in alkali-chloride electrolyte, with chlorine recovered for feed preparation. Lower operating temperature and compact bipolar-cell designs are genuine potential advantages, but they move substantial complexity upstream and into gas containment (Welch, 1999; ASME Technical Working Group, 1999).

### A. Feed preparation must be included in the energy and emissions boundary

A representative carbon-assisted chlorination step is

\[
\mathrm{Al_2O_3+3C+3Cl_2\rightarrow2AlCl_3+3CO},
\]

while electrolysis is

\[
\mathrm{2AlCl_3\rightarrow2Al+3Cl_2}.
\]

Combining them cancels recycled chlorine and aluminium chloride:

\[
\mathrm{Al_2O_3+3C\rightarrow2Al+3CO}.
\]

This does not establish the energy use of every possible chloride process, but it demonstrates why **electrolyzer electricity alone is an incomplete comparison**. Carbon and energy may have moved upstream rather than disappeared. The assessment must include chlorination, purification, CO/CO₂ handling, chlorine drying and recycle, auxiliary heat and environmental controls.

### B. Dry, high-purity feed handling is a first-order problem

AlCl₃ is volatile and moisture-sensitive. Moisture ingress produces corrosive hydrolysis products and oxygen-containing species that can foul or destabilize the cell. Volatile impurity chlorides must also be separated or purged: otherwise elements more readily reduced than aluminium can contaminate the product.

Consequently, conventional alumina point feeding is replaced by a chain of sealed feed production, purification, transfer and storage operations. Cold spots, desublimation, salt freezing and maintenance-related air ingress matter at plant scale, not just in bench chemistry.

### C. The chlorine loop is large even when chlorine is fully recycled

From the electrolysis stoichiometry,

\[
\frac{3M_{\mathrm{Cl_2}}}{2M_{\mathrm{Al}}}
=\frac{3(70.906)}{2(26.9815)}
=3.94\ \mathrm{kg\ Cl_2/kg\ Al}.
\]

Thus approximately **3.94 tonnes of chlorine circulate per tonne of aluminium per pass**. This is not net chlorine consumption under perfect recycle, but it shows why recovery efficiency, leak-tightness, inventory control and purge management are central. Chlorine sale cannot simply be assumed away as an unlimited sink: any offtake depends on a suitably sized, reliable local market, while the smelter itself must still be able to operate safely through recycle upsets and downstream outages.

### D. Corrosion, product separation and maintainability must be solved together

The plant must keep a dry chloride electrolyte, hot chlorine and reactive molten aluminium separated. Chlorine surviving near the cathode or contacting withdrawn metal can recombine with aluminium, wasting current and reagent. AlCl₃ volatility and condensation can obstruct gas passages, while moisture-related corrosion can attack piping, seals, valves and feed equipment.

Lower electrolysis temperature therefore changes the materials problem rather than eliminating it. Industrial acceptance requires durable cell construction, reliable product withdrawal, effective chlorine collection and safe recovery from leaks, freezing, power interruptions and maintenance. A few efficient cell runs do not demonstrate those capabilities.

### E. The energy advantage must repay a much larger capital discontinuity

A chloride smelter generally requires new or extensively altered feed preparation, chloride purification, electrolysis cells, chlorine recovery and recycle, gas treatment, materials supply and safety systems. Unlike a possible anode retrofit, it cannot rely on most of the incumbent’s alumina-feeding and fluoride-cell infrastructure.

Its lower-temperature or lower-cell-electricity advantage must consequently repay the **whole integrated plant**, not just the electrolyzer. Historical assessments of chloride development identify scale-up, maintenance, corrosion and containment economics—not inability to electrolyse AlCl₃—as central obstacles (ASME Technical Working Group, 1999).

---

## Bottom line

Hall–Héroult persists because carbon, cryolite, the liquid metal pad, the frozen ledge and the surrounding supply chain solve several difficult problems together. Carbon supplies a substantial thermodynamic voltage credit; cryolite permits alumina electrolysis and metal collection; resistive losses support the thermal balance; and the architecture is supported by mature, continuously improving industrial operations.

The displacement test is therefore **cost, emissions and reliability per tonne of saleable aluminium over commercially meaningful operating campaigns**, using a common system boundary:

- **Inert anodes:** demonstrate long anode and connection life without excessive metal contamination; compensate for the lost carbon voltage credit; preserve current efficiency and heat balance; and manufacture, retrofit and maintain the system economically.
- **Chloride routes:** demonstrate economical anhydrous feed production and purification; near-complete, safe chlorine recycle; corrosion-resistant and maintainable equipment; effective aluminium–chlorine separation; and a full-plant energy, emissions and capital advantage.

Neither route needs to win on electricity consumption alone. It can win if savings in emissions, consumables, maintenance or capital outweigh an energy penalty—or lose despite an efficient electrolysis cell if the rest of the plant consumes the advantage.

# The Physical and Economic Lock-In of Hall–Héroult Electrolysis and the Technological Barriers to Alternative Routes

## Executive Summary

The Hall–Héroult process has maintained an industrial monopoly over primary aluminium production since its independent invention by Charles Martin Hall and Paul Héroult in 1886 because it is not merely a single chemical reaction, but a tightly coupled physical, thermodynamic, material, and economic stack. In this system:
1. **Molten cryolite** ($\mathrm{Na_3AlF_6}$) acts as a unique solvent that dissolves alumina ($\mathrm{Al_2O_3}$) at manageable temperatures (~950–980 °C), conducts ionic current rapidly, and permits liquid metal to settle below the bath.
2. **Consumable carbon anodes** double as chemical fuel, supplying a ~1.03 V thermodynamic depolarization subsidy ($\approx 3.1\text{ kWh/kg Al}$) by evolving $\mathrm{CO_2}$ instead of $\mathrm{O_2}$.
3. **Resistive cell overpotentials** ($I^2R$ dissipation across a ~4.0–4.5 cm electrode gap) generate the autothermal heat budget required to keep the bath liquid and maintain a self-passivating frozen side-ledge against wall corrosion.

Displacing this technology requires beating the **full-system lifecycle cost per tonne of saleable metal** at multi-hundred-kiloampere scale, not merely lowering cell-level voltage or demonstrating oxygen evolution in a pilot vessel:
- **Inert-anode routes** (e.g., ELYSIS) must repay the +1.03 V oxygen-evolution penalty by shortening the anode-cathode distance (ACD) to <2.0 cm using titanium diboride ($\mathrm{TiB_2}$) wetted drained cathodes, while achieving anode corrosion rates low enough (<1 mm/yr) to meet commercial purity standards (e.g., P1020 grade: $\mathrm{Fe} \le 0.15\text{ wt\%}$, $\mathrm{Cu/Ni} \le 0.03\text{ wt\%}$) over multi-year continuous campaigns.
- **Chloride-based routes** (e.g., the historical Alcoa Smelting Process) operate at lower cell voltages and temperatures (~700 °C, ~9.5 kWh/kg), but shift the economic and environmental burden upstream into carbothermal chlorination, anhydrous $\mathrm{AlCl}_3$ sublimation and violent moisture hydrolysis, closed-loop chlorine gas containment, and organochlorine byproduct remediation.

---

## 1. Physical Constraints Governing the Operating Envelope (960–1000 °C, 13–14 kWh/kg)

```
========================================================================================
                         HALL–HÉROULT CELL PHYSICAL & THERMAL STACK
========================================================================================

                                Carbon Anodes (+)
                         [===]        [===]        [===]
                         | CO2 Gas Evolution       |
  +----------------------|-------------------------|-----------------------------------+
  | Solidified Cryolite Ledge ("Freeze")           v                                   |
  | (Self-healing autogenous wall insulation)   Molten Cryolite Bath (950–960 °C)     |
  |                                             rho ~ 2.10 g/cm³                       |
  |                                             -------------------------------------  |
  |                                             Liquid Aluminium Pad (Cathode, -)      |
  |                                             rho ~ 2.30 g/cm³                       |
  |                                             =====================================  |
  +------------------------------------------------------------------------------------+
  | Carbon Cathode Blocks & Steel Shell                                                |
  +------------------------------------------------------------------------------------+
```

### A. Cryolite Solvency and Temperature Phase Equilibria
Pure alumina ($\mathrm{Al_2O_3}$) melts at 2072 °C, a temperature at which structural containment and thermal radiation losses become unmanageable. Molten synthetic cryolite ($\mathrm{Na_3AlF_6}$) dissolves alumina into oxyfluoride complex anions (such as $[\mathrm{Al_2OF_6}]^{2-}$ and $[\mathrm{Al_2O_2F_4}]^{2-}$) at temperatures accessible to industrial alloys and refractories (Grjotheim & Kvande, 1993; Thonstad et al., 2001).

- **The Liquidus Window:** Pure cryolite melts at 1009 °C. Industrial cells operate with an acidic bath containing excess aluminium fluoride ($\mathrm{AlF_3}$, 8–12 wt%) and calcium fluoride ($\mathrm{CaF}_2$, 4–6 wt%), which depresses the liquidus temperature to 940–950 °C (Tabereaux & Peterson, 2014).
- **Alumina Solubility Boundary:** Below ~950 °C, $\mathrm{Al_2O_3}$ solubility drops precipitously (falling below 3–4 wt%). Solute starvation triggers mass-transfer polarization and catastrophic **anode effects** (voltage spikes >30 V with perfluorocarbon $\mathrm{CF_4}/\mathrm{C_2F_6}$ emissions). Undissolved alumina settles as an electrically resistive sludge ("muck") on the cathode floor, destabilizing current distribution.
- **Faradaic Efficiency Boundary:** Operating above ~980 °C accelerates the dissolution of metallic aluminium into the fluoride melt (forming subvalent species such as dissolved $\mathrm{Al}^+$ and $\mathrm{Na}$). These species diffuse upward across the inter-electrode gap and re-oxidize with anode gas:
  $$\mathrm{2 Al_{(dissolved)} + 3 CO_{2(g)} \longrightarrow Al_2O_{3(bath)} + 3 CO_{(g)}}$$
  This back-reaction is the primary source of Faradaic current efficiency loss (Kvande & Drabløs, 2014). The ~950–960 °C window represents a tightly constrained optimum balancing solubility against metal re-oxidation.

### B. Density Inversion and Continuous Phase Separation
At operating temperatures (950–960 °C), the density of the molten fluoride bath is $\approx 2.08\text{--}2.12\text{ g/cm}^3$, whereas liquid elemental aluminium has a density of $\approx 2.28\text{--}2.30\text{ g/cm}^3$ (Thonstad et al., 2001). 
- Because $\rho_{\mathrm{metal}} > \rho_{\mathrm{bath}}$ by $\sim 0.20\text{ g/cm}^3$, product aluminium pools naturally at the bottom of the pot.
- This liquid metal pad acts as the physical cathode, protected from ambient oxidation by the overlying electrolyte bath, allowing continuous tapping without interrupting pot operation.

### C. Self-Passivation via the Frozen Side-Ledge
Molten fluoride salts dissolve virtually all structural refractories and metals. The Hall–Héroult pot survives because heat loss through the outer steel shell and sidewall blocks (typically SiC or anthracite carbon) forces a layer of cryolite and alumina to crystallize along the interior walls (Taylor, 2014). This dynamic, autogenous "frozen ledge" isolates the sidewalls from chemical attack and electrical short-circuiting.

### D. The Thermodynamic Carbon Depolarization Subsidy
Direct electrochemical decomposition of alumina into its elements evolves pure oxygen gas:
$$\mathrm{\frac{1}{2} Al_2O_3(dissolved) \longrightarrow Al(l) + \frac{3}{4} O_2(g)}, \quad \Delta G^\circ_{1233\text{K}} \approx +640\text{ kJ/mol Al}, \quad E^\circ_{\mathrm{rev}} \approx -2.21\text{ V}$$

In the Hall–Héroult cell, coupling the anodic reaction to carbon oxidation converts the overall process into:
$$\mathrm{\frac{1}{2} Al_2O_3(dissolved) + \frac{3}{4} C(s) \longrightarrow Al(l) + \frac{3}{4} CO_2(g)}, \quad \Delta G^\circ_{1233\text{K}} \approx +340\text{ kJ/mol Al}, \quad E^\circ_{\mathrm{rev}} \approx -1.18\text{ V}$$

Consuming carbon pays a thermodynamic dividend of $\Delta E \approx 1.03\text{ V}$ (Grjotheim & Kvande, 1993). Carbon acts as an in-situ chemical co-fuel, supplying roughly 47% of the total energy required to split the aluminium–oxygen bond.

### E. Magnetohydrodynamic (MHD) Physics and the 13–14 kWh/kg Energy Floor
Faraday's law dictates that producing 1 kg of aluminium requires a theoretical charge of:
$$Q = \frac{1000\text{ g}}{26.9815\text{ g/mol}} \times 3 \times 96485.3\text{ C/mol} \times \frac{1\text{ Ah}}{3600\text{ C}} \approx 2980.6\text{ Ah/kg Al}$$

At a standard current efficiency ($\eta_{\mathrm{CE}}$) of 94–96%, the specific electrical energy consumption ($w$, in kWh/kg Al) depends directly on total cell voltage ($V_{\mathrm{cell}}$):
$$w = \frac{V_{\mathrm{cell}} \times 2.9806}{\eta_{\mathrm{CE}}}$$

```
========================================================================================
                      INDUSTRIAL HALL–HÉROULT VOLTAGE BREAKDOWN (~4.20 V)
========================================================================================
Reversible Decomposition Potential (E_rev):   [==== 1.18 V ====] (28.1%)
Anodic Overpotential (reaction & bubble):     [=== 0.50 V ===]   (11.9%)
Cathodic Overpotential:                       [= 0.05 V =]       ( 1.2%)
Ohmic Bath Drop (IR_bath across 4.5 cm ACD):  [====== 1.45 V ======] (34.5%)
External Busbars, Anode Stubs, & Cathode IR:  [==== 1.02 V ====] (24.3%)
========================================================================================
```

To achieve 13.0–13.5 kWh/kg Al at 95% current efficiency, total cell voltage must remain between 4.15 V and 4.30 V:
$$w = \frac{4.20\text{ V} \times 2.9806}{0.95} \approx 13.18\text{ kWh/kg Al}$$

The largest single voltage drop is the **ohmic bath potential** ($I \cdot R_{\mathrm{bath}} \approx 1.30\text{--}1.60\text{ V}$ across an ACD of 4.0–4.5 cm). This distance cannot be shortened in conventional horizontal cells: high direct currents (300 to 600+ kA) intersecting stray magnetic fields create Lorentz forces ($\vec{J} \times \vec{B}$) that induce standing waves and turbulence in the liquid metal pad (Kenjereš et al., 2013). Narrowing the ACD below ~4.0 cm causes metal wave peaks to touch the anode face, triggering localized short circuits and re-oxidizing the metal pad.

Furthermore, the ~3.0 V of total overvoltage and resistive losses is not wasted; its Joule heating ($I^2R$) provides the thermal input required to maintain the 960 °C bath temperature and preserve the protective frozen side-ledge against ambient heat loss.

## 2. Economic Dynamics of Incumbent Lock-In

| Economic Factor | Mechanism of System-Level Lock-In |
| :--- | :--- |
| **Capital Intensity & Asset Lifespans** | Greenfield prebake smelters require US\$4,000–\$5,500 of capital expenditure per annual tonne of capacity (International Aluminium Institute [IAI], 2024). Potlines operate continuously for 30–50 years, with individual pot cells relined every 5–8 years. High sunk costs discourage greenfield technology adoption. |
| **Operating Cost Structure** | Electricity constitutes 30–40% of cash operating costs (US\$650–\$1,120/t Al at standard industrial tariffs of \$0.05–\$0.08/kWh). Carbon anodes represent 10–15% of cash costs. Smelters are sited near low-cost power (hydropower or captive generation), where incremental efficiency gains yield modest financial returns relative to capital risk. |
| **Feedstock Integration** | Calcined petroleum coke (CPC) and coal-tar pitch (CTP) are low-cost residual byproducts of petroleum refining and steelmaking coke production. The carbon supply chain is fully integrated into smelter operations. |
| **Maturity & Scale Economies** | Modern potlines achieve >95% Faradaic efficiency, run with automated point-feeders, and utilize dry scrubbers that capture and recycle >99% of gaseous fluoride emissions back into the bath. |
