## Direct answer

Carbon-anode Hall–Héroult electrolysis still dominates because it is the only route that has ever combined, at industrial scale, a solvent that dissolves alumina well below its 2072 °C melting point, a self-renewing anode that doubles as a chemical fuel, an autothermal heat balance, and a century of sunk capital and operating know-how. The 960–1000 °C window and ~13–14 kWh/kg are not arbitrary: they are the equilibrium point of those constraints. An inert-anode or chloride route does not merely have to work electrochemically — it has to beat the incumbent's delivered cost per tonne across a plant that today produces, globally, about 73 million tonnes a year.

## 1. Why the temperature and energy figures are locked in

**The solvent sets the temperature floor.** Pure alumina melts at 2072 °C; molten cryolite (Na3AlF6) with excess AlF3 and CaF2 dissolves 2–6 wt% alumina and melts near 950–960 °C. That is why the cell sits at 960–1000 °C: colder and the bath freezes and alumina will not dissolve fast enough; hotter and heat loss, bath attack on materials, and aluminium re-dissolving into the bath (which destroys current efficiency) all rise steeply. The temperature is a system compromise, not a setpoint that can be dialled down independently.

**The solvent itself is now synthetic — a quiet proof of how entrenched the process is.** Natural cryolite came from essentially one commercial deposit, Ivittuut in Greenland, which yielded roughly 3.7–3.8 million tonnes of ore at ~58% cryolite grade between 1854 and 1987, peaking at 86,000 tonnes shipped in 1942, before the deposit ran out and the mine closed in 1987. Rather than abandon the process, the industry switched to synthetic sodium aluminium fluoride, and production continued uninterrupted (Mining North, "Cryolite: Greenland's forgotten icy mineral", https://www.miningnewsnorth.com/story/2025/08/01/mining-history/cryolite-greenlands-forgotten-icy-mineral/9197.html). A process that survives the commercial extinction of its namesake mineral is not easily displaced.

**The 13–14 kWh/kg follows from Faraday's law plus unavoidable losses.** Producing 1 kg of aluminium requires 2.98 kAh of charge at 100% current efficiency (3 electrons per Al atom, Faraday constant 96,485 C/mol, molar mass 26.98 g/mol). At a typical 95% current efficiency that is ~3.14 kAh/kg, so 13–14 kWh/kg implies an average cell voltage of ~4.1–4.5 V. The thermodynamic minimum for the carbon-assisted reaction is only ~1.2 V; the rest is anode overpotential (~0.5 V), ohmic drop across the anode–cathode gap (~1.4–1.6 V), and hardware resistance. Those losses are also the cell's only heat source — the cell is autothermal, with no external heater — so cutting voltage without adding heat elsewhere would freeze the bath. This is the trap: efficiency gains and thermal survival pull in opposite directions.

**Carbon is a fuel, not just an electrode.** The carbon anode is oxidised to CO2, which lowers the reversible potential from ~2.2 V (direct alumina decomposition) to ~1.2 V — carbon donates roughly 1 V of thermodynamic driving force. Stoichiometrically that costs at least 0.334 kg of carbon and emits at least 1.22 kg of CO2 per kg of aluminium. An inert anode gives up that ~1 V and must win it back through lower resistive losses or better cell geometry — a demanding trade, since the voltage it must recover is comparable to the entire ohmic drop of a modern cell.

## 2. The economic lock-in: scale and sunk capital

The incumbent's real moat is scale. Global primary aluminium production reached 72.76 million tonnes in 2024, up 2.89% year on year, according to the International Aluminium Institute (Mysteel, 21 Jan 2025, https://www.mysteel.net/news/5074920-iai-global-primary-al-output-reaches-73-million-t-in-2024-up-3-yoy). China alone produced about 43 million tonnes — roughly 60% of world output — and operates under a government capacity cap of 45 million tonnes set in 2017, running at about 98.2% utilisation (Reuters/Andy Home, 25 Apr 2025, http://energynews.oedigital.com/mining/2025/04/25/what-next-as-china-approaches-peak-aluminum-production-andy-home). Every tonne of that output sits in smelters whose potlines, anode plants, alumina refineries, fluoride recovery, power contracts and maintenance routines are built around Hall–Héroult. A challenger must compete against the *marginal* cost of already-paid-for incumbent capacity, not against the cost of building a new Hall–Héroult plant from scratch. Roughly 2 tonnes of alumina feed each tonne of aluminium, so the challenger must also slot into a Bayer-refinery supply chain that produces ~138 million tonnes of metallurgical alumina a year.

## 3. What an inert-anode route must overcome — and where it actually stands

The decisive recent datapoint: on 13 November 2025, ELYSIS (the Alcoa–Rio Tinto joint venture, launched 2018) started up a 450 kA inert-anode cell at Rio Tinto's Alma smelter in Québec — the first inert-anode cell at commercial amperage, i.e. the current level used in modern full-scale potlines (ELYSIS press release, 13 Nov 2025, https://elysis.com/en/elysis-achieves-breakthrough-with-commercial-size-cell-a-first-in-aluminium-production-using-the). That is a genuine milestone: the previous pilot was 100 kA (first metal November 2021), and its metal went into Apple laptops and iPhones, Michelob Ultra cans and Audi e-tron wheels. ELYSIS has raised over CAD 650 million (~US$460 million), including Canadian and Québec government funding (Canary Media, 25 Nov 2025, https://www.canarymedia.com/articles/clean-aluminum/alcoa-riotinto-hit-low-carbon-production-milestone).

But the milestone also measures the remaining gap:

- **Durability is unproven at scale.** The 450 kA cell is a single cell at the end of an existing potline, and ELYSIS says it will undergo "several more years of testing" to validate performance. One cell proving oxygen evolution is not a potline proving multi-year anode life, stable current efficiency and metal purity.
- **The demonstration plant is tiny relative to the industry.** The Arvida demonstration plant, under ELYSIS's first technology licence (June 2024), is ten 100 kA cells with a nameplate capacity of up to 2,500 tonnes per year, first production targeted by 2027, at a total investment of US$285 million (CAD$375 million). A modern smelter produces 300,000–500,000 tonnes per year — roughly 150–200 times that. The 2027 target has had no public reaffirmation since the November 2025 announcement, which should be read as absence of evidence, not confirmation.
- **The voltage penalty is real.** Replacing carbon oxidation with oxygen evolution forfeits carbon's ~1 V thermodynamic contribution. The inert anode must therefore run a materially more efficient cell (tighter anode–cathode distance, lower resistance, better current efficiency) just to match the incumbent's energy use — while surviving hot fluoride attack, thermal cycling and electrical-contact degradation without contaminating the metal. Even slow anode dissolution matters: at 73 million tonnes a year, trace contamination becomes a product-specification failure.
- **The prize is direct emissions only.** An inert anode eliminates the ~1.22 kg CO2/kg Al from anode oxidation and the perfluorocarbon emissions of anode effects, but it does nothing about electricity-related emissions — which dominate the footprint wherever power is fossil — or about alumina refining. Its business case therefore depends on cheap clean power and a carbon price, not on electrochemistry alone.

## 4. What a chloride route must overcome — and why it already lost once

The chloride route is the older challenger, and its history is the strongest evidence for how high the bar is. Alcoa developed it from the 1960s into the 1980s: alumina is chlorinated to aluminium chloride, which is then electrolysed in a molten-salt bath at typically ~720 °C — about 240 °C cooler than Hall–Héroult — using graphite electrodes that are inert in that chemistry (SINTEF blog, updated 10 Dec 2024, https://blog.sintef.com/energy/could-the-chloride-process-replace-the-hall-heroult-process-in-aluminium-production/). The process is more compact, runs cooler, and a 1976 Arthur D. Little assessment for the US government estimated it could save about 10% of the energy at the same or slightly lower operating cost than a Hall cell plant (OSTI, https://www.osti.gov/biblio/6537260).

It still never commercialised, and the reasons are exactly the constraints a revived chloride route must overcome:

- **Feed preparation eats the advantage.** Anhydrous AlCl3 must be made and kept rigorously dry — moisture causes unwanted reactions — and purified to remove iron, silicon and titanium chlorides. The US Bureau of Mines' state-of-the-art review concluded that "an acceptable chemical means has not been found to extract aluminum from clay as a highly pure anhydrous aluminum chloride" (Landsberg, Information Circular 8923, https://archive.org/stream/aluminumfromdome00land/aluminumfromdome00land_djvu.txt). Any carbon-assisted chlorination also consumes carbon and produces CO, so the cell's low electricity figure understates the full-plant energy and carbon balance.
- **Impurities and side reactions.** The chloride process is adversely affected by raw-material impurities; side reactions occur, and gaseous chlorine compounds are toxic. Formation of chlorinated alkanes (PAHs) and biphenyls (PCBs) has been reported (SINTEF, same source). Chlorine must be recycled with very low losses and contained safely, including during failures and maintenance — a containment problem the fluoride bath does not have, since cryolite is a molten salt, not a toxic gas.
- **Materials and corrosion.** Hot chlorides and chlorine attack equipment throughout the plant, not just the cell. Durable, affordable materials for the chlorinator, the cell and the chlorine loop remain a cost and reliability problem.
- **It was tried at pilot scale and still lost.** Pilot-scale AlCl3 reduction cells operated in the 1970s–80s, and interest faded for decades before a recent reassessment at Norway's HighEFF centre. A route that was piloted, costed at a ~10% energy saving, and still abandoned tells us the incumbent's advantage is in the full plant — feed, containment, materials, reliability — not in the cell voltage.

## 5. Bottom line

Hall–Héroult dominates because its constraints are mutually reinforcing: cryolite fixes the temperature, carbon fixes the voltage, Joule heating fixes the thermal balance, and 73 million tonnes a year of sunk capital fixes the economics. The temperature and the 13–14 kWh/kg are the visible surface of that equilibrium.

For an inert anode to displace it, the technology must demonstrate, together: multi-year anode life at 300–600 kA with no metal contamination; a cell voltage that recovers carbon's ~1 V without breaking the autothermal heat balance; and a full-potline cost per tonne below the marginal cost of existing smelters. ELYSIS's 450 kA cell (November 2025) proves the first step — commercial amperage — but the 2,500 tpy Arvida demonstration and "several more years of testing" show how far the remaining steps are.

For a chloride route, the bar is higher in one sense and already measured: it must make dry, pure AlCl3 cheaply, recycle chlorine near-losslessly and safely, survive hot-chloride corrosion, and prove a full-plant energy and emissions advantage — all of which Alcoa's 1960s–1980s programme, despite a cooler cell and an estimated ~10% energy saving, failed to do at commercial scale.

**Prediction (inference, not a verified fact):** Hall–Héroult will still produce the large majority of primary aluminium in 2035. Inert anodes are the more plausible challenger — ELYSIS has real capital, a commercial-amperage cell, and a licensed demonstration plant — but I estimate only a ~25–35% chance that an inert-anode plant produces more than 100,000 tonnes in any single year before 2032, because durability, voltage recovery and potline-scale economics remain unproven. A chloride route displacing Hall–Héroult at industrial scale before 2035 I estimate at under 5%: it would have to solve feed purification and chlorine containment problems that defeated a well-funded, decades-long industrial programme. Confidence in the qualitative ranking (inert anode ahead of chloride, incumbent dominant to 2035): ~70%.

## Why Hall–Héroult has survived 140 years — and what would actually have to change

The verified answer already covers the core electrochemistry: carbon lowers the decomposition voltage, the bath must stay molten, and the cell's own resistive losses supply its heat. This answer adds what it does not establish — the measured scale of the process, the chemistry that pins the temperature window so tightly, the emissions problem that is not CO2 from the anode, and how far the two challenger routes have actually got. Those are the facts that decide whether an alternative can displace the incumbent.

## 1. The numbers behind the question are real — and revealing

The question's 13–14 kWh/kg is not an approximation. The International Aluminium Institute reports the global average for smelting at just under 14 kWh per kg in 2024, and its earlier published global average was 14.21 kWh/kg; efficient modern smelters run at roughly 13 MWh per tonne, with the industry range usually quoted as 13–15 kWh/kg. Against that, the thermodynamic floor is far lower: the theoretical DC power consumption is about 6.34 kWh/kg. A modern cell therefore uses roughly twice the thermodynamic minimum, and roughly half the energy entering a smelter leaves as waste heat.

That energy dominates the economics: electricity can account for up to 40% of the total cost of producing primary aluminium. Global primary production is about 70 million tonnes a year (69.0 Mt in 2022, with China producing 59% of it), and smelting consumes roughly 3–4% of all the world's electricity — about 7% of China's national electricity demand. Any challenger therefore competes against an industry whose cheapest plants sit next to hydroelectric dams because power price, not cell chemistry, is the largest single cost line.

## 2. Why the temperature is pinned at 960–1,000 °C

Pure cryolite, Na3AlF6, melts at 1,011–1,012 °C, while pure alumina melts at about 2,072 °C. Dissolving alumina in cryolite brings the working temperature down by a thousand degrees, but the bath that actually runs in a modern high-amperage cell is not pure cryolite. Published bath surveys show modern cells using 10–12% excess aluminium fluoride (AlF3), 4–6% calcium fluoride (CaF2, mostly arriving as an impurity from the alumina feed), and 2–4% dissolved alumina, operating at 955–965 °C. Alumina solubility in molten cryolite at 1,000 °C is about 10 wt%, but the cell deliberately runs far leaner, at 2–4%, because that is where the operating window is stable.

Every additive that lowers the liquidus temperature also lowers alumina solubility — the central trade-off of bath chemistry. Add AlF3 and the bath melts cooler, but it holds less alumina, so the cell risks running dry and triggering an anode effect. The temperature therefore cannot simply be dialled down: go cooler and the bath stops dissolving enough alumina and stops flowing; go hotter and heat loss, attack on the lining, and dissolution of aluminium back into the bath all rise. The frozen electrolyte ledge that protects the cell sidewalls only exists inside this narrow thermal balance. A lower-temperature process is a different electrolyte system, not a colder version of the same one.

## 3. The carbon anode costs more than its stoichiometry — and the real emissions problem is not only CO2

The verified answer correctly derives the stoichiometric minimum of 0.334 kg of carbon and 1.22 kg of CO2 per kg of aluminium. In practice, real carbon consumption is more than 400 g per kg of aluminium — roughly a fifth above the ideal — because anodes also burn in air, react with CO2, and shed dust. Anode manufacture adds about 0.3 kg CO2 per kg of aluminium, and the anode reaction about 1.0 kg.

But the more distinctive emissions problem is the perfluorocarbons. When dissolved alumina falls below a critical level, the cell enters an "anode effect": voltage spikes and the cryolite itself reacts with the carbon anode, producing tetrafluoromethane (CF4) and hexafluoroethane (C2F6). Their global warming potentials are about 6,500 and 9,200 times that of CO2 on the commonly used industry figures (newer assessments put them at 6,630 and 11,100), and CF4 persists in the atmosphere for roughly 50,000 years. In 1990 the industry's average PFC burden was 3.65 tonnes of CO2-equivalent per tonne of aluminium; the best technology of the time achieved 0.35 tonnes. Modern process control has cut that dramatically, but online monitoring has also revealed that low concentrations of PFCs leak continuously during normal operation, not only during anode effects, and these background emissions may account for as much as 50% of the total. An inert anode eliminates both the CO2 and the PFCs at a stroke — a larger environmental prize than the carbon arithmetic alone suggests.

## 4. The incumbent is a system, not a cell

A modern prebaked-anode cell runs at 300,000–500,000 amperes and roughly 4.0–4.5 volts. Hundreds of such cells are wired in series in a potline, sharing rectifiers, alumina handling, anode baking plants, fluoride scrubbers and casthouses. A smelter's capital is largely sunk: the comparison that matters for an existing plant is the alternative's cost against the incumbent's operating cost, not its full replacement cost. That is a much harder bar than beating a pilot cell's energy figure, and it is the main reason a century of better chemistry has not displaced a process whose chemistry has barely changed since 1886.

## 5. Inert anodes: the furthest any challenger has ever got

An inert anode must do something no material has yet done cheaply for years at a time: evolve oxygen in a 960 °C fluoride melt without dissolving, oxidising, cracking under thermal cycling, or contaminating the metal. The leading materials are cermets — ceramic–metal composites, typically nickel ferrite with copper — and metal alloys such as copper–nickel. Even slow dissolution matters, because iron, nickel or copper leaking into the bath degrades aluminium purity, and the most valuable grades tolerate only parts-per-million contamination.

The state of the art has moved decisively since the review literature the verified answer cites. ELYSIS, the Alcoa–Rio Tinto joint venture founded in 2018, produced aluminium in a 100 kA inert-anode cell in November 2021, and in November 2025 it started up a 450 kA cell at the end of an existing potline at Rio Tinto's Alma smelter in Quebec — the first inert-anode cell at the current used in modern full-scale smelters, emitting oxygen instead of CO2 and PFCs. Metal from the smaller pilot has gone into Apple laptops and iPhones, Michelob Ultra cans and Audi electric-car wheels. A separate ten-cell demonstration plant at Arvida, Quebec — 100 kA cells, up to 2,500 tonnes a year, about US$285 million — is targeted for first production by 2027. RUSAL has run inert-anode cells at its Krasnoyarsk smelter since 2017, producing about 6,000 tonnes of commercial-grade metal; its ALLOW INERTA brand was independently verified in 2023 at 0.01 tonnes of CO2-equivalent per tonne of metal (Scope 1 and 2) using hydroelectric power, and in March 2026 it commissioned its first industrial electrolyser with inert anodes, releasing roughly 900 kg of oxygen per tonne of aluminium.

That is real progress — but note what it is not. Neither project has yet run a full potline of inert-anode cells for years, published a verified anode lifetime at commercial amperage, or demonstrated the total cost per tonne against a carbon-anode potline on the same power contract. The voltage penalty is the open question: oxygen evolution gives up carbon's thermodynamic advantage, so the cell must recover that voltage through lower resistive losses, tighter electrode spacing, or a redesigned cell. Until a multi-cell plant runs long enough to measure anode replacement cost, metal purity, current efficiency and maintenance downtime together, inert anodes remain a demonstrated technology rather than a displaced incumbent.

## 6. The drained cathode: the quiet efficiency lever the alternatives depend on

In a conventional cell the liquid aluminium pool is the cathode, and the gap to the anode must be kept at about 5 cm to avoid short circuits from waves in the metal pad. The cryolite in that gap has a resistivity of about 0.42 ohm-cm, so the gap alone wastes a large share of the cell's power. A "drained" or wetted cathode — a solid surface that molten aluminium wets and drains off, rather than a deep pool — could shrink the gap to 1–2 cm, saving an estimated 2–4 kWh per kg of aluminium, up to 25% of the power, and raising current efficiency by 5–20%.

Titanium diboride (TiB2) is the leading wettable-cathode material: highly wettable by aluminium, electrically conductive, wear-resistant and chemically stable. Results so far are encouraging but partial: TiB2/carbon cathodes in a 92 kA drained cell at Comalco achieved a lowest reported energy consumption of 12.8 kWh/kg, and a TiB2/carbon composite coating in a 300 kA cell at the Yichuan smelter in China saved about 0.4 kWh/kg and improved current efficiency by 1–2.5%. The unresolved problem is lifetime: the coating must resist electrolyte penetration and survive three to five years in service, and most full-size trials have delivered shorter lives. Low-temperature electrolytes (around 800 °C) would help both inert anodes and TiB2 cathodes last longer, but they dissolve less alumina — the same solubility trade-off that pins the conventional bath. The anode, the cathode and the bath must all change together, which is why incremental cell improvements have historically won and radical redesigns have not.

## 7. Chloride route: a proven pilot that lost on the whole plant, not on the cell

The chloride route is the most serious historical challenger. Alcoa developed it from the 1960s into the 1980s: alumina is carbochlorinated to aluminium chloride, which is dissolved in a molten salt bath and electrolysed at about 720 °C — roughly 240 °C cooler than Hall–Héroult — using graphite electrodes that are inert in the chloride melt. The electrolysis step was reported at about 9.6 kWh/kg against 13.4 kWh/kg for Hall–Héroult at the time, a saving of 25–30%. The metal was also purer, because the sodium contamination characteristic of cryolite cells is absent, and chloride cells tolerate power interruptions better than fluoride cells.

It never displaced the incumbent, for reasons that map exactly onto the question's test. First, the feed step consumes the apparent saving: carbochlorination reacts alumina with carbon and chlorine to make AlCl3 and CO2, so the process produces about the same CO2 per kg of aluminium as Hall–Héroult unless the CO2 is captured — although the concentrated process gas does make capture easier, which is why SINTEF has recently reassessed the route. Second, aluminium chloride is volatile, hygroscopic and highly corrosive: the feed must be made and kept rigorously dry, chlorine must be recycled with very low losses, and the plant must contain a toxic gas safely through failures and maintenance. Third, feed impurities cause side reactions, including formation of chlorinated alkanes and biphenyls (PCBs), and moisture triggers unwanted reactions. Fourth, the claimed energy advantage was measured at the electrolysis cell, not at the plant gate: once chlorination, chlorine recovery, drying, corrosion-resistant materials and emissions control are charged to the process, the advantage narrowed to the point where no producer would finance a full-scale plant. A challenger must win on the full-plant cost and emissions boundary, including feed preparation, not on the electrolysis step alone.

## 8. The displacement test, stated plainly

Hall–Héroult persists because it is a system that is good enough on every dimension at once: a solvent that dissolves alumina at a manageable temperature, an anode that is cheap and replaceable rather than durable, a cell that generates its own heat, a supply chain and workforce built over a century, and an installed base whose capital is already paid for. Its weaknesses are real and measurable: roughly twice the thermodynamic minimum energy, more than 400 g of carbon per kg of metal, and PFC emissions with a 50,000-year atmospheric lifetime.

An inert-anode route displaces it only when it demonstrates, together and at multi-cell scale: anode life measured in years at commercial amperage with metal purity maintained; a total cell voltage that compensates for the lost carbon depolarisation, most plausibly through drained cathodes or vertical electrodes; and a full-plant cost per tonne below the incumbent's operating cost on the same power. A chloride route displaces it only when it demonstrates: dry AlCl3 production at scale with chlorine losses near zero; safe containment of chlorine and chlorinated by-products; corrosion-resistant construction that survives years of service; and a plant-gate energy and CO2 balance, including carbochlorination, that beats Hall–Héroult rather than merely beating its electrolysis cell. The ELYSIS 450 kA cell and RUSAL's industrial electrolyser are the first demonstrations to put the inert-anode route within sight of that test. Until one of them passes it over a full operating life, carbon-anode electrolysis in molten cryolite will remain dominant — not because it is the best chemistry, but because it is the only chemistry that has ever survived the whole plant.

The Hall–Héroult process has remained the dominant primary aluminium production technology for over 140 years not because it is a perfect chemical reaction, but because it is a self-optimizing industrial system. The 960–1000 °C operating window, the ~13–14 kWh/kg energy consumption, and the consumable carbon anode are not arbitrary choices; they are the equilibrium points of a system where each component solves a constraint that would otherwise stop the process.

### 1. The Physical Constraints: Why the Process is Locked In

**The Solvent-Temperature Constraint:**
Pure alumina ($\text{Al}_2\text{O}_3$) melts at 2,072 °C, which is too high for industrial containment. Molten cryolite ($\text{Na}_3\text{AlF}_6$) is the only solvent that simultaneously:
*   Dissolves alumina (up to ~8 wt% at 960 °C).
*   Conducts electricity via $\text{Na}^+$ ions.
*   Is less dense than liquid aluminium (~2.1 g/cm³ vs ~2.3 g/cm³), allowing the metal to pool at the bottom for tapping.
*   Allows the formation of a "frozen ledge" (a self-healing crust of solidified bath) that protects the cell walls from the corrosive fluoride melt.

The 960–1000 °C window is the narrow range where the bath is fluid enough to dissolve alumina and conduct current, but cool enough to maintain the frozen ledge and prevent excessive dissolution of the product metal back into the bath (which would collapse current efficiency).

**The Carbon Anode Constraint:**
The carbon anode is not just an electrode; it is a chemical reductant. The reaction $2\text{Al}_2\text{O}_3 + 3\text{C} \rightarrow 4\text{Al} + 3\text{CO}_2$ has a reversible potential of ~1.2 V, whereas oxygen evolution ($2\text{Al}_2\text{O}_3 \rightarrow 4\text{Al} + 3\text{O}_2$) requires ~2.2 V. Carbon provides a ~1 V "voltage discount" (worth ~3 kWh/kg). Furthermore, carbon is cheap, conductive, and self-renewing through a mature supply chain.

**The Energy Constraint:**
The 13–14 kWh/kg figure is the sum of the electrochemical reaction, the ohmic resistance of the bath, and the heat required to maintain the frozen ledge. Roughly half the input energy leaves as waste heat. This is not "wasted" energy; it is the heat required to keep the bath molten and the ledge stable. A cell that was perfectly insulated would melt its own walls; a cell that lost too much heat would freeze.

### 2. Hurdles for Alternative Routes

To displace Hall–Héroult, an alternative must beat the *entire system* cost, not just the electrolysis step.

**Inert Anodes (Oxygen Evolution):**
*   **The Voltage Penalty:** By evolving oxygen, the cell loses the ~1 V carbon discount. To remain energy-competitive, the cell must recover this voltage by shrinking the anode-cathode distance (ACD).
*   **The MHD Limit:** In conventional cells, the ACD cannot be shrunk below ~4 cm because Lorentz forces ($\mathbf{J} \times \mathbf{B}$) create waves in the liquid metal pad that would short-circuit the cell.
*   **The Solution:** Inert anodes require a "drained" or "wettable" cathode (e.g., $\text{TiB}_2$) to eliminate the deep metal pad. This is a total cell redesign, not a drop-in replacement.
*   **Durability:** The anode must survive years in 960 °C fluoride without dissolving, which would contaminate the aluminium with Fe, Ni, or Cu, violating purity standards (P1020). As of late 2025, commercial-amperage cells (e.g., ELYSIS 450 kA) are in multi-year testing; durability remains the primary hurdle.

**Chloride-Based Routes:**
*   **Feed Preparation:** Alumina must be converted to anhydrous $\text{AlCl}_3$ via carbochlorination. This is an energy-intensive, corrosive, and toxic upstream process that produces CO and chlorinated byproducts.
*   **Containment:** $\text{AlCl}_3$ is volatile and hygroscopic. Moisture ingress creates HCl, which corrodes equipment. Chlorine gas must be recycled in a closed loop.
*   **Economic Reality:** The Alcoa Smelting Process (ASP) demonstrated lower cell energy (~9.5 kWh/kg) in the 1970s but failed because the upstream feed plant and chlorine containment costs exceeded the savings from the cell.

### Conclusion
Hall–Héroult persists because it is a self-consistent system where the carbon anode, the cryolite bath, and the frozen ledge support one another. Inert anodes are the most plausible challenger, but they require a coupled redesign (drained cathodes) and multi-year durability proof. Chloride routes face a "system-level" barrier: the electrolysis cell is efficient, but the feed-preparation and containment plant is not.

## Direct answer

Hall–Héroult is not held in place by one number. It is held by a coupled budget in which each apparent inefficiency performs a necessary function:

- The **cryolite bath** is a solvent, an ion conductor, a density separator, and — through the frozen side ledge — the cell’s own corrosion-resistant container.
- The **carbon anode** is not merely an electrode. It is a chemical fuel worth roughly **0.9–1.0 V** of decomposition voltage, a scheduled consumable, and a distributed control actuator that operators adjust to steer current and temperature.
- The **cell’s ohmic heat** is not pure waste. It is the furnace that keeps the bath molten and maintains the frozen ledge.
- The **MHD-limited anode–cathode gap** is why the largest single voltage loss cannot simply be designed away.
- The **installed capital and power contracts** mean a challenger must beat the *best* incumbent smelters, not the global average.

An inert-anode route must replace carbon’s chemical energy, recover the lost heat, survive fluoride/oxygen attack with very low contamination, control current without adjustable anode heights, and handle a very large pure-oxygen stream. A chloride route must win on the **whole plant** — chlorination, drying, purification, chlorine containment and corrosion — not on the electrolysis cell alone.

## 1. The temperature is a narrow superheat window

The 960–1000 °C figure is often described as “where cryolite melts.” That is incomplete. Pure cryolite melts near 1009–1012 °C; industrial baths add excess AlF₃ and CaF₂ to depress the liquidus to roughly 940–960 °C, and the cell runs only about **10–20 °C above its own liquidus**.

That narrow margin is the real constraint:

- **Colder:** alumina solubility falls, bath viscosity rises, alumina dissolution slows, sludge forms on the cathode, and local alumina starvation triggers anode effects.
- **Hotter:** aluminium dissolves into the bath and re-oxidises at the anode, lowering current efficiency; fluoride volatility, materials attack, and heat loss rise; the frozen side ledge can melt back.

## Direct answer

The verified answers in this arena settle the chemistry: carbon anodes survive because they donate ~1 V of decomposition voltage, molten cryolite is the only workable solvent, and an inert anode must repay that ~3 kWh/kg penalty while surviving years in hot fluoride. What none of them tests is the displacement condition itself — and it has already been tested twice, in 2022–2026, by events rather than by pilots. Both tests say the same thing: **the binding constraint on displacing Hall–Héroult is the power contract and market access, not the anode.** A challenger must beat the incumbent on delivered dollars per tonne at the marginal producer, and it must be allowed to sell where it claims to displace. On both counts the record since 2022 is against the challengers, and it quantifies how large the gap is.

## 1. The displacement test already ran — on power price, not on chemistry

**Europe, 2022–2026.** Norsk Hydro states that 50 percent of EU primary aluminium production has been curtailed since 2022 (Hydro, 2026). The mechanism was power price, not anode chemistry. Slovalco (Slovakia, 175,000 t/yr capacity, Hydro 55.3%) curtailed 40% of capacity in late 2021–early 2022 and closed primary production entirely by September 2022 because of high electricity prices and the absence of a competitive CO2-compensation framework; Hydro said the plant "would incur substantial financial losses if it continued its operation beyond 2022" (Hydro, 2022). Four years later it is restarting only 75,000 t/yr — 43% of capacity — in Q4 2026, after a €100 million investment, a ten-year power purchase agreement with the state hydropower company, and conditional on European Commission approval of an updated indirect-carbon-cost compensation scheme; the remaining 100,000 t/yr depends on framework conditions beyond 2030 (Hydro, 2026).

**Mozal, Mozambique, March 2026.** South32 placed Mozal — ~580,000 t/yr, Mozambique's largest industrial facility — on care and maintenance on 15 March 2026 after six years of engagement failed to secure "sufficient and affordable power supply" beyond March 2026; the smelter needs ~950 MW continuously (South32, 2026). Output had already fallen 30% in FY2026 to 248,000 t (from 355,000 t), and the April–June 2026 quarter recorded zero production (South32, reported 2026). The price that killed it is on the record: the smelter argued for a tariff of ~$51/MWh against ~$100/MWh proposed by suppliers (Diário Económico, reported 2026). Drought at Cahora Bassa constrained hydro availability as well — so this is a test of power price *and* power availability, and the smelter failed both.

**Why this decides the question.** At the question's own 13–14 kWh/kg, the Mozal price gap is worth 13.5 kWh/kg × ($100 − $51)/MWh ≈ **$660 per tonne of aluminium**. Compare that with the two prizes the earlier answers quantify: the chloride route's whole energy advantage (~3.8 kWh/kg) is worth only ~$100–150/t at $30–40/MWh, and the inert anode's avoided ~1.5 t CO2/t is worth ~$150/t at a $100/t CO2 price and ~$300/t at $200/t. The power-price swing that actually kills smelters is roughly **four to six times the chloride energy prize and two to four times the inert anode's carbon value**. An alternative route that wins on chemistry but needs cheap power loses to the same force that closed Slovalco and Mozal — and it competes for the same scarce cheap hydro the incumbents already occupy. The displacement condition is therefore not "beat 13–14 kWh/kg" but "survive a power market where the viable price is ~$50/MWh and the killer price is ~$100/MWh, on a long-term contract."

Two honest caveats. First, curtailment is reversible when the power contract is fixed: Slovalco's restart proves the constraint is contractual, not geological. Second, CBAM — the policy meant to price the incumbent's direct emissions — entered its definitive regime on 1 January 2026, *after* half of EU production had already been curtailed; the carbon price arrived too late to save the smelters it was meant to protect, which is itself evidence that the binding variable was power all along.

## 2. Market access is a separate displacement constraint — proven by RUSAL

The latest verified answer establishes that RUSAL is the furthest-advanced inert-anode programme in commercial terms: cells at Krasnoyarsk since 2017, ~6,000 tonnes of commercial-grade metal, ALLOW INERTA verified by TÜV AUSTRIA at 0.01 t CO2e/t (Scope 1 and 2, hydro power), and the first industrial electrolyser commissioned in March 2026. What it does not record is that this metal is being progressively locked out of the markets it would have to displace Hall–Héroult in. The EU's 16th sanctions package (Regulation (EU) 2025/395, February 2025) banned Russian unwrought aluminium, with a 275,000-tonne quota — 80% of 2024 EU imports — for February 2025 to February 2026, then only ≤50,000 tonnes under pre-existing contracts until 31 December 2026, and full prohibition from that date; the LME suspended warranting of the listed Russian brands in EU warehouses from 25 February 2026 (LME, 2026). The US and UK had already banned Russian metal imports in 2024.

The scale puts the point beyond argument: ~6,000 tonnes over nine years is about **0.008% of a single year's world output** (~72.8 Mt in 2024). RUSAL's metal does find buyers — a 25-tonne batch went to a major Chinese customer in late 2025 — but China already produces ~60% of world primary aluminium (43 Mt of ~72 Mt) under a government capacity cap of 45 Mt running at ~98% utilisation, so inert-anode metal sold there adds to a capped system rather than displacing a tonne of Hall–Héroult output. A technology can be commercially implemented and still displace nothing, if the markets where it could displace are closed to it and the markets open to it are capped. Any displacement claim for an inert-anode route must therefore clear a market-access test alongside the durability test — and ELYSIS, whose first commercial-amperage cell started at Alma in November 2025 with its ten-cell Arvida demonstration targeted for 2027, is the programme that can still pass it, because it sells into Western markets.

## 3. The displacement conditions, restated with the two new tests

A route displaces Hall–Héroult at industrial scale only when it passes **all** of these, not just the chemistry ones the verified answers establish:

1. **Durability at commercial amperage, over years** — one 450 kA cell (ELYSIS, November 2025) and one industrial electrolyser (RUSAL, March 2026) do not answer the multi-year anode-life and metal-purity question; Arvida (2027+) is the first real test.
2. **A power contract, not just a kWh/kg figure** — survival at ~$50/MWh long-term power, in a market where ~$100/MWh closes a 580,000 t/yr smelter. A route whose economics assume $30–40/MWh power is competing for the same scarce cheap hydro as the incumbents.
3. **Market access where it claims to displace** — LME-deliverable status and freedom from import bans in the target market; RUSAL shows that commercial implementation without market access displaces nothing.
4. **A carbon price (or green premium) above the ~$150–250/t CO2 breakeven** established in this arena — necessary, but as Slovalco and Mozal show, not sufficient: a carbon price does not save a smelter that cannot buy power.

Until a challenger passes all four, carbon-anode electrolysis in molten cryolite remains dominant — not because it is the best chemistry, but because it is the only route that has ever survived the whole plant, the whole power contract, and the whole market.

**Direct answer.** Hall–Héroult persists because bath, consumable carbon anode and cell heat balance are one interlocking system: the carbon anode is simultaneously the cheapest oxygen sink, a ~1 V voltage subsidy, and the fuel that keeps the cell autothermal. An inert anode removes all three at once; a chloride route must win at the plant gate, not at the cell.

**1. Temperature is pinned by a narrow superheat window.** Aluminium cannot be electrowon from water — it is far more reactive than hydrogen, so hydrogen evolves instead — which forces a molten-salt solvent. Pure cryolite melts near 1,010 °C; AlF₃ and CaF₂ additions depress the liquidus to roughly 950–960 °C, and cells run only ~10–20 °C above it (Thonstad et al., 2001). Colder, alumina solubility and bath conductivity fall, sludge settles, and local alumina starvation triggers anode effects with CF₄/C₂F₆ emissions. Hotter, fluoride volatility, corrosion and aluminium back-dissolution rise, and the frozen sidewall ledge — the cell's self-repairing lining, since molten cryolite attacks nearly all refractories — melts back. The temperature is not chosen; it is the interval in which the bath dissolves enough alumina, carries hundreds of kiloamperes, and still freezes its own container.

**2. Most of the 13–14 kWh/kg is deliberate heat, not waste.** Faraday's law fixes charge at 3 F per mol Al: 2.98 kAh/kg at 100% current efficiency, ~3.1 kAh/kg at the 93–96% of modern cells (Thonstad et al., 2001). At ~4.2 V that is ~13 kWh/kg; the International Aluminium Institute reports industry-average smelting energy near 14,000 kWh/t because the fleet includes older cells (International Aluminium Institute, n.d.). Only ~1.2 V is reversible decomposition voltage; the remainder is overpotential, bath resistance and busbar loss — and it is the heater. The cell has no external heat source, so voltage cannot simply be cut.

**3. The inert anode's penalty is thermal.** From NIST-JANAF standard enthalpies (ΔHf Al₂O₃ = −1675.7, CO₂ = −393.5 kJ/mol), Al₂O₃ + 1.5C → 2Al + 1.5CO₂ releases ~1,085 kJ per 6 F, an enthalpy voltage of ~1.9 V, against ~2.9 V for oxygen evolution. At the same 4.2 V an idealised inert cell therefore converts ~1 V more electricity into chemical work and releases ~3 kWh/kg less heat (1.0 V × 2.98 kAh/kg ÷ 0.95). It would run colder and risk freezing its ledge unless voltage rises ~1 V — giving the saving back — or the cell is redesigned with a drained/wetted cathode, tighter anode–cathode spacing and better insulation. Spacing cannot simply close: at hundreds of kiloamperes the metal pad waves under magnetohydrodynamic forcing and shorts against the anode. The inert anode is a system redesign whose honest selling point is CO₂ and PFC elimination, not energy.

**4. Economic lock-in.** The fleet's capital is sunk; anode plants, pitch supply and butt recycling are integrated; power contracts are baseload and electricity dominates operating cost. A consumable anode is a predictable operating cost; a durable anode converts it into capital and maintenance risk with an unknown replacement interval, which financiers discount heavily.

**5. Chloride route.** Alcoa's chloride process electrolysed AlCl₃ in a molten chloride bath well below cryolite temperatures, with graphite electrodes effectively inert there, and was reported at substantially lower cell energy than Hall–Héroult at the time (SINTEF, n.d.). It failed at the plant boundary: carbochlorination consumes carbon and chlorine, so CO₂ per tonne is similar unless captured; AlCl₃ is volatile, hygroscopic and corrosive; chlorine must be recycled with near-zero loss and contained through failures; chlorinated by-products form. The cell-level energy win did not survive whole-plant accounting.

**6. What would change the answer.** A carbon price high enough to price the anode's CO₂ (~1.5 t CO₂ per tonne Al on ~0.4 t carbon consumed; Thonstad et al., 2001); demonstrated multi-year anode life at commercial amperage with acceptable metal purity; and a heat-balanced low-temperature cell. ELYSIS (an Alcoa–Rio Tinto venture) reports industrial-scale inert-anode cell development, but on the public record this is demonstration, not fleet conversion — that judgement is my assessment, not a cited finding. My confidence that inert anodes take a large share of capacity before 2035 is low-to-moderate: physics is not the obstacle; durability-and-heat-balance economics is.

## What the verified answers leave out — and why it matters

The three verified answers converge on the right constraint stack: the ~1 V carbon credit, cryolite's solvent bundle, the MHD-limited anode–cathode gap, the frozen ledge, the cathode campaign, and the CBAM breakeven arithmetic. I do not dispute any of it. This answer adds six things none of them contains: the last displacement, a third challenger route, a different inert-anode architecture, the incumbent learning to flex, recycling as live displacement, and a policy cap moving tonnes geographically.

## 1. The last displacement: price collapsed, chemistry followed

Hall–Héroult did not displace the Deville sodium process by being a better cell. It displaced it by collapsing the price: Deville's process sold aluminium at $32 per pound in 1855 — more than gold — and still $15 per pound thirty years later, while the 1884 capstone of the Washington Monument used just 6 pounds, about one-thousandth of the world's entire annual output. Within three years of Hall's 1886 patent the price had fallen to about $2 per pound, and by 1914 to 18 cents a pound. The lesson: a challenger needs one decisive cost collapse, not a marginal improvement on a single metric — and none of the current challengers has yet shown one.

## 2. Carbothermic reduction: the route the question omits

There is a third route besides inert anodes and chloride, and it is the oldest challenger of all. Carbothermic reduction reacts alumina directly with carbon — Al2O3 + 3C → 2Al + 3CO — with no electrolysis and no fluoride bath at all. It proceeds in two stages: alumina and carbon first form aluminium carbide (2Al2O3 + 9C → Al4C3 + 6CO) at roughly 1,875–2,000 °C, and the carbide then reacts with more alumina to yield metal (Al2O3 + Al4C3 → 6Al + 3CO) above about 2,050 °C. Alcoa pursued it for decades, with Elkem, and the claimed prize was large: a successful carbothermic process was projected to cut capital investment by 50–70% and operating costs by 25–35% against the electrolytic route, while eliminating fluoride emissions entirely.

It has never worked commercially. At the temperatures required, aluminium itself vaporises, and side reactions producing aluminium suboxide (Al2O) and oxy-carbides steal the yield: reviews conclude that no industrial carbothermic process has succeeded because carbide and oxy-carbide formation and aluminium vaporisation keep yields low. The engineering problems are the mirror image of Hall–Héroult's: instead of containing a corrosive liquid at 960 °C, the plant must recover volatilised aluminium from a 2,000 °C-plus gas stream, limit refractory loss, and handle a large volume of carbon monoxide. Newer concepts try running the reduction under vacuum to lower the required temperature and suppress the side reactions, but they remain laboratory-scale. The binding constraint on a non-electrolytic route is not energy but yield — the metal keeps escaping as vapour or carbide before it can be tapped.

## 3. Solid oxide membrane electrolysis: an inert anode behind a wall

The inert-anode discussion in the verified answers assumes the anode sits in the fluoride bath. There is an architecture that avoids that entirely. In solid oxide membrane (SOM) electrolysis, developed at Boston University by Uday Pal and co-workers, an oxygen-ion-conducting tube of yttria-stabilised zirconia (YSZ) separates the molten flux from the anode assembly inside it. Alumina dissolved in a magnesium fluoride–calcium fluoride flux is reduced at the cathode while oxygen ions migrate through the YSZ membrane and are oxidised at the anode — a liquid silver anode with an LSM (lanthanum strontium manganite)–Inconel current collector — so the anode never touches fluoride at all, and pure oxygen is collected as a byproduct.

The proof of concept, published in 2017, ran at 1,200 °C — hotter than Hall–Héroult, not colder — in a flux of 45 wt% MgF2–55 wt% CaF2 with 6 wt% CaO, 3 wt% Al2O3 and 4 wt% YF3, the last added to stop yttrium leaching out of the membrane. It produced high-purity aluminium (over 99 wt%) deposited on a TiB2 cathode, and the membrane was confirmed chemically and electrochemically stable after 28 hours of electrolysis. The same SOM approach has been demonstrated for magnesium, titanium, tantalum and silicon — but 28 hours is not a campaign, the membrane adds its own ionic resistance to the cell voltage, and nothing has been shown at kiloampere scale. SOM's displacement test is therefore distinct from ELYSIS's: membrane life in months at industrial current density, and a cell voltage that absorbs both the oxygen-evolution penalty and the membrane resistance, before it can claim to solve anode corrosion by sidestepping it.

## 4. The incumbent is learning to flex — and that raises the bar

At its Essen smelter in Germany, TRIMET has converted 120 pots into a "virtual battery" using controllable shell heat exchangers (EnPot technology, developed with the University of Wuppertal) fitted to the cell sidewalls. By artificially varying heat loss, the smelter can consume 25% more or 25% less electricity for up to 48 hours without interrupting production — and can cut demand to zero for up to an hour — storing up to about 2,000 MWh, comparable to a medium-sized pumped-storage plant. The €36 million trial lets the smelter sell flexibility back to the grid at peak prices and absorb surplus wind and solar power. TRIMET is now rolling its METRICS control system across its furnaces, aiming to control all 998 electrolysis furnaces at its four smelters by 2028 — and it is simultaneously researching an inert anode of its own.

The implication cuts both ways. A challenger that needs a flat baseload contract is competing against an incumbent that no longer strictly needs one, which narrows the economic case for any replacement that cannot also flex — and any new cell designed from scratch would have to be built flexible as well, on top of the durability and energy tests, not instead of them.

## 5. Recycling is already displacing primary metal — from the demand side

The verified answers frame displacement as a contest between smelting chemistries. The displacement that is actually happening is different: secondary aluminium already supplies roughly a third of new metal, at about 5% of the energy. The International Aluminium Institute puts primary production at 186 GJ per tonne (mine to cast house, 2019) against 8.3 GJ per tonne for recycled metal, and 15.1 tonnes of CO2-equivalent per tonne of primary against 0.52 tonnes for recycling (2022). In the United States in 2022, secondary aluminium accounted for 34% of total new supply including imports.

But recycling has a ceiling that protects primary smelting, and it is chemical, not logistical. Iron, copper, zinc and manganese are difficult to remove from molten aluminium, and they accumulate with every recycling loop. The standard countermeasure, documented by Gaustad, Olivetti and Kirchain (2012), is dilution with primary aluminium — which caps how much scrap any melt can absorb. A die-casting alloy such as EN AC-46000 tolerates iron up to 1.3% and copper at 2–4%, so it can be made largely from scrap, while a low-impurity wrought alloy such as EN AC-42100 caps iron at 0.19% and copper at 0.05%, requiring primary metal or very clean scrap. Sorting technology — handheld LIBS and XRF analysers, eddy-current and X-ray separators — pushes the ceiling up by keeping alloy streams separate, but it cannot remove tramp elements already mixed in. Recycling therefore displaces primary tonnes where specifications are loose, and entrenches Hall–Héroult where they are tight.

## 6. The cap that is moving tonnes: geography, not chemistry

The final missing constraint is political, and it is already reshaping the industry faster than any new cell. China capped domestic primary smelting capacity at 45 million tonnes a year under a 2017 policy to curb overcapacity and pollution, and producers are operating close to that ceiling: in 2025 China produced about 44.2 million tonnes of the global 73.78 million, roughly 60%. With no legal room to grow at home, capacity migrated to hydropower — Yunnan province held about a fifth of China's electrolytic capacity by the end of 2021 — and now overseas: Chinese producers have announced or planned at least 15 million tonnes a year of new primary capacity in Southeast Asia, the Middle East, Central Asia and Africa, with 2.85 million tonnes already under construction. The power-contract constraint also bites in reverse: the Mozal smelter in Mozambique, which consumes 43% of the country's electricity, halted production in March 2026 after electricity price negotiations failed. Hall–Héroult's dominance is therefore being tested less in the laboratory than by whether cheap, flat, low-carbon power exists anywhere at the scale a smelter needs — and the answer is increasingly "not where the smelters are." A challenger that uses materially less electricity, or that can run on intermittent renewables, would not need to beat the incumbent's cost in Quebec or Yunnan; it would need to beat it where power is expensive or unavailable. That is a lower bar, and it is the one the chloride route's ~30% electrolysis energy saving and the flexible-potline concept are both, in different ways, aimed at.

## The displacement test, restated with the new evidence

Hall–Héroult persists because it is a system that is good enough on every dimension at once — the verified answers establish that, and the history in section 1 shows what it takes to break such a lock: a cost collapse, not a marginal improvement. The new evidence adds four tests. A carbothermic route must show it can recover volatilised aluminium and suppress carbide and suboxide formation at yields that survive 2,000 °C operation. A solid oxide membrane route must show membrane life in months and a voltage that absorbs both the oxygen penalty and the membrane resistance, at kiloampere scale. Any challenger must match the incumbent's new flexibility — TRIMET's ±25% for 48 hours — or accept a narrower market. And every route must reckon with recycling, which already takes the loose-specification tonnes and leaves the challenger fighting for the high-purity end. On the inert-anode front itself, the latest public evidence as of September 2026 is silence: no update on the Arvida ten-cell demonstration plant has been issued since the November 2025 Alma start-up, while Rio Tinto began commissioning a conventional AP60 expansion at the same Arvida complex in March 2026, with 96 new pots due by the end of the year. Until a challenger passes its whole checklist at multi-pot scale — or a cost collapse arrives the way it did in 1886 — carbon-anode electrolysis in molten cryolite will remain dominant, not because it is the best chemistry, but because it is the only chemistry that has ever survived the whole plant, the whole grid, and the whole market.

The Hall–Héroult process persists not merely because it is the most efficient chemical reaction, but because it is a **coupled physical and kinetic system** where every apparent inefficiency performs a mechanical or thermal function. The constraints of 960–1000 °C and 13–14 kWh/kg Al represent a "systemic lock" where the carbon anode, fluoride bath, and magnetic stability limits form a self-optimizing equilibrium. 

To displace this at an industrial scale, alternative routes must overcome not only the thermodynamic penalty but also the mechanical mixing, thermal insulation, and "shunt current" problems that the incumbent process solves "for free."

---

### 1. The Physical Lock: Why 960–1000 °C is Pinning the Process

While the melting point of pure cryolite is 1011 ± 1 °C, the industry runs at 950–970 °C (often cited as the 960–1000 °C range in the premise) because of a specific **kinetic trade-off between alumina solubility and the "Stefan Problem" of the side-ledge.**

#### A. The Bubble-Driven Mixing Constraint
A critical constraint under-discussed in the previous answers is the **gas-lift effect**. As the carbon anode is consumed, it evolves CO₂ bubbles (roughly 0.15–0.20 m³ per kg of Al). These bubbles are not merely waste; they provide the primary mixing energy for the bath. This turbulence is essential to ensure that the alumina feed dissolves instantaneously and stays in suspension.
*   **The Hurdle for Inert Anodes:** Inert anodes evolve O₂, which has a different surface tension and bubble diameter than CO₂. Research indicates that O₂ bubbles are smaller and detach differently, which can significantly reduce the **mass transfer coefficient** ($k_m$) for alumina dissolution (Thonstad et al., 2001). To displace the incumbent, an inert-anode plant must redesign the feeding mechanics to compensate for the lost "CO₂ gas-lift" or risk "sludging" (undissolved alumina settling at the bottom).

#### B. The Stefan Problem: The Frozen Ledge
The "ledge" (frozen electrolyte on the side walls) is the only reason the pot shell does not melt. Its thickness is governed by the heat balance: $Q_{in} = Q_{loss}$. 
*   **The Temperature Floor:** If the temperature drops below ~940 °C, the ledge grows inward, reducing the effective volume of the cell and causing "muck" to form. 
*   **The Temperature Ceiling:** If it exceeds ~980 °C, the ledge thins, the side wall is attacked by the bath, and the "back-reaction" ($2Al + 3CO_2 \rightarrow Al_2O_3 + 3CO$) accelerates, destroying current efficiency (Kvande & Drabløs, 2014).
*   **Conclusion:** The temperature is pinned by the narrow window (10–20 °C of superheat) where the bath is fluid enough to dissolve alumina but cool enough to maintain its own container.

---

### 2. The Economic Lock: The 13–14 kWh/kg "Digital Goalpost"

The 13–14 kWh/kg figure is the equilibrium point between the **thermodynamic decomposition energy (~6.3 kWh/kg)** and the **magnetic stability limit**.

#### A. The Magnetic Goalpost and "Digital Twins"
Historically, the anode–cathode distance (ACD) was kept at 4–5 cm because the massive currents (up to 600 kA) create magnetic fields that induce waves in the liquid metal. If a wave touches the anode, it causes a short circuit.
*   **The 2024-2026 Shift:** Modern smelters are now using **Digital Twin** modeling and **Busbar 4.0** designs to compensate for magnetic fields in real-time. This has allowed some modern pots (like Rio Tinto’s AP60) to operate closer to 12.5–12.8 kWh/kg (International Aluminium Institute, 2024). 
*   **The Hurdle:** This "moving goalpost" makes the economic case for inert anodes harder. If the incumbent can drop to 12 kWh/kg through software and magnetic design, the 1V (~3 kWh/kg) thermodynamic penalty of switching to inert anodes (oxygen evolution) becomes an even larger hurdle to overcome.

---

### 3. Constraints Alternatives Must Overcome to Displace the Incumbent

#### A. Inert Anodes: The "Purity Ratchet" and the "Heat Deficit"
To displace carbon at scale, inert anodes (like the ELYSIS cermet anodes) must survive the "Purity Ratchet."
*   **The Purity Ratchet:** In a carbon-anode cell, impurities in the coke (Fe, Si) are predictable. In an inert cell, the anode material (e.g., Ni-Fe spinel) slowly dissolves. Because Fe and Ni are nobler than Al, 100% of the dissolved anode material ends up in the metal pad (Kvande, 1999). 
*   **The Constraint:** To meet P1020 grade specifications (Fe < 0.15%), the anode corrosion rate must be less than **1 mm/year**. As of November 2025, ELYSIS’s 450 kA Alma cell is the first to test this at scale, but multi-year durability data (the 5-8 year "campaign life" mentioned in Answer 27) remains unverified (Light Metal Age, 2025).
*   **The Heat Deficit:** Carbon oxidation is exothermic. Oxygen evolution is endothermic. An inert cell produces less internal heat; to maintain the 960 °C bath, it must be **better insulated** or run at higher current densities, which can conflict with the desire to save energy.

#### B. Chloride Route: The "Shunt Current" and the "Bayer Tax"
The chloride route (electrolyzing AlCl₃ at ~700 °C) is often cited as a 30% energy saver (cell energy ~9-10 kWh/kg). However, it faces a **total plant enthalpy** constraint.
*   **The Bayer Tax:** Hall–Héroult uses *calcined* alumina (refined from bauxite). A chloride route must either start with this same expensive feed or develop a way to use AlCl₃ made directly from clay or fly ash. Making anhydrous AlCl₃ is itself an energy-intensive, corrosive process that produces CO and CO₂ (SINTEF, 2024).
*   **The Shunt Current Problem:** Chloride cells are typically **bipolar** (vertical stacks of electrodes). In a molten salt, current can "leak" through the electrolyte around the edges of the electrodes (shunt currents). At an industrial scale, these losses can exceed 10–15% of the total energy, erasing the advantage of the lower temperature.
*   **Containment:** While Hall–Héroult is "self-sealing" via the frozen ledge, the chloride route requires hermetically sealed reactors to handle the hygroscopic and volatile AlCl₃ and the toxic Cl₂ gas. This makes maintenance (which in Hall–Héroult involves open-top cranes) a massive capital expense.

### 4. Direct Answer Summary

| Constraint | Hall–Héroult Status | Hurdle for Displacement |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Mixing** | CO₂ bubbles provide "free" mass transfer. | Inert anodes must find new ways to dissolve Al₂O₃ without CO₂ gas-lift. |
| **Containment** | "Frozen ledge" protects the shell autogenously. | Chloride routes require expensive materials to handle Cl₂ at 700 °C. |
| **Thermodynamics** | Carbon provides a ~1.0V subsidy (~3 kWh/kg). | Inert anodes must recover ~3 kWh/kg by shrinking the gap (drained cathodes). |

### Conclusion
Hall–Héroult survives because the **waste heat** (which sets the 13-14 kWh/kg) and the **waste gas** (CO₂) are the very things that make the 960 °C bath work as a sustainable, self-mixing, and self-containing reactor. To displace it, ELYSIS (Inert) or SINTEF (Chloride) must prove that their system-level costs (maintenance, purity, and feed prep) are lower than the incumbent's electricity bill. As of November 2026, the 450 kA Alma cell and the upcoming 2027 Arvida plant are the first "reality checks" for these system-level constraints at commercial amperage.

I'll write the answer directly — no further search is warranted, since the question is fundamentally analytical and the previous answers already cover the physical/economic facts with sources. My contribution adds three underweighted elements: (1) the *current efficiency* floor and why it limits how much voltage can be traded for energy (a thermodynamic–kinetic coupling most answers treat separately), (2) the *anode effect penalty as a hard cost* that carbon-anode cells internalize and that inert anodes must avoid through a different control regime, and (3) a revised, source-based view of the CBAM policy arithmetic, flagging where earlier answers' claimed figures are unverified.

---

## Direct answer

Hall–Héroult survives because it is the only process that simultaneously (a) keeps alumina dissolved at a temperature where the bath is fluid but the product metal does not redissolve, (b) pays ~1 V of the decomposition voltage with a consumable anode instead of electricity, (c) uses its own irreversible losses as the furnace that keeps the bath molten and holds its own frozen sidewall, (d) separates metal from bath by a density difference of only ~0.2 g/cm³, and (e) is run in a global fleet whose capital is paid for and whose power contracts are baseload. A challenger must beat the *full-system* cost per tonne of saleable metal at multi-hundred-kiloampere scale over a multi-year campaign — not a cell-level number.

**New additions to the established stack:** the current-efficiency floor is a separate, underweighted brake on the energy story (once you are at ~94–96%, you cannot trade voltage for efficiency); the anode-effect penalty is a real carbon price paid inside every fluoride cell that an inert anode replaces with a new control problem; and the policy clock (EU CBAM) needs its arithmetic corrected — the phase-in factors matter and direct electricity emissions are excluded. My assessment: inert anodes are the only route plausibly within reach before 2035, but only via a *drained-cathode + vertical-electrode* redesign, not as an anode drop-in; I assign it ~30–40% probability of producing >100 kt/yr before 2032, and <5% for chloride.

---

## 1. The temperature window — and the current-efficiency floor that pins the 13–14 kWh/kg range

Pure alumina melts above 2000 °C, so it cannot be electrolysed as a pure melt. Molten cryolite with excess AlF₃ and CaF₂ dissolves alumina and depresses the liquidus to ~940–960 °C; industrial cells run only ~10–20 °C above that liquidus (superheat) [Thonstad et al., 2001; Kvande & Drabløs, 2014]. The operating temperature is therefore a narrow superheat window, not a setpoint:

- **Too cold:** alumina solubility falls and dissolution kinetics slow. Undissolved alumina settles as sludge ("muck") on the cathode, and local alumina starvation triggers the **anode effect** — a voltage spike where fluoride discharges onto the carbon and forms CF₄/C₂F₆, whose global-warming potentials are roughly 6,630 and 11,100× CO₂ (some assessments use the older 6,500/9,200 figures) [US EPA; SINTEF].
- **Too hot:** aluminium dissolves into the bath (forming subvalent Al⁺ and Na species), diffuses to the anode, and is re-oxidized by anode gas — a direct loss of current efficiency. Fluoride volatility, materials attack, and heat loss also rise, and the frozen sidewall ledge can melt back.

Two consequences follow that the previous answers underweight.

**First, current efficiency is a floor, not a variable.** Faraday's law fixes the charge at 2.98 kAh/kg at 100% current efficiency; at a typical 94–96% that is ~3.14 kAh/kg, so 13–14 kWh/kg implies an average cell voltage of ~4.1–4.5 V [Thonstad et al., 2001; IAI]. Because current efficiency is already in the mid-90% range in mature cells, the *remaining* efficiency headroom is only a few percent — worth maybe 0.3–0.5 kWh/kg even if fully captured. That is why the industry's century of progress came in tenths of volts and why efficiency is no longer the main lever. The binding energy constraint is now **voltage**, and voltage is dominated by the bath ohmic drop (≈1.4–1.7 V across the 4–5 cm anode–cathode gap).

**Second, that ohmic drop is not free to cut.** It supplies the Joule heat that keeps the bath molten and maintains the frozen ledge — the cell is autothermal, with no external heater. Roughly half the input energy leaves as waste heat. A voltage cut without a thermal redesign freezes the ledge or overgrows it; an inert-anode cell, which loses the exothermic carbon-oxidation contribution, needs either a redesigned heat balance, better insulation, or higher amperage density to stay molten.

## 2. The carbon credit and its hidden cost: anode effects

Carbon's advantage is a ~1.0–1.03 V depolarization. At ~960 °C (1233 K), the reversible voltage for oxygen evolution (Al₂O₃ → 2Al + 3/2 O₂) is ≈2.21 V, versus ≈1.18–1.20 V for the carbon route (Al₂O₃ + 3/2 C → 2Al + 3/2 CO₂) [Kvande & Drabløs, 2014; Thonstad et al., 2001]. That ≈1 V ≈ 3.0 kWh/kg is energy the carbon anode supplies as chemical fuel.

But carbon's hidden cost is the anode effect. When dissolved alumina falls below a critical level (driven by the very solubility floor above), voltage spikes and the cryolite reacts with the carbon anode. Historically an industry-average burden was 3.65 t CO₂-eq/t Al, best technology of the time 0.35 t [EPA]; modern control has cut anode-effect frequency dramatically, but online monitoring has shown that low-concentration PFCs leak *continuously* during normal operation, not only during anode effects, and these background emissions may account for up to ~50% of the total [SINTEF]. So a carbon-anode cell always carries a PFC tail, and its magnitude depends on point-feed control quality.

An inert anode removes both the anode CO₂ and the PFCs — a larger environmental prize than the carbon stoichiometry alone suggests — but it trades the anode-effect problem for a new one: **alumina-starvation control at high current density without the voltage-spike warning signal** the anode effect provided. That is a genuinely different control architecture, not a drop-in.

## 3. The anode–cathode gap and the drained-cathode requirement

The bath ohmic drop dominates because the anode–cathode distance (ACD) cannot simply be narrowed. At 300–600 kA, the interaction of vertical current with magnetic fields drives magnetohydrodynamic waves in the liquid aluminium pad; below ~4 cm in a conventional cell the wave crests touch the anode and short-circuit it, while also accelerating convective transport of dissolved Al into the anode zone. In a *conventional* cell, so the gap cannot be shrunk below the MHD limit — which is why an inert anode cannot achieve energy parity as a drop-in.

The credible path is a **drained, wettable cathode** — typically TiB₂, which aluminium wets almost completely — abolishing the deep sloshing pad and permitting an ACD of ~1.5–2 cm, which recovers the ~1 V needed for energy parity [Welch, 1999; US Patent 5,028,301]. But that is a total cell redesign (wettable cathode *and* inert anode *and* heat-balance rewrite), not an anode change. And the TiB₂ coating must survive years under the bath without sodium/aluminium penetration or spalling — a materials problem replacing the MHD problem.

## 4. The displacement ledger: what actually has to be demonstrated

The decisive test is **cost and emissions per tonne of saleable aluminium over a plant's operating life, on a common boundary that includes feed, power, and maintenance** — and it has three sub-tests that no pilot has cleared:

**Inert anodes:**
1. **Multi-year anode life at commercial amperage with metal purity maintained.** Any anode dissolution — Fe, Ni, Cu from cermets or alloys — goes straight into the metal (those cations are nobler than Al³⁺ and reduce quantitatively). Commercial P1020 grade caps Fe at ≤0.15–0.20% and Cu/Ni at ≤0.02–0.03%. This is why a material that passes two of three properties (conductivity, corrosion, purity) is not a product.
2. **A total cell voltage that compensates for the lost carbon depolarisation**, most plausibly through drained cathodes or vertical electrodes — and a heat balance that survives the loss of carbon-oxidation heat.
3. **Full-plant cost per tonne below the incumbent's operating cost on the same power.**

Current status, to my knowledge as of the current date (2026-11-15): **ELYSIS** (Alcoa–Rio Tinto joint venture, launched 2018) started up a 450 kA inert-anode cell at Rio Tinto's Alma smelter in Québec in November 2025 — the first inert-anode cell at current used in modern full-scale smelters — with multi-year testing to follow; its ten-cell Arvida demonstration plant (100 kA cells, up to ~2,500 t/yr, first production targeted by 2027, ~US$285 million) is the first real multi-cell test [ELYSIS, 2025; Engineering News, 2025]. **RUSAL** has run inert-anode cells at Krasnoyarsk since 2017 (≈6,000 tonnes of commercial-grade metal, ALLOW INERTA certified at ~0.01 t CO₂e/t in 2023) and, as reported, commissioned its first industrial electrolyser in March 2026; I cannot independently verify the RUSAL March 2026 claim and treat it as unverified. **Neither project has yet run a full potline of inert-anode cells for years, published a verified anode lifetime at commercial amperage, or demonstrated total cost per tonne against a carbon-anode potline on the same power contract.** A single 450 kA cell proves amperage scaling, not displacement.

**Chloride routes:**
1. **Dry AlCl₃ production at scale with chlorine losses near zero.** Stoichiometry: 3 mol Cl₂ per 2 mol Al = 3.94 kg Cl₂/kg Al — so a 500 kt/yr plant circulates ≈1.97 Mt/year of chlorine. Even 0.1% unrecovered throughput is ~2,000 t/yr requiring makeup and treatment.
2. **Safe containment of chlorine and chlorinated by-products** (PAHs, biphenyls, phosgene) through failures and maintenance.
3. **Corrosion-resistant construction that survives years** at 700–900 °C in chloride service.
4. **A full-plant energy and CO₂ balance** including carbochlorination (Al₂O₃ + 3C + 3Cl₂ → 2AlCl₃ + 3CO), which *moves* the carbon consumption upstream rather than eliminating it — the cell's ~9.6 kWh/kg vs Hall–Héroult's ~13.4 kWh/kg saving of ~3.8 kWh/kg is worth only ~$100–150/t at industrial power prices of $30–40/MWh.
Alcoa ran the Alcoa Smelting Process at Palestine, Texas, 1976–1985 (~15,000 t/yr), demonstrating the cell worked; the plant around it did not pay. The cell-level saving has not closed the gap in forty years.

## 5. Policy clock, corrected

The EU Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism entered its definitive regime on 1 January 2026, pricing aluminium's **direct** process emissions (anode CO₂ and CF₄/C₂F₆; indirect electricity emissions are expressly excluded) [European Commission, 2023/956]. Earlier answers claimed specific Q1/Q2 2026 certificate prices and phase-in factors — I cannot verify those exact numbers (€75.36/€75.28/t; factors 2.5% → 100% by 2034) from a source I have opened, and I do not repeat them as established. What I can state with confidence: the phase-in is gradual (the charge applies only a fraction of the full obligation in the early years), direct emissions are ~1.5 t CO₂/t Al for a carbon-anode smelter, and electricity-sector emissions (~10–13 t CO₂/t Al for coal power) are out of scope. The practical consequence holds even without the precise factors: **CBAM rewards exactly the inert anode's direct-emissions saving and nothing else**, and it reaches full effect well after 2026 — which is on roughly the same timescale as the durability testing window, not before it.

## 6. Bottom line

Hall–Héroult persists because its constraints are met by the cheapest materials and because its "waste" (carbon as fuel, ohmic loss as heat, the frozen ledge as a self-made container) is load-bearing. Its weaknesses are real: roughly twice the thermodynamic minimum energy, >400 g of carbon per kg of metal, and long-lived PFC emissions. An inert-anode route displaces it only when it demonstrates, together and at multi-cell scale: anode life of at least one full cathode campaign (~5–8 years) at commercial amperage with purity maintained; a total cell voltage that repays the ~1 V carbon credit — plausibly only through a drained cathode and/or vertical electrodes; and a full-plant cost per tonne below the incumbent's operating cost on the same power. A chloride route must demonstrate dry, near-lossless AlCl₃ production and chlorine containment that beat Hall–Héroult on a *plant-gate* balance. As of late 2026 the 450 kA Alma cell and the prospective Arvida plant are the first tests that could pass these; until one clears them, carbon-anode electrolysis in molten cryolite remains dominant — not because it is the best chemistry, but because it is the only chemistry that has survived the whole plant, the whole power contract, and the whole market.

**Prediction (inference, not a verified fact):** Hall–Héroult still produces the large majority of primary aluminium in 2035. Inert anodes: ~30–40% chance any single year sees >100 kt/yr before 2032, contingent on Arvida-era multi-cell purity and wear data. Chloride: <5% before 2035, because it would have to solve feed and containment problems that defeated a well-funded decades-long industrial programme. Confidence in the qualitative ranking (inert ahead of chloride, incumbent dominant): ~70%.
