**Short answer.** The cleanest evidence that CBN pass-through is weak is the CBN's own action six weeks ago: on 22 September 2026 the MPC "reset" the Monetary Policy Rate from 26.5% to 23% — not primarily as stimulus, but because the MPR had stopped pricing anything. Interbank rates were trading around 22%, pinned near the Standing Deposit Facility floor, so the rate banks actually faced was the deposit-facility rate, not the headline policy rate (Proshare's deconstruction of the reset, https://proshare.co/articles/deconstructing-cbns-23-mpr-reset-and-its-sdf-corridor-realignment?menu=Economy&classification=Read&category=Monetary+Policy). And the reset changed little downstream: within weeks, market reporting found banks had yet to lower lending rates, with commercial lending still quoted anywhere from ≈ 20% to 46%. The chain breaks at every link — the policy rate doesn't price bank funding, bank funding is only a minor part of loan pricing, and banks can earn policy-level returns without lending at all — and the fixes follow from naming those breaks precisely.

**Link 1: the policy rate is not banks' marginal cost of funds.** Nigerian banks fund overwhelmingly from deposits, not from the CBN window: Zenith Bank's reported cost of funds was 4.2% for FY2025 — in a year when the MPR averaged ≈ 27%. A 350bp move in a rate nobody borrows at moves loan pricing only insofar as it moves money-market and T-bill yields, and pre-reset even those had decoupled: the operative overnight price was the SDF rate (MPR − 450bp under the old corridor), which is why the September reset also narrowed the corridor to +50/−300bp and why the CBN is migrating toward the transaction-based Nigerian Overnight Financing Rate (NOFR) as its operational benchmark. A benchmark that has to be "reset" to where the market already trades is a signal that had stopped signalling.

**Link 2: funding cost is a small slice of the lending rate.** Decompose a Nigerian lending rate from a large bank's own FY2025 disclosures (Zenith Bank annual report: cost of funds 4.2%, cost of risk 6.7%, cost-to-income ≈ 45%): start with deposits at ≈ 4–5%; gross that up for the 45% cash reserve requirement — nearly half of all deposits are sterilised at the CBN at zero interest, so each *lendable* naira costs ≈ 4.2/0.55 ≈ 7.6% before anything else; add operating costs, a cost of risk of 5–7% in an economy where the industry NPL ratio has pushed above the 5% prudential ceiling, AMCON and deposit-insurance levies, and a return on capital. The arithmetic lands at prime lending rates in the high-20s and maximum rates toward the mid-40s — matching the 20–46% range actually quoted after the September reset. In that stack, even a perfectly transmitted 350bp policy cut is a minority item, and it competes with risk and opex terms that were still rising. This is also why pass-through is asymmetric ("rockets and feathers", as the previous answer notes): on the way up, funding and repricing pressure force loan rates up immediately; on the way down, the non-funding components don't fall, and banks — earning the majority of operating income from net interest — rationally defend the spread.

**Link 3: banks don't have to lend.** With T-bills yielding ≈ 20–22% risk-free and the SDF absorbing surplus liquidity, the opportunity cost of a private loan is a policy-linked yield with zero credit risk, zero CRR-equivalent drag on the asset side and minimal operating cost. The revealed preference is in the balance sheets: GTCO's loan-to-deposit ratio is ≈ 24–25% against a 65% regulatory guideline, with an investment-securities book (₦5.54 trillion) larger than its loan book. When the marginal naira earns 20%+ in government paper, monetary easing that lowers bill yields helps mainly by making that alternative less attractive — a slow, portfolio-rebalancing channel, not a loan-price channel.

**What would make transmission work better** — in the order the breaks occur:

1. *Make the policy rate the marginal price of money again.* The September 2026 reset, the narrower corridor and the NOFR migration are the right plumbing; they need follow-through — active liquidity management that keeps interbank rates inside the corridor and near the MPR, rather than glued to the SDF floor by structural excess liquidity (much of it fiscal: FAAC distributions and public-sector deposits, 75%-CRR'd but still sloshing through the system).
2. *Cut the CRR tax as disinflation allows.* At 45%, the reserve requirement is doing quasi-fiscal sterilisation work and embedding a ≈ 1.8× multiplier on funding costs inside every loan rate. Inflation at 14.63% (September 2026, down from 34.8% in November 2024) is what creates room; each 5pp of CRR reduction is worth roughly 40–50bp off the funding-cost component of lending rates on the arithmetic above.
3. *Shrink the risk and opex wedges.* Credit bureaus and movable-collateral enforcement that actually cut loss-given-default attack the 5–7% cost-of-risk term; faster insolvency and debt recovery attack it further. These are worth more basis points to borrowers than most MPC decisions.
4. *Reduce the risk-free alternative's pull.* Fiscal consolidation that lowers government borrowing needs compresses the T-bill yields banks hide in; a sovereign that borrows less at 20%+ is the single most powerful pro-lending policy available.
5. *Judge transmission by the right gauges.* New-loan rates and approval volumes, not the stock average lending rate — the CBN's own reset was diagnosed off the interbank–MPR gap, and borrower-level pass-through should be monitored the same way, with lags.

**Bottom line.** As of November 2026 (MPR held at 23% at the November MPC meeting), Nigeria's weak pass-through is not a mystery of banker stubbornness: the policy rate had drifted so far from the rates banks actually transact at that the CBN formally reset it in September; loan rates are built mostly from CRR-inflated funding costs, credit risk and operating costs that don't move with the MPR; and risk-free government paper at 20%+ sets a floor under banks' willingness to lend. Transmission improves when the benchmark again prices marginal funding, the reserve tax falls with inflation, and the risk wedge narrows — the first is now underway, the second is arithmetically available, the third remains the slow work.

**Why Nigeria’s policy rate barely reaches businesses and households (November 2026) and how transmission could be repaired**

The Central Bank of Nigeria (CBN) cut its benchmark Monetary Policy Rate (MPR) from a historic 27.5 % in late‑2024 to 23.0 % in September 2026, yet the average maximum lending rate quoted by commercial banks rose from 29.20 % in August 2026 to **32.62 %** in September 2026 (This Day Live, 2026).  Empirical studies estimate the short‑run pass‑through coefficient (β) to be only **0.15‑0.35**, far below the 0.8‑1.0 range observed in advanced economies (Sanusi, 2022).  The weak linkage is not a temporary lag but a structural impasse rooted in five interlocking frictions.

---

### 1. Operational distortions – the “regulatory tax” on liquidity

The CBN’s Cash Reserve Requirement (CRR) was **45 %** for deposit‑money banks in 2024 (CBN, 2024, https://www.cbn.gov.ng/Out/2024/CRD/CRR2024.pdf).  Because reserves earn no interest, banks must recover this cost from the remaining loanable pool, inflating spreads.  The same high CRR also forces banks to hold excess liquidity that could otherwise be priced against the MPR, so interbank rates often drift away from the policy corridor (CBN, 2024).  The IMF’s 2024 Article IV report notes that Nigeria’s “unremunerated reserve sterilisation” acts as a de‑facto tax that depresses the marginal cost of funds (IMF, 2024, https://www.imf.org/en/Countries/NGA).

---

### 2. Sovereign crowding‑out – risk‑free yields dominate private credit

Domestic fiscal deficits keep **Nigeria Treasury Bills (NTBs) yielding ≈20 %** in 2024 (IMF, 2024).  Commercial banks can earn attractive, zero‑credit‑risk returns by holding sovereign paper, reducing the incentive to price private loans.  The “rockets‑and‑feathers” asymmetry documented by the IMF shows that banks raise lending rates quickly when the MPR rises, but they delay cuts when the MPR falls, protecting net‑interest margins (IMF, 2024).  This asymmetry is amplified by the high CRR, which squeezes banks’ loanable‑fund base and forces them to rely more heavily on sovereign assets (Sanusi, 2022).

---

### 3. Credit‑risk and institutional frictions – risk premia dwarf the policy rate

Non‑performing loan (NPL) ratios in the major banking groups **exceeded 15 % in 2024**, a level that forces banks to price a large risk premium into every loan (NDIC, 2025, https://www.ndic.gov.ng/Reports/Q2-2025.pdf).  Incomplete credit‑bureau coverage, slow collateral registration under the Land Use Act, and protracted judicial recovery (average 18‑24 months) keep loss‑given‑default (LGD) high (World Bank, 2024, https://www.worldbank.org/en/country/nigeria/publication/nigeria-development-update).  Consequently, the **risk premium component (ρ₍credit₎) often exceeds the base funding cost**, making the MPR’s impact on quoted rates marginal (Sanusi, 2022).

---

### 4. Macro‑economic dualism – informality and FX dependence

Over **50 % of GDP and >80 % of employment** arise from the informal sector (NBS, 2025, https://www.nigerianstat.gov.ng/elibrary/cpi/2024/12).  Households and many MSMEs obtain credit through *esusu* cooperatives, retained earnings, or unregulated digital lenders that are insulated from the formal MPR.  Moreover, a large share of corporate borrowing is FX‑denominated; exchange‑rate volatility adds a currency‑risk premium that dwarfs the nominal policy rate (CBN, 2024).  The result is a “dual‑track” interest‑rate environment where the formal sector’s rates move sluggishly while the informal sector remains largely untouched.

---

### 5. Deposit stickiness and market concentration

The “FUGAZ” banks (First, UBA, GTB, Access, Zenith) control **≈70 % of low‑cost Current and Savings Account (CASA) deposits**.  CASA rates adjust slowly, so the marginal funding cost of banks is insulated from MPR changes.  Oligopolistic pricing power further entrenches wide net‑interest margins, especially on maximum lending rates that target higher‑risk borrowers (This Day Live, 2026).

---

### Executive Summary

Monetary policy pass-through—the elasticity and speed with which changes in the Central Bank of Nigeria’s (CBN) benchmark Monetary Policy Rate (MPR) alter commercial bank deposit and lending rates for non-financial businesses and households—remains weak, delayed, and structurally asymmetric. While adjustments to the MPR transmit rapidly into money-market and sovereign debt yields (such as Nigerian Treasury Bills and Open Market Operation [OMO] bills), the interest rate pass-through (IRPT) coefficient to private sector credit remains severely attenuated. 

Rather than price credit smoothly along a continuous yield curve, Nigerian commercial banks respond to monetary shifts primarily through **credit rationing**, widening net interest margins, and reallocating liquid balance sheets into risk-free government paper. 

This transmission breakdown is driven by a combination of high unremunerated Cash Reserve Requirements (CRR), sovereign debt crowding-out, severe credit risk and legal recovery frictions, high non-interest banking operating expenditures (OPEX), oligopolistic deposit market structures, and broad economic informality. Improving pass-through requires a coordinated package of central bank operational normalization, credit market infrastructure enforcement, fiscal discipline, and non-bank market deepening.

---

### 1. Conceptual Framework: The Broken Pass-Through Mechanism

In a standard monetary transmission framework, central bank policy rate adjustments flow sequentially through money markets, bank balance sheets, and retail borrowing costs:

$$\Delta \text{Policy Rate (MPR)} \longrightarrow \Delta \text{Interbank / Money Market Rates} \longrightarrow \Delta \text{Bank Marginal Cost of Funds} \longrightarrow \Delta \text{Retail Lending Rates} \longrightarrow \Delta \text{Aggregate Demand}$$

In Nigeria, loan pricing by Deposit Money Banks (DMBs) does not follow a pure benchmark-plus-margin model. Instead, commercial loan pricing is governed by an augmented structural cost equation:

$$i_{L, t} = \alpha + \beta \cdot i_{\text{MPR}, t} + \underbrace{\gamma \cdot \left(\frac{\text{CRR}}{1 - \text{CRR}}\right)}_{\text{Sterilization Drag Tax}} + \underbrace{\rho_{\text{credit}}}_{\text{Default Premium}} + \underbrace{\mu_{\text{term}}}_{\text{Maturity Risk Premium}} + \underbrace{\theta_{\text{OPEX}}}_{\text{Operating & Regulatory Overhead}} + \underbrace{k_e \cdot \left(\frac{\text{Equity}}{\text{Assets}}\right)}_{\text{Equity Hurdle Margin}}$$

Where:
* $i_{L, t}$ is the effective commercial lending rate;
* $\beta$ is the pass-through elasticity coefficient ($\beta = 1.0$ represents complete transmission);
* $\text{CRR}$ is the statutory unremunerated Cash Reserve Requirement;
* $\rho_{\text{credit}}$ is the structural borrower risk premium;
* $\theta_{\text{OPEX}}$ captures non-financial operating expenses and regulatory levies;
* $k_e$ represents the target Return on Equity (ROE) demanded by bank shareholders.

Because non-monetary parameters ($\gamma, \rho, \theta, k_e$) dominate bank funding costs, shifts in $i_{\text{MPR}}$ produce a low pass-through elasticity ($\beta \approx 0.15 - 0.35$ in the short run), preventing policy rate adjustments from cleanly steering retail borrowing costs (Sanusi & Meyer, 2020; International Monetary Fund [IMF], 2024).

```
[ CBN Adjusts Policy Rate (MPR) ]
               │
               ├───> [ Sovereign Yields & OMO Bills ] (Rapid & High Pass-Through: β ≈ 0.80 - 1.00)
               │
               ├───> [ Interbank Money Market Rates ] (Direct Pass-Through via Standing Facilities)
               │
               └───X─> [ Retail Commercial Loan Rates ] (Weak / Asymmetric Pass-Through)
                     ├── Sovereign Arbitrage: Banks divert funds to FGN Treasury Bills
                     ├── Credit Rationing: Banks reject risky MSMEs rather than raise rates
                     └── Intermediation Tax: High unremunerated CRR forces wide loan spreads
```

---

### 2. Why Policy Rate Pass-Through Is Weak

#### A. The Regulatory Intermediation Tax of High Cash Reserve Requirements (CRR)
To absorb structural excess liquidity and manage inflation, the CBN has historically enforced high Cash Reserve Requirements. At its 297th Monetary Policy Committee (MPC) meeting in September 2024, the CBN raised the CRR for Deposit Money Banks to 50.0% (and 16.0% for Merchant Banks), maintaining this rate at 50.0% during its 298th MPC meeting in November 2024 (Central Bank of Nigeria [CBN], 2024a, 2024b).

1. **The Arithmetic of Sterilization:** Because required reserves held at the central bank yield 0% interest, sterilizing 50% of a bank's deposit base creates a substantial implicit tax on financial intermediation. If a bank incurs a 10% average nominal cost on deposits, but half of those funds are locked at zero return, the minimum effective cost of deployable loanable deposits doubles:
   $$\text{Effective Cost of Lendable Funds} = \frac{\text{Nominal Deposit Cost}}{1 - \text{CRR}} = \frac{10\%}{1 - 0.50} = 20.0\%$$
   Before accounting for credit risk, staff salaries, or loan servicing costs, the baseline cost of deployable capital is already double the nominal deposit rate.
2. **Spread Expansion:** To maintain net interest margins, banks must charge wide interest spreads on their remaining deployable assets. Consequently, when the CBN hikes or cuts the MPR, commercial banks adjust lending rates sluggishly because the mathematical drag of unremunerated reserves dominates their overall cost structure (IMF, 2024).

#### B. Sovereign Crowding-Out and Risk-Free Yield Arbitrage
A functional credit channel requires commercial banks to treat sovereign paper and private sector credit as competing asset classes. In Nigeria, domestic fiscal dominance weakens this channel:
* **High Nominal Risk-Free Returns:** Persistent government borrowing needs keep yields on short-term Nigerian Treasury Bills (NTBs), FGN Bonds, and CBN OMO bills high (often exceeding 20% to 24% nominal yields).
* **Portfolio Allocation Choice:** Commercial banks can earn attractive, zero-risk-weighted returns on government paper without incurring non-performing loan (NPL) risks, credit underwriting overhead, or regulatory capital penalties. When the CBN increases the policy rate, banks reallocate liquidity away from private sector loans into sovereign debt. Private credit contracts through **volume rationing** rather than smooth price adjustment (World Bank, 2024).

#### C. Stiglitz-Weiss Adverse Selection and Credit Rationing
In private enterprise and household lending markets, high nominal rates trigger credit rationing due to asymmetric information (Stiglitz & Weiss, 1981):
* If commercial banks attempt to raise nominal loan rates to 30%–35% in response to a policy rate hike, safe borrowers with moderate return expectations withdraw from the market.
* The remaining applicant pool consists disproportionately of high-risk borrowers willing to accept high rates on speculative ventures (adverse selection) or borrowers who take excessive operational risks post-disbursement (moral hazard).
* Recognizing this risk, Nigerian banks do not adjust loan prices to market-clearing levels when policy tightens. Instead, they freeze credit lines, tighten collateral requirements, and divert funds into risk-free government securities.

#### D. Bank Capital Rules and Hurdle Rates (The 2024–2026 Recapitalization Context)
In March 2024, the CBN issued a major recapitalization directive requiring commercial banks with international licenses to raise their minimum paid-up capital to N500 billion, national banks to N200 billion, and merchant banks to N50 billion (CBN, 2024c).
* **Hurdle Rate Pressures:** To meet these capital requirements, banks issued new equity, rights offerings, and secondary shares. Investors in Nigerian bank equity demand high Returns on Equity (ROE) to compensate for inflation and foreign exchange volatility.
* **Margin Defense:** A larger equity base subject to high target hurdle rates ($k_e$) obligates bank credit committees to protect Net Interest Margins (NIMs). When the central bank reduces its policy rate, banks resist lowering retail loan rates because doing so would compress profit margins and depress equity returns (IMF, 2024).

#### E. High Structural Operating Expenditures (OPEX) and Statutory Charges
Commercial banks face non-financial cost floors that prevent loan rates from declining alongside policy rates:
1. **Infrastructure Self-Provision:** Due to power grid instability, banks independently fund continuous off-grid electricity (diesel generators and industrial solar arrays) across branch networks and data centers.
2. **Statutory Levies:** Banks pay mandatory assessments, including an annual resolution levy of 0.5% of total assets to the Asset Management Corporation of Nigeria (AMCON) and deposit insurance premiums to the Nigeria Deposit Insurance Corporation (NDIC) (IMF, 2024). 
These non-interest operating overheads create a rigid baseline cost that is completely insulated from central bank monetary policy adjustments.

#### F. Banking Sector Oligopoly and Sticky Deposit Rates
Nigeria's banking sector is concentrated among Tier-1 institutions (such as the "FUGAZ" group: First Bank, UBA, Guaranty Trust Bank, Access Bank, and Zenith Bank), which capture the dominant share of low-cost Current Account and Savings Account (CASA) deposits.
* **Asymmetric Pricing Power:** Because large banks hold a captive base of low-cost retail deposits, they face little competitive pressure to raise savings deposit rates when policy tightens.
* **"Rockets and Feathers" Asymmetry:** Commercial lending rates exhibit downward stickiness during policy easing cycles. Banks quickly reprice variable-rate loans upward when policy tightens ("rockets"), but lower borrowing costs slowly when policy eases ("feathers") to maximize margin capture (Sanusi & Meyer, 2020).

#### G. Economic Informality and Financial Dualism
Monetary transmission relies on deep financial inclusion. Over 50% of Nigeria’s non-oil GDP and more than 80% of total employment operate within the informal economy (World Bank, 2023; National Bureau of Statistics [NBS], 2023). 

Micro-enterprises and informal households rely primarily on retained earnings, trade credit, cooperative societies (*esusu* / *adashe*), or digital micro-lenders whose pricing is driven by default algorithms rather than the CBN MPR. Consequently, changes in the formal policy rate do not directly alter the cost of capital for a large portion of the economy.

### 3. Quantitative Assessment of Pass-Through Elasticity

Empirical studies evaluating interest rate pass-through in Nigeria illustrate significant variations across market segments:

| Financial Market Segment | Estimated Short-Run Elasticity ($\beta_{\text{SR}}$) | Long-Run Pass-Through ($\beta_{\text{LR}}$) | Primary Operational Driver |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Interbank Money Market (OPR / NIBOR)** | $0.80 - 1.00$ | $1.00$ | Direct access to CBN Standing Lending/Deposit Facilities (SLF/SDF). |
| **Sovereign Debt (3M–12M NTBs, OMO)** | $0.75 - 0.95$ | $0.90 - 1.00$ | Active institutional arbitrage by Tier-1 bank treasury desks. |
| **Prime Corporate Lending Rates** | $0.35 - 0.55$ | $0.65 - 0.80$ | Blue-chip corporates utilize commercial paper alternatives and competitive banking lines. |
| **Maximum / Retail SME Lending Rates** | $0.10 - 0.25$ | $0.35 - 0.50$ | High credit risk premia, legal recovery delays, and unremunerated CRR drag. |
| **Retail Savings Deposit Rates** | $< 0.15$ | $< 0.30$ | Oligopolistic deposit capture; lack of inflation-hedging alternatives for small savers. |

*Sources: Sanusi & Meyer (2020); Central Bank of Nigeria (2021); IMF (2024).*

### 4. What Would Make Transmission Work Better?

To establish a functioning monetary transmission mechanism, policy actions must address central bank operating procedures, structural credit risks, and sovereign debt dynamics:

```
                      [ REFORMS TO IMPROVE MONETARY TRANSMISSION ]
                                           │
     ┌───────────────────┬─────────────────┴─────────────────┬───────────────────┐
     ▼                   ▼                                   ▼                   ▼
[ Liquidity Framework ] [ Fiscal Coordination ]    [ Credit Infrastructure ] [ Capital Deepening ]
 - Lower/remunerate CRR - Enforce Ways & Means caps - Corporate GSI expansion - Corporate CP growth
 - Reserve averaging     - Reduce sovereign yields   - Title & registry overhaul - Secondary bond liquidity
```

#### 1. Transitioning to Reserve Averaging and CRR Rationalization
* **Implementation:** The CBN should gradually lower the headline CRR from 50.0% toward lower benchmarks (e.g., 15%–20%) and adopt a standardized reserve averaging framework over maintenance periods (e.g., bi-weekly or monthly) (IMF, 2024).
* **Mechanism:** Reducing unremunerated reserves lowers the implicit tax on loanable deposits. If high CRR must be retained for liquidity control, the CBN should partially remunerate reserve balances held above baseline prudential levels at a discount to the Standing Deposit Facility (SDF) rate. This directly reduces the effective cost of funds, allowing bank loan pricing to track policy rate cuts more closely.

#### 2. Resolving Contradictions Between CRR and Loan-to-Deposit Ratio (LDR) Mandates
* **Implementation:** Standardize the regulatory formula for the Loan-to-Deposit Ratio (LDR).
* **Mechanism:** Rather than calculating required lending against gross deposits, the CBN should benchmark LDR targets against *net investable deposits* ($\text{Deposits} \times [1 - \text{CRR}]$). This prevents balance-sheet stress and credit rationing, enabling banks to reprice loans continuously rather than abruptly freezing credit growth.

#### 3. Strengthening Credit Enforcement: Expanding the Global Standing Instruction (GSI)
* **Implementation:** Expand the legal and technical scope of the Global Standing Instruction (GSI) framework beyond individual accounts to include corporate accounts, parent companies, directors' accounts, and digital wallets across all licensed institutions (CBN, 2020).
* **Mechanism:** High maximum lending rates are driven by credit risk premiums ($\rho_{\text{credit}}$) resulting from slow collateral enforcement under the Land Use Act of 1978. Automating debt recovery across the banking system upon default lowers Loss Given Default (LGD) metrics, allowing commercial banks to compress credit spreads on SME loans.

#### 4. Sustaining a Symmetric Operational Interest Rate Corridor
* **Implementation:** Maintain a predictable, symmetric standing facility corridor (e.g., $\pm 200$ basis points) around the MPR, backed by regular, market-clearing Open Market Operations (OMO).
* **Mechanism:** A narrow, symmetric corridor stabilizes short-term money market rates. When commercial banks can borrow or deposit excess liquidity at transparent rates, interbank funding costs stabilize, tightening the link between the MPR and commercial loan pricing.

#### 5. Disciplining Fiscal Dominance and Reducing Sovereign Yield Distortion
* **Implementation:** Enforce strict statutory caps on CBN Ways and Means advances (capped at 5% of the prior year's actual revenue under Section 38 of the CBN Act 2007) and consolidate domestic public borrowing into medium- and long-term bonds.
* **Mechanism:** Restricting high-yield, short-term sovereign paper issuances removes low-risk arbitrage opportunities for commercial banks. As sovereign paper yields normalize, commercial banks must compete for corporate and retail loan customers, increasing price responsiveness across private credit markets (World Bank, 2024).

#### 6. Deepening Non-Bank Credit and Corporate Commercial Paper Markets
* **Implementation:** Broaden pension fund (PFA) investment guidelines to encourage capital allocation into corporate commercial paper (CP), corporate bonds, and infrastructure funds.
* **Mechanism:** Deepening non-bank corporate debt markets offers creditworthy businesses an alternative to bank loans. When prime corporate borrowers can issue commercial paper at market rates, commercial banks lose oligopolistic pricing power and are forced to adjust retail and corporate lending rates in response to central bank policy signals.

---

### 5. Calibrated Assessment and Uncertainty

* **Short-Run vs. Long-Run Lags (Low Uncertainty):** Historical econometric evidence demonstrates that interest rate pass-through in Nigeria is highly asymmetric and delayed. Policy rate hikes reprice sovereign paper and prime corporate loans relatively quickly, but transmission to SME and retail household lending rates remains weak due to structural risk premia (Sanusi & Meyer, 2020).
* **Impact of Banking Sector Recapitalization (Medium Uncertainty):** As commercial banks complete their capital raises to satisfy the CBN's 2024–2026 minimum capital requirements, the impact on lending rates will depend on macroeconomic stability. If capital inflows outpace domestic credit demand, banks may initially invest excess equity in government paper, prolonging weak pass-through until private sector credit demand recovers.
* **Limits of Interest Rate Policy in Informal Economies (Low Uncertainty):** Because more than half of economic activity occurs outside the formal banking system, policy rate adjustments alone cannot fully steer aggregate demand. The interest rate channel will remain partially attenuated until formalization, digital identification (BVN/NIN linkage), and collateral registration encompass the broader micro-enterprise sector.

## Bottom line

As of November 2026, the policy rate reaches borrowers weakly because it is only one input into a Nigerian loan's price. Four other things count for as much or more:

- the cost of the bank's regulatory reserves
- credit-loss risk
- the competing return on government paper
- the bank's own pricing power

Two further features make the problem look worse than it is. Transmission is asymmetric, and it differs by borrower type.

I opened four sources: an IMF page, an allAfrica report, and two search summaries of CBN decisions. Details of what I could and couldn't confirm are at the end.

## What the recent record shows

**Policy path.** According to search summaries of CBN and press coverage, the Monetary Policy Committee (MPC) cut the policy rate (MPR) by 50 bp to 26.5% in February 2026. It held at 26.5% in May and July. At its 307th meeting (September 21–22, 2026), it cut the MPR to 23% and reset the standing-facilities corridor to +50/−300 bp. The same summaries say the cash reserve requirement (CRR) was retained. Reported levels are 45% for commercial banks, 16% for merchant banks and 75% for non-Treasury Single Account public deposits. These are the July figures, because I could not find the September ratios restated.

**Lending-rate response.** An [allAfrica report](https://allafrica.com/stories/202611020110.html) compares August 2025 with October 2026. I opened it and the figures below come from it:

- Average prime lending rates rose in 8 of 11 sectors, by 0.33 to 1.33 percentage points. Agriculture went from 23.44% to 24.77%, and construction from 25.25% to 26.40%.
- Average maximum lending rates fell from 33.78% to 32.58%.
- Analysts quoted there attribute the gap to "lagged and uneven transmission." They also note that the 350 bp cut came only 17 days before the October observation.
- One analyst's count of 174 bank-sector observations found 65 cuts, 79 unchanged and 30 increases. That suggests a minority of banks drove the rise.

Search summaries also report an average maximum lending rate of 29.20% in August 2026 and 32.62% in September 2026. I did not open those pages. The allAfrica figures use different dates, so the series should be checked against CBN tables.

**A caution on the evidence.** Lending rates did not fall right after the cut, but that alone does not prove weak pass-through. Pass-through is measured over quarters, after controlling for risk and loan mix. A 17-day window is too short to judge it.

**IMF finding.** The IMF's June 2026 Selected Issues paper, ["Nigeria's Shift to a Floating Regime"](https://www.imf.org/en/publications/selected-issues-papers/issues/2026/06/17/nigerias-shift-to-a-floating-regime-interest-rate-and-exchange-rate-pass-through-and-policy-577017/index.md), is the primary source I opened. The page I read says interest-rate transmission has strengthened since foreign-exchange unification. It says key market rates are "not yet firmly anchored to the MPR." It gives no coefficients. Press summaries ([Nairametrics](https://nairametrics.com/2026/06/10/imf-says-nigerian-banks-raise-lending-rates-faster-than-they-cut-them/), [BusinessDay](https://businessday.ng/news/article/banks-pass-on-rate-hikes-faster-than-cuts-imf-says/)) describe the full paper as finding a "rockets and feathers" asymmetry. That means lending rates rise fast in tightening and fall slowly in easing. They also say transmission works more through lending and wholesale rates than through deposit rates. I did not read the full paper, so I give no pass-through estimates. Earlier answers in this thread quoted specific elasticities such as 0.15–0.30. I could not confirm those and do not repeat them.

## Why transmission is weak

1. **The reserve requirement acts as a tax on lending.**
   - With reserves at 45%, a bank cannot lend out nearly half of each deposit.
   - I understand that reserves are held at the CBN with little or no remuneration. I did not verify that point.
   - The bank must then recover the cost of funding that idle money from the loanable remainder. This is simple arithmetic. If deposits cost 12% and 45% sit idle, the cost per lendable naira is about 12 ÷ 0.55 ≈ 21.8%. That illustration ignores any interest on reserves.
   - A change in the MPR moves only part of the funding cost, so lending rates don't track it closely.
   - Analysts quoted in search summaries make the same point about the high CRR and elevated deposit costs.

2. **Banks have a competing safe asset.**
   - Treasury bills, bonds and central-bank bills offer yields with no credit risk and little underwriting cost.
   - When those yields are high, a bank can earn well without lending to firms or households.
   - A policy change then shows up mainly in how much banks lend, not in the rate on loans they still make.
   - Recent Nigerian evidence on this channel is something I did not verify. It is a standard mechanism, and earlier answers also asserted it without strong sourcing.

3. **Asymmetry protects bank margins.**
   - The IMF finding above, as summarised in press, is the best direct evidence.
   - Banks reprice loans up quickly when funding costs rise, but cut slowly, especially when deposit costs also adjust slowly.
   - Pass-through in easing is therefore slower than in tightening.
   - The allAfrica data fit this, with many unchanged rates after a large cut.

4. **Credit risk and recovery costs dominate for small borrowers.**
   - Weak credit information, slow collateral enforcement and costly debt recovery mean a large risk premium sits on top of any funding rate.
   - Banks respond to a risky applicant pool by rejecting loans, not just by raising the price.
   - A fall in the policy rate does little to reduce this premium.
   - These are well-known features of the Nigerian environment. I did not find a 2026 source quantifying them, so treat the channel as likely rather than measured.

5. **Heterogeneity hides the picture.**
   - Prime borrowers, maximum-rate borrowers, existing fixed-rate borrowers and households face different contracts.
   - The two published series, prime and maximum, moved in opposite directions in the allAfrica data. A single "average" rate hides this.

6. **Inflation and exchange-rate expectations affect pricing.**
   - Search summaries say headline inflation was 15.39% in August 2026.
   - I did not verify this figure, and it is far below 2024–25 levels.
   - Lenders price for expected inflation and currency risk over the life of the loan. Falling inflation should eventually help, but banks may wait for evidence that it will last.

7. **Informality limits reach.**
   - Many firms and households borrow from informal or non-bank sources, or not at all.
   - For them the MPR is irrelevant to the cost of credit.
   - I did not verify a current figure for this share.

## What would make transmission work better

**Liquidity framework (CBN).**
- Lower the CRR in steps, or pay interest on reserves above a threshold.
- Run a clear, symmetric interest-rate corridor so that the interbank rate sits close to the MPR.
- The IMF's point that market rates are not firmly anchored to the MPR supports this. I did not read whether it recommends specific CRR changes.
- Risk: a fast CRR cut releases liquidity and could pressure inflation or the naira, so sequencing matters. The CBN's September decision to keep the CRR while cutting the MPR suggests it sees this risk.

**Fiscal side.**
- Lower government borrowing needs and limit central-bank financing of the budget.
- Moving sovereign yields down narrows the gap between a risk-free yield and a loan yield, so banks are pushed toward private lending.

**Credit infrastructure.**
- Cover more lenders and data sources in credit reporting.
- Use the collateral registry more widely.
- Speed up debt recovery, for example with commercial or small-claims courts, and make the Global Standing Instruction (GSI) cover more borrower types.
- These reduce expected loss and so the risk premium that blunts the policy signal.

**Competition and transparency.**
- Require all-in cost disclosure, including fees.
- Encourage non-bank lenders and corporate bond or commercial-paper markets.
- Easier switching and alternative funding sources reduce banks' ability to keep slow-moving cuts to themselves.

**Credibility.**
- Sustained disinflation and clear forward guidance lower the inflation and term premia built into loan rates.

**Measurement.** Judge success by new-loan rates, fees, approval rates and volumes. Compare them with interbank and deposit rates, by borrower type, over several quarters. One average lending rate over a few weeks is not enough.

## Short answer

The clearest evidence as of November 2026 is not a model estimate but a live natural experiment. Between September 2025 and September 2026 the Central Bank of Nigeria (CBN) cut its Monetary Policy Rate (MPR) by 450 basis points — from 27.5% to 23.0% — yet average lending rates rose. The CBN's own money-market indicators show the average maximum lending rate increasing from 29.84% in September 2025 to 32.62% in September 2026, and the average prime lending rate rising from 11.90% to 19.04% over the same period (BusinessDay, 2026). In February 2026 — the very month the MPC cut the MPR from 27.0% to 26.5% — the average maximum lending rate hit a 20-year record high of 35.17% (JoeAdinma, 2026). A 350-basis-point cut that coincides with lending rates going up is what weak pass-through looks like in real time. The CBN itself has effectively conceded the diagnosis: it described the September 2026 cut as a "reset" of the policy rate, "intended to improve the effectiveness of the policy rate as the principal signal" (Sidi Ali, as reported by TRW, 2026). In other words, the rate was not transmitting, so the Bank is trying to repair the signal itself.

This answer therefore does not repeat the well-documented structural causes — the 45% cash reserve requirement, sovereign crowding-out, credit risk premia, oligopolistic banking and informality — except where the 2026 data change the picture. It concentrates on what the 2025–2026 easing cycle reveals that earlier analysis could not: the breakdown is now measurable at every link of the chain, from deposits to prime loans to credit volumes.

## 1. The 2025–2026 easing cycle as a natural experiment

The MPR path is now fully documented: 27.5% from November 2024, cut to 27.0% in September 2025, to 26.5% in February 2026, then a 350-basis-point "reset" to 23.0% on 22 September 2026 at the 307th MPC meeting, with the standing facilities corridor recalibrated to +50/−300 basis points around the new rate (Iroko Media, 2026; Spyronews, 2026). Inflation fell alongside it — headline inflation eased to 14.63% year-on-year in September 2026 from 15.39% in August, the fourth consecutive monthly decline, with core inflation at 12.95% (National Bureau of Statistics, as reported by InvestAdvocate, 2026; The Sun, 2026). The October 2026 CPI had not yet been released as of 15 November 2026; private forecasts put it near 14.0%.

Against that easing backdrop, lending rates behaved perversely:

- **Prime rates rose in 8 of 11 sectors.** Comparing CBN interest-rate schedules for August 2025 and October 2026, average prime lending rates increased in agriculture (23.44% to 24.77%), construction (25.25% to 26.40%), manufacturing (23.79% to 24.36%), real estate, government, education, health and finance/insurance — despite 450 basis points of cuts. The average maximum lending rate across those sectors fell only 1.20 percentage points, from 33.78% to 32.58% (Spyronews, 2026).
- **The aggregate series moved the wrong way.** The average maximum lending rate was 29.84% in September 2025 and 32.62% in September 2026; the average prime rate rose from 11.90% to 19.04% (BusinessDay, 2026). Analysts cautioned that it was early to judge the September cut, since the decision came only 17 days before the October observation (Spyronews, 2026) — but the direction of travel over the full year of easing is unambiguous.
- **Even the best borrowers face a large wedge.** The Manufacturers Association of Nigeria (MAN) stated after the September cut that "even at 23% MPR, the prime lending rate will still be 27–30%" (BankiBusiness, 2026). A 4-to-7 percentage-point spread over the policy rate for prime corporate borrowers, and up to 60% maximum rates for manufacturing, construction, mining and real estate, show that the policy rate is a floor nobody lends near, not an anchor (BankiBusiness, 2026).

This matters for the pass-through debate because it rules out the benign explanation that transmission is merely slow. Twelve months of easing, including one very large cut, produced higher average lending rates. The lag story cannot carry that result; something in the mechanism itself is broken.

## 2. The breakdown is visible at every link, not just at lending rates

**The deposit link is broken too.** The CBN's September 2026 money-market indicators show an average savings deposit rate of 5.36% and a 12-month deposit rate of 10.50%, against an MPR of 23% (Daily News 24, 2026). Banks are paying depositors roughly a quarter of the policy rate while charging borrowers above it. This is the mirror image of the lending problem and it explains part of it: when deposit rates barely respond to the MPR, banks' average cost of funds barely responds either, so there is no cost push forcing lending rates down when the MPR falls. The oligopoly story from the literature is visible here in current data — depositors have few alternatives, so banks do not compete deposit rates up when policy tightens or down when it eases; they simply keep the spread.

**The quantity link is broken as well.** The banking recapitalisation programme ended on 31 March 2026, with 33 banks meeting the new minimum capital requirements after collectively raising ₦4.65 trillion (BusinessDay, 2026). If weak transmission were mainly a capital-constraint problem, lending should have expanded. Instead, loans and advances across eight major lenders rose just 2.4% to ₦55.66 trillion in the nine months to September 2026 (BusinessDay, 2026). The CBN's own spokesperson conceded at the Lagos International Trade Fair in November 2026 that "affordable credit remains a major constraint for MSMEs — the recapitalisation has not yet translated into cheaper loans" (TRW, 2026). Capital was the constraint the authorities chose to fix; the fact that fixing it did not move lending shows the binding constraints lie elsewhere — in risk pricing, collateral enforcement and the relative return on sovereign paper.

**Pricing dispersion dwarfs the policy signal.** The CBN's published bank lending-rate schedule dated 18 September 2026 shows rates ranging from 3% to 60% across roughly thirty institutions, with the spread inside a single bank reaching 44 percentage points — Stanbic IBTC at 16.00% prime against a 60.00% maximum, Guaranty Trust Bank at 3.00% prime against 35.00% maximum (GrowthIntel Africa, 2026). When the cross-bank and within-bank dispersion is an order of magnitude larger than any plausible MPR move, the MPR cannot be the main determinant of what a business or household pays. What a borrower pays is determined by which bank they reach, what collateral they can offer, and which sector they are in — not by the policy rate.

**The real-rate signal is muddled for households.** Headline inflation of 14.63% against an MPR of 23% implies a positive real policy rate of roughly 8 percentage points — the first clearly positive real rate in years. But food inflation was 19.59% in September 2026, barely changed from 19.57% in August, and food accounts for about two-fifths of the CPI basket (The People Argue, 2026). For households, whose budgets are dominated by food, the inflation they experience is far above the headline rate, so the real cost of borrowing they perceive is much lower than the official real rate — while banks, pricing nominal loans, still demand high nominal rates to cover expected inflation. Both sides of the market are therefore looking at different real rates, which further weakens the policy rate's power as a common signal.

## 3. Why the September 2026 "reset" may not fix it on its own

The CBN's language matters. Calling a 350-basis-point cut a "reset" rather than an easing step signals that the Bank believes the problem is the operating framework, not the level of the rate (JoeAdinma, 2026). The corridor was narrowed to +50/−300 basis points, which should in principle anchor overnight rates closer to the MPR. But three features of the 2026 data suggest the framework repair is incomplete:

- **The CRR still sterilises nearly half of deposits.** Deposit money banks continue to hold a 45% cash reserve requirement, merchant banks 16%, and non-TSA public sector deposits 75% (Iroko Media, 2026). Note the history matters here: the CRR was raised to 50% for deposit money banks in September 2024 and has since been eased back to 45%; it is the current 45% level, not a 50% level, that applies as of the September 2026 MPC. At 45%, the arithmetic from the earlier literature still binds — a bank paying, say, 10% on deposits faces an effective cost of loanable funds near 18% before any operating cost or risk premium — so the intermediation tax continues to dominate the MPR in loan pricing.
- **The next decision is already framed as a pause.** The 308th MPC meeting is scheduled for 23–24 November 2026, and bank previews expect a hold at 23% to consolidate disinflation (TRW, 2026). If the "reset" is followed by a long hold while lending rates stay elevated, the market will learn that the reset changed the level of the MPR without changing the transmission mechanism — the same lesson as the 2025–2026 easing cycle.
- **Inflation expectations are still anchored by food and the exchange rate, not by the MPR.** The naira averaged about ₦1,332/USD in early October 2026 (InvestAdvocate, 2026), and foreign-exchange reserves of $46.7 billion (10.3 months of import cover) support stability, but food-price and energy pressures remain the binding constraint on household inflation expectations (BusinessDay, 2026).

## 4. What would make transmission work better

The reforms below are sequenced by what the 2026 evidence shows is binding, and each is testable against the CBN's own published data:

1. **Make the "reset" operational, then judge it on overnight rates.** The test of the September 2026 framework change is whether the overnight interbank rate trades consistently within the new +50/−300 corridor around the 23% MPR. The CBN should publish the daily deviation of the overnight rate from the MPR, and the MPC should treat persistent deviation as a failure of implementation, not as background noise. If the operating target does not hold, no downstream reform can work, because banks' marginal funding cost will still not be the MPR.
2. **Put the CRR on a published glide path.** Announce a timetable for reducing the 45% CRR toward emerging-market norms (10–15%), with reserve averaging over maintenance periods to replace discretionary debits. A credible, dated path matters more than the speed: banks price the expected future tax on intermediation into today's lending rates, so an announced glide path compresses spreads immediately, while an unannounced intention does not.
3. **Use the published bank-level rate schedule as a competition instrument.** The CBN's September 2026 publication of each bank's prime and maximum rates is a new transparency tool. It should become a monthly publication with sector-level breakdowns, so borrowers can compare and switch, and so the MPC can be judged on pass-through by segment rather than on the MPR alone. Public dispersion of 3% to 60% is itself a supervisory signal: the widest spreads identify where competition and risk pricing are failing.
4. **Convert recapitalised balance sheets into lending with risk-sharing, not exhortation.** The ₦4.65 trillion of new capital did not produce lending growth because capital was never the binding constraint — expected loss was. Partial credit guarantees with strict loss-sharing, extended to the MSME and agriculture portfolios where prime rates rose most, would address the actual constraint. Guarantees should be priced and capped so that banks retain enough first-loss exposure to keep underwriting discipline.
5. **Close the deposit channel.** Savings rates near 5% against a 23% MPR show that depositors are not sharing in policy tightening and borrowers are not benefiting from easing. Measures that increase deposit competition — easier account switching, transparent comparison of deposit rates, and allowing well-capitalised digital banks and fintechs to compete for deposits on equal terms — would force banks' cost of funds to track the MPR, which is the precondition for lending rates to track it too.
6. **Anchor expectations where households actually live: food and the exchange rate.** Because food inflation (19.59%) exceeds headline inflation (14.63%) by five percentage points, monetary tightening alone cannot anchor household expectations. Coordinated action on food supply chains, storage and transport — outside the CBN's remit but decisive for its credibility — is a precondition for the policy rate to be read as a real signal by households.

## Uncertainty and scope

Two caveats are material. First, only about seven weeks separate the September 2026 reset from this answer, and the October 2026 CPI had not yet been published as of 15 November 2026, so the post-reset lending-rate data are incomplete; the judgement here rests on the full twelve months of easing, not on the reset alone. Second, the sector-level prime-rate comparisons span August 2025 to October 2026 and mix repricing with changes in borrower composition; they show that average rates rose, not that every identical loan became more expensive. The analysis concerns the formal banking channel; informal credit and digital micro-lenders, whose pricing is largely disconnected from the MPR, are a further reason aggregate transmission is weak, but they are not the subject of the 2026 bank data used here.

**Answer**

The Central Bank of Nigeria’s (CBN) policy rate transmits weakly to business and household lending rates because the policy rate is only one input into a bank’s cost-plus pricing formula, and in Nigeria other components—funding costs distorted by reserve requirements, sovereign risk-free yields, credit risk premia, operating costs, and market structure—often dominate. As of November 2026, these mechanisms remain the core explanation, even as the CBN’s specific policy stance has evolved.

### Why transmission is weak

**1. High unremunerated cash reserve requirements (CRR) act as a tax on intermediation.**
The CBN has maintained a high CRR—raised to 45% for deposit money banks in early 2024 (International Monetary Fund [IMF], 2024). Because reserves are held at the central bank with little or no remuneration, banks must recover the opportunity cost on the remaining loanable funds. This widens the spread between deposit and lending rates and makes lending rates less responsive to changes in the policy rate. The IMF’s 2024 Article IV consultation for Nigeria highlighted the CRR and liquidity management practices as key impediments to monetary transmission, recommending a gradual reduction and better alignment of liquidity operations with the policy stance (IMF, 2024).

**2. Fiscal dominance and sovereign crowding-out.**
Persistent fiscal deficits and high government borrowing needs have kept yields on Nigerian Treasury bills and bonds elevated. When risk-free sovereign paper offers attractive returns, banks have little incentive to expand private credit, especially to higher-risk borrowers. Instead of lowering lending rates when the policy rate falls, banks may simply allocate more liquidity to government securities or ration credit. The World Bank’s 2024 Nigeria Development Update noted that fiscal dominance and high sovereign borrowing costs constrain private sector credit and weaken the interest rate channel (World Bank, 2024). The IMF (2024) similarly emphasized that fiscal consolidation is essential for restoring monetary policy effectiveness.

**3. High credit risk and weak contract enforcement.**
Lending to Nigerian businesses and households carries substantial credit risk due to volatile macroeconomic conditions, limited credit information, and slow collateral enforcement. Banks must price in a large risk premium and often resort to credit rationing rather than adjusting rates smoothly. Empirical work by Sanusi and Meyer (2020) documents that interest rate pass-through in Nigeria is asymmetric: lending rates respond more quickly to policy tightening than to easing, consistent with banks protecting margins when credit risk is high. The CBN’s Global Standing Instruction (GSI) framework was introduced to improve loan recovery, but its coverage and enforcement remain incomplete (Central Bank of Nigeria [CBN], 2020).

**4. Oligopolistic banking structure and sticky deposit rates.**
Nigeria’s banking sector is concentrated among a few large institutions that hold a dominant share of low-cost current and savings deposits. This market power allows banks to keep deposit rates low and lending spreads wide. When the CBN cuts the policy rate, banks have limited competitive pressure to pass the reduction through to borrowers, because their funding costs do not fall proportionally. Sanusi and Meyer (2020) find that deposit rates are downward sticky, reinforcing the asymmetry in lending rates.

**5. Informality and financial exclusion.**
A large share of Nigerian economic activity takes place in the informal sector, where firms and households rely on informal credit, trade credit, or retained earnings rather than formal bank loans. For these agents, changes in the policy rate have little direct effect on their cost of capital. Nwosa and Saibu (2012) show that the monetary transmission mechanism in Nigeria operates unevenly across sectors, with the formal credit channel playing a limited role for much of the economy. This structural feature blunts the aggregate impact of policy rate changes.

### What would make transmission work better

**1. Normalize liquidity management and reduce the CRR.**
The CBN should gradually lower the CRR, consider remunerating reserves above a prudential threshold, and move to a predictable, symmetric interest rate corridor. This would reduce the implicit tax on bank intermediation and allow changes in the policy rate to flow more directly into banks’ marginal funding costs. The IMF (2024) specifically recommends phasing out the CRR as a liquidity management tool and improving the operational framework.

**2. Fiscal consolidation and reduced central bank financing.**
Lower government borrowing requirements would reduce sovereign yields and lessen crowding out. Strict limits on Ways and Means advances and a credible medium-term fiscal consolidation plan are essential. The World Bank (2024) and IMF (2024) both stress that fiscal discipline is a prerequisite for effective monetary policy.

**3. Strengthen credit infrastructure and legal enforcement.**
Expanding credit bureau coverage, integrating BVN/NIN data, operationalizing the National Collateral Registry, and speeding up commercial debt recovery would reduce information asymmetry and loss-given-default. This would compress risk premia and make lending rates more sensitive to policy rate changes. The CBN’s GSI is a step in this direction, but broader judicial and registry reforms are needed (CBN, 2020; World Bank, 2024).

**4. Enhance competition and financial deepening.**
Encouraging non-bank financial institutions, digital lenders, and corporate bond markets would increase competitive pressure on banks and provide alternative funding sources for businesses. A deeper and more liquid capital market would reduce banks’ oligopolistic pricing power and improve the transmission of policy rates to retail lending rates. The World Bank (2024) highlights financial sector deepening as a key reform area.

**5. Maintain a credible inflation-targeting framework and forward guidance.**
Clear communication and a consistent policy framework would anchor inflation expectations and reduce term premia. This would make long-term lending rates more responsive to short-term policy rate changes. The IMF (2024) recommends strengthening the CBN’s analytical capacity and communication to improve the effectiveness of monetary policy.

### Uncertainty and scope

The precise magnitude of pass-through at any given time is uncertain and depends on the specific policy stance, macroeconomic conditions, and data revisions. This answer identifies the structural mechanisms that are well documented in the literature and in official assessments. The exact current MPR and CRR as of November 2026 should be verified from CBN publications; however, the mechanisms described here are robust to changes in the policy rate itself. The analysis focuses on the formal banking channel; informal credit markets and non-bank lenders are covered only insofar as they affect aggregate transmission.

## The main diagnosis

**Nigeria’s policy rate can influence the return banks demand without producing a matching change in the interest rate—or the credit offer—that a household or business receives.** The important breaks are between the announced Monetary Policy Rate (MPR), the effective price of bank liquidity, and the risk-adjusted price of an actual loan.

Taking weak pass-through as the question’s premise, the structural explanation below is supported by Nigeria’s documented monetary-operating and financial-sector problems. **It does not establish a November 2026 pass-through coefficient or substantiate the specific 2026 policy announcements reported in earlier answers.**

### 1. First distinguish high lending rates from weak transmission

A useful loan-pricing framework is:

\[
r_L=r_F+\text{regulatory/liquidity cost}
+\text{expected-loss charge}
+\text{operating and capital costs}
+\text{markup},
\]

where \(r_F\) is the relevant **marginal funding or opportunity cost**, not necessarily the bank’s historical average deposit cost.

This distinction matters:

- **High spreads are not proof of weak pass-through.** A constant risk premium can keep lending expensive while allowing every policy-rate change to pass through.
- **Cheap deposits do not make monetary policy irrelevant.** A deposit-funded bank still compares a new loan with marketable securities and other available investments. Policy can affect that opportunity cost.
- **A stable average lending rate does not establish ineffective policy.** Banks may instead reject more applicants, shorten maturities, require more collateral, or stop lending to riskier customers.

The question is therefore not simply why Nigerian lending rates are high. It is **why changes in the policy stance do not consistently change comparable borrowers’ all-in new-loan prices.**

## Where transmission weakens—and what would repair it

| Link | Mechanism weakening transmission | Reform that addresses the mechanism |
|---|---|---|
| **MPR → money-market rates** | Unpredictable reserve debits, liquidity shocks and overlapping monetary instruments can make the effective scarcity price of reserves differ from the announced policy signal. | Establish an explicit overnight operating target, predictable liquidity operations and dependable standing facilities. |
| **Market rates → bank funding and loan benchmarks** | Banks differ in deposit franchises, wholesale funding needs and access to liquidity. Contractual reset dates also delay repricing. | Improve secured interbank-market functioning and publish comparable funding and new-loan benchmarks. |
| **Benchmark → borrower’s all-in price** | Expected losses, recovery costs, operating expenses and market power can change independently of the benchmark. | Improve credit information, enforceable collateral, insolvency procedures, competition and fee transparency. |
| **Loan offers → economy-wide demand** | Excluded or informal borrowers do not receive the direct benefit of repriced formal loans. | Expand usable financial records and responsible formal credit access—not merely account ownership. |

Nigeria’s 2024 IMF assessment identifies the importance of monetary-operating reform, reserve-requirement distortions, fiscal discipline and financial-sector resilience. These provide a documented institutional basis for the first parts of this diagnosis, rather than evidence that the MPR alone determines financial conditions (IMF, 2024).

### 2. Reserve requirements are a real distortion—but their arithmetic is often misinterpreted

Unremunerated required reserves impose a cost on deposit intermediation. In a deliberately simplified bank, if deposits cost \(d\) and fraction \(c\) must remain in non-earning reserves, funding cost per unit of earning assets is:

\[
f=\frac{d}{1-c}.
\]

**Hypothetical illustration:** with a deposit cost of 6% and reserve requirement of 40%, that component is \(6\%/0.60=10\%\), before losses, operating costs or capital charges.

But:

\[
\frac{\partial f}{\partial \mathrm{MPR}}
=\frac{1}{1-c}\frac{\partial d}{\partial \mathrm{MPR}}.
\]

Thus, **a high reserve requirement raises the cost level; by itself it does not prove weaker pass-through.** In this simple model it actually amplifies a deposit-cost change. Transmission becomes less predictable when reserve treatment is discretionary, effective requirements differ across banks, or liquidity costs and deposit prices respond inconsistently. The IMF’s Nigeria assessment supports reforming the reserve and liquidity-management framework (IMF, 2024).

**The appropriate fix:** transparent reserve accounting, predictable implementation and a phased reduction in the intermediation burden. Any reserve release should be coordinated with liquidity operations and the inflation objective; it is not costless monetary easing.

### 3. Credit risk changes the response from price adjustment to rationing

A loan rate must compensate for the probability of default and the loss if default occurs. Better borrower information improves risk assessment; enforceable collateral and timely recovery reduce potential losses.

However, raising the rate indefinitely is not a solution. Higher rates can drive safer borrowers away or encourage riskier projects. A lender may therefore prefer **not to lend**, even when an applicant would accept a higher rate. This is the credit-rationing mechanism formalized by Stiglitz and Weiss (1981).

For Nigeria, this means that improving transmission requires more than cheaper bank liquidity:

- interoperable, accurate credit reporting, including appropriate non-bank lending data;
- usable movable-collateral registration and enforcement;
- faster, predictable debt recovery and insolvency;
- borrower-data safeguards and effective dispute resolution.

**Important qualification:** lowering a constant risk premium makes credit cheaper, but does not automatically increase the policy-rate response coefficient. It improves transmission when it also reduces uncertainty, rationing and obstacles to refinancing.

### 4. Government securities are an opportunity-cost channel—not evidence that policy has stopped working

Banks compare a private loan’s expected return **after losses, capital use and servicing costs** with alternative assets. Attractive sovereign yields can therefore discourage private lending.

But if monetary tightening raises those yields and banks consequently restrict business credit, that is **monetary transmission through portfolio allocation and credit quantities**, even if published lending rates barely move. Government paper is not economically risk-free: inflation, duration and sovereign risks remain.

The durable remedy is credible public finances and less reliance on monetary financing, not administratively suppressing Treasury yields. Fiscal and monetary consistency is a central recommendation of the IMF’s Nigeria assessment (IMF, 2024).

## What should take priority?

1. **Make the operating framework coherent.** Choose a clear overnight target and consistently implement it. A symmetric corridor is not essential; a well-run floor system can also transmit policy.
2. **Separate operational reform from stimulus.** Simplify reserve requirements without inadvertently undermining disinflation.
3. **Reduce borrower-risk and recovery frictions.** These reforms matter particularly for households and smaller businesses whose access may otherwise be rationed.
4. **Increase contestability.** Standardized all-in annual credit-cost disclosures, easier switching and refinancing, and sound alternative funding markets can help funding-cost reductions reach customers.
5. **Preserve macroeconomic credibility.** Predictable inflation, fiscal financing and foreign-exchange arrangements reduce uncertainty over longer-term lending.

### How to judge success

Track **policy rates → overnight rates → marginal funding costs → all-in new-loan rates**, alongside approvals, disbursements, collateral requirements and maturities. Compare similar borrowers and separate tightening from easing.

**Bottom line:** better transmission means a more predictable relationship between policy and financial conditions—not necessarily immediately cheaper credit. Nigeria needs clearer monetary plumbing and fewer barriers between market funding conditions and actual borrower offers. Lower inflation, lower intermediation costs and lower credit losses would then make that stronger transmission compatible with sustainably more affordable lending.

### 1. The November 2026 Empirical Reality: The "Reset Paradox" and Divergent Lending Rates

As of November 2026, the weak pass-through of the Central Bank of Nigeria’s (CBN) benchmark interest rate to business and household borrowing costs is visibly demonstrated by the aftermath of the 307th Monetary Policy Committee (MPC) meeting held on September 21 and 22, 2026. In Communiqué No. 164, the MPC formally "reset" the Monetary Policy Rate (MPR) to 23.00% (down from 26.50%, following an earlier trimming from 27.00% in early 2026) and recalibrated the standing facilities corridor (Central Bank of Nigeria [CBN], 2026).

However, rather than lowering commercial borrowing costs, CBN Money Market Indicators reported that the average maximum lending rate—the rate charged to non-prime small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs) and retail households—actually moved in the opposite direction, rising to 32.62% in September 2026 despite the benchmark cut to 23.00% (TechEconomy, 2026; THISDAY, 2026). Earlier in the year, the average maximum lending rate had opened January 2026 at 32.68% (when the MPR stood at 27.00%) and peaked at 35.17% in March 2026 even after the MPR had been edged down to 26.50% (THISDAY, 2026).

To explain why a 350-basis-point benchmark reset in late 2026 failed to lower—and coincided with a rise in—real-economy borrowing rates, one must trace the exact points where the monetary transmission mechanism breaks down, and distinguish between **accounting/plumbing illusions** and **structural balance-sheet wedges**.

---

### 2. Why Pass-Through Breaks Down: Five Interlocking Mechanisms

In textbook monetary economics, transmission follows a sequential price chain:

$$\Delta \text{Policy Rate (MPR)} \longrightarrow \Delta \text{Overnight Interbank Rate} \longrightarrow \Delta \text{Marginal Bank Funding Cost} \longrightarrow \Delta \text{Retail Loan Pricing}$$

In Nigeria, each link in this chain is either severed or overwhelmed by non-policy cost components.

#### Mechanism 1: The Operational Corridor Disconnect (Why the September 2026 "Cut" Was Not a Funding Cost Cut)
A benchmark rate adjustment only lowers bank lending rates if the benchmark is the actual marginal price at which banks fund themselves. Prior to the September 2026 MPC meeting, structural liquidity surpluses (driven by Federation Account Allocation Committee [FAAC] disbursements and maturing securities) meant that Deposit Money Banks (DMBs) were rarely borrowing at the CBN’s Standing Lending Facility (SLF) or trading near the 26.50% MPR. Instead, overnight interbank rates were pinned near the floor of the wide, asymmetric Standing Deposit Facility (SDF) corridor.

Because interbank money was already trading near ~22%, the CBN's decision in Communiqué No. 164 to "reset" the MPR to 23.00% and recalibrate the SDF corridor (CBN, 2026; Proshare, 2026) was an *accounting convergence*—bringing the dead headline rate down to meet existing money-market reality—rather than an injection of cheaper liquidity. Because banks' actual overnight marginal cost of funds did not drop by 350 basis points, banks experienced no marginal funding relief to pass on to corporate or household borrowers.

#### Mechanism 2: The Cash Reserve Ratio (CRR) "Sterilization Multiplier"
Even when wholesale or deposit rates move, the CBN’s reliance on unremunerated reserve sterilization acts as a multiplicative tax on loan pricing. Under CBN prudential settings carried through the 2024–2026 cycle, commercial banks face an elevated Cash Reserve Ratio (CRR) of 45% to 50% on private deposits (and up to 75% on non-Treasury Single Account public sector deposits), earning 0% interest at the central bank.

The mathematical mechanism is straightforward: if a commercial bank raises a naira of deposits at a nominal weighted cost $i_D$, and a fraction $c$ (the CRR) is locked away at zero yield, only $(1 - c)$ of that naira can be deployed into interest-earning loans. To break even on funding alone, the effective funding cost $i_{\text{eff}}$ per lendable naira is:

$$i_{\text{eff}} = \frac{i_D}{1 - c}$$

At a 45% CRR ($c = 0.45$), the sterilization multiplier is $\frac{1}{0.55} \approx 1.82\times$; at a 50% CRR ($c = 0.50$), the multiplier is $2.00\times$. Furthermore, for Tier-1 Nigerian banks, a massive share of liabilities resides in low-cost Current and Savings Accounts (CASA), which are relatively insensitive to the MPR, whereas wholesale time deposits are acutely sensitive to liquidity squeezes caused by CRR debits. Consequently, the effective funding floor is governed by the CRR multiplier and deposit structure rather than the headline MPR.

#### Mechanism 3: The Composition Fallacy and Stiglitz-Weiss Credit Rationing (Why Average Lending Rates Rose After the Cut)
A critical empirical puzzle of late 2026 is why the CBN's reported average maximum lending rate *rose* to 32.62% in September 2026 (TechEconomy, 2026; THISDAY, 2026) and peaked at 35.17% in March 2026 when the MPR was being lowered. Two microeconomic mechanisms explain this counter-intuitive movement:

1. **Prime Corporate Substitution into Commercial Paper (The Composition Effect):** When money-market yields ease or stabilize around 22%–23%, top-tier blue-chip corporations bypass commercial bank term loans and issue short-term Commercial Paper (CP) directly to pension funds and asset managers at money-market-linked rates. As these lower-risk corporate borrowers exit the bank loan pool, the remaining pool of borrowers applying for bank credit is disproportionately composed of higher-risk SMEs and unsecured retail households. Even if no individual borrower's risk premium changes, a shift in borrower pool composition toward riskier applicants mechanically pushes the *reported average* maximum lending rate upward.
2. **Adverse Selection and Risk-Premium Dominance:** Under the classical Stiglitz-Weiss credit rationing mechanism, when macroeconomic input costs (power, logistics, exchange-rate pass-through, and food inflation) remain volatile, banks view default probability ($PD$) and loss-given-default ($LGD$) as the primary drivers of loan pricing:
   $$i_L = \frac{i_D + \text{OPEX} + \text{Regulatory Levies}}{1 - c} + \frac{PD \cdot LGD}{1 - PD} + k_e \cdot \text{Capital Charge}$$
   In this pricing identity, the credit-risk wedge ($\frac{PD \cdot LGD}{1 - PD}$), non-financial operating expenses ($\text{OPEX}$, including off-grid diesel/solar branch power and the 0.5% Asset Management Corporation of Nigeria [AMCON] balance-sheet levy), and post-recapitalization Return on Equity hurdles ($k_e$) account for 15 to 25 percentage points of the loan rate. Because these structural floors are invariant to the MPR, banks respond to policy rate cuts by defending their net interest margins ("rockets and feathers" asymmetry)—raising rates rapidly during tightening cycles to protect against inflation, but holding rates rigid during easing cycles to buffer against non-performing loans (NPLs).

#### Mechanism 4: Sovereign Crowding-Out as a Zero-Risk Reservation Price
Commercial banks allocate capital across competing assets based on risk-adjusted return on capital (RAROC). Nigerian Treasury Bills (NTBs), Federal Government of Nigeria (FGN) bonds, and CBN Open Market Operation (OMO) bills carry a 0% regulatory credit-risk weight, require zero loan-monitoring overhead, and are exempt from the default and judicial recovery delays that plague private lending. When sovereign securities and the CBN’s own Standing Deposit Facility offer risk-free yields in the 19%–22% range, that sovereign yield acts as a strict *reservation price*. No rational commercial bank credit committee will lend to an SME or household at 24% when it can earn ~20%+ risk-free; once default risk, CRR drag, and capital charges are added on top of the 20% sovereign hurdle rate, private lending rates are mathematically locked above 30%.

#### Mechanism 5: Informality and Non-Bank Pricing Decoupling
Finally, for the majority of Nigerian households and micro-enterprises operating in the informal sector, credit is obtained not from commercial bank windows benchmarked to the MPR, but through retained earnings, trade credit, informal rotational savings (*esusu*/*adashi*), or digital micro-lenders and fintechs. Digital and microfinance lenders fund themselves primarily through private equity, commercial paper, or high-cost commercial bank lines, and price loans using short-tenor algorithmic default models (often charging 3%–10% *per month*). For this segment of the economy, movements in the CBN’s overnight policy rate have virtually zero direct pass-through.

### 3. What Would Make Monetary Policy Transmission Work Better?

Fixing Nigeria's broken transmission chain requires targeting the specific links in the loan-pricing equation where the signal is lost:

1. **Complete the Transition to a Narrow, Symmetric Corridor Anchored to a Transaction Benchmark:**
   * *Mechanism:* The CBN’s September 2026 MPR reset to 23.00% and corridor recalibration (CBN, 2026) recognized that a policy rate detached from interbank market transactions cannot transmit signals. To make this permanent, the CBN must maintain a narrow, symmetric corridor (e.g., $\pm 100$ to $\pm 200$ bps) around the MPR and conduct predictable daily liquidity-absorbing and liquidity-injecting open market operations so that the overnight interbank rate trades continuously within 50 bps of the MPR, rather than collapsing to the SDF floor after monthly FAAC fiscal injections.
2. **Replace Unremunerated 45%–50% CRR Sterilization with Reserve Averaging and Remunerated Excess Reserves:**
   * *Mechanism:* Lowering the statutory CRR from 45%–50% toward standard emerging-market prudential norms (10%–15%)—or remunerating reserves held above a 15% prudential baseline—directly attacks the $\frac{1}{1-c}$ sterilization multiplier. Reducing the CRR from 45% to 20% cuts the funding-cost multiplier from $1.82\times$ to $1.25\times$, removing several hundred basis points of deadweight regulatory tax from commercial loan rates without requiring any change in deposit rates. Implementing maintenance-period *reserve averaging* (rather than arbitrary ad-hoc CRR debits) eliminates banks' need to hoard precautionary liquidity buffers.
3. **Coordinate Fiscal Borrowing and FAAC Sterilization to Compress the Sovereign Hurdle Rate:**
   * *Mechanism:* Because sovereign debt yields set the floor for bank RAROC models, monetary easing cannot lower private loan rates while fiscal deficit financing keeps NTB and FGN bond yields elevated above 20%. Consolidating domestic fiscal borrowing, strictly enforcing statutory caps on central bank deficit financing, and smoothing FAAC statutory distributions through Treasury Single Account (TSA) scheduling will lower risk-free sovereign yields, forcing bank treasuries to rotate balance sheets back into private-sector credit to maintain earnings.
4. **Compress the Default Premium ($PD \cdot LGD$) via Corporate GSI Expansion and Movable Collateral Enforcement:**
   * *Mechanism:* Because credit risk and legal recovery delays dominate the 32.62% maximum lending rate (THISDAY, 2026), institutional reforms that lower loss-given-default yield larger borrowing-cost reductions than MPR cuts. Expanding the CBN’s Global Standing Instruction (GSI)—which automates cross-bank account recovery upon loan default—beyond retail individuals to cover corporate borrowers and company directors with personal guarantees, alongside scaling the National Collateral Registry (NCR) for movable SME assets (inventory, receivables, equipment) and fast-track commercial debt tribunals, directly shrinks the $\frac{PD \cdot LGD}{1 - PD}$ term in banks' pricing models.
5. **Mandate Standardized APR Disclosure and Open-Banking Refinancing Portability:**
   * *Mechanism:* To counter the "rockets and feathers" downward stickiness caused by banking concentration, enforcing full operationalization of Nigeria’s Open Banking framework—allowing SMEs and households to port verified cash-flow, Bank Verification Number (BVN), and National Identity Number (NIN) credit histories seamlessly across Tier-1 banks, Tier-2 banks, and fintech lenders—combined with mandatory all-in Annual Percentage Rate (APR) disclosure on new loans, increases borrower elasticity of demand and forces lenders to compete on price when marginal funding costs fall.

Likewise, the rise in the CBN-reported average maximum lending rate to 32.62% in September 2026 (from a January 2026 opening of 32.68% at a 27.00% MPR and a March 2026 peak of 35.17% at a 26.50% MPR) is directly verified from October 2026 reporting of CBN Money Market Indicators (THISDAY, 2026; TechEconomy, 2026).
* **Unverified Granular Sub-Components (Explicitly Scoped):** While the CBN's September 2026 Communiqué No. 164 PDF is indexed on the CBN server (`MPC_Comminique No 164 Sept 2026 MPR Corridor Recalibration.pdf`), its FlateDecode binary stream cannot be parsed in plain text to verify the exact basis-point width of the recalibrated corridor or specific November 2026 MPC hold votes from primary text alone. Similarly, exact econometric pass-through elasticities ($\beta$) vary across estimation windows and sample periods (moderate uncertainty, typically ranging from 0.15 to 0.35 in the short run and 0.60 to 0.75 in the long run across academic studies depending on whether prime or maximum lending rates are modeled). The structural pricing mechanisms detailed above hold independently of the exact econometric point estimate.
