A coordinated policy sequencing—anchoring fiscal deficit monetization, narrowing the Standing Deposit Facility/Standing Lending Facility corridor, migrating the Cash Reserve Ratio toward an actively remunerated open-market framework, expanding corporate Global Standing Instruction and movable-asset enforcement, and operationalizing open-banking portability—provides the necessary structural transmission channels to translate future Monetary Policy Rate adjustments into lower real-sector borrowing costs.

## Bottom line

Previous answers explain the weak pass-through with the right ingredients — the CRR tax, asymmetric repricing, crowding-out by government paper, and thin credit information. Two dated, quantified mechanisms are still missing from them, and they change the diagnosis: **the CBN itself loosened the quantity channel while it tightened the price channel**, and **the risk premium on household/SME loans is unobservable for most borrowers, so it cannot move with the MPR**. Until those two are fixed, MPR cuts will keep arriving at borrowers late, unevenly, or not at all.

## 1. The quantity ratios moved against the price signal: the April 2024 LDR cut

Answer 10 states the CRR-plus-LDR arithmetic correctly (45–50% of deposits sterilised plus a 50–65% lending floor exhausts nearly all deposit funding). What no previous answer records is the dated policy event that made that arithmetic *worse* while the MPR was being hiked:

- On **18 April 2024** the CBN issued circular **BSD/DIR/PUB/LAB/017/005** directing all Deposit Money Banks to cut their minimum loan-to-deposit ratio (LDR) from **65% to 50%**, effective immediately, explicitly "to align with the current monetary tightening" (Stren & Blan, 2024; BusinessDay, 2024). The floor had been raised to 60% in July 2019 and 65% in September 2019 to force lending to the real sector; the April 2024 cut reversed that direction (Omaplex Law Firm, 2024).
- Under the same regime, commercial banks must hold **45%** of deposits as CRR (14% for merchant banks), with compliance assessed on **average daily** LDR figures (Stren & Blan, 2024).
- The arithmetic: 45% sterilised at the CBN (earning 0%) plus a 50% lending floor leaves roughly **5% of deposits discretionary**. The MPR is a price signal, but the balance sheet is almost fully pre-committed by two quantity ratios — so banks respond to MPR changes by rationing credit and defending spreads, not by repricing loans smoothly. That is exactly the mechanism Answer 10 derives; the April 2024 cut is the dated evidence that the CBN chose to tighten the quantity side at the same time as it tightened price.
- The floor's bite is a penalty, not a loan: a bank missing the LDR faces an **additional CRR charge of 50% of the lending shortfall** (Omaplex Law Firm, 2024). A bank therefore compares the penalty against the expected loss on a marginal loan — and when the expected loss is larger, it rationally pays the penalty instead of lending. The floor then transmits nothing to borrowers; it transmits a tax to the bank.
- One correction to the record: Answer 12 cites a "**65% regulatory guideline**" for LDR. That figure is stale — the floor has been **50% since April 2024**. Answer 12 also reports GTCO's LDR at roughly 24–25% (I have not independently verified that figure). If it is right, it is telling: a large bank's actual lending sits far below even the lowered 50% floor, so the floor does not bind through lending volumes at all — it binds only through the penalty.

## 2. The risk premium is unobservable for most borrowers, so it cannot move with the MPR

Answers 3 and 7 propose deepening credit bureaus and scaling the National Collateral Registry, but only qualitatively. The numbers show why this is the binding constraint for households and SMEs, not a secondary reform:

- **Credit bureau coverage was about 14% of adults** (World Bank Doing Business, cited by CRC Credit Bureau's Managing Director, Dr Tunde Popoola, in 2020). Fewer than **25 million Nigerians had enjoyed credit in the previous decade** (Credit Bureau Association of Nigeria, reported by MSME Africa Online, 2020).
- **SMEs are over 96% of businesses but received under 1% of total commercial bank credit** (CBN statistics for 2018, cited in the same report), and fewer than 5% of SMEs could access adequate finance for working capital (National Bureau of Statistics, cited in the same report).
- As recently as **2024, only 6.1% of adults borrowed from a formal financial institution** (World Bank Global Findex, indicator fin22a).
- The position has not improved: EFInA's 2026 survey finds formal financial inclusion at 73% of adults, but only **10% access formal credit**, and total consumer credit **shrank 19.92% to ₦3.78 trillion in 2025** (TechCabal, 2026, reporting CBN data). Non-performing loans reached **8.03% in January 2026** (CBN, via TechCabal, 2026) — realised losses, not just perceived risk.

The mechanism: a loan price is funding cost plus expected loss plus operating cost plus return on capital. When roughly 86% of adults have no bureau record and SMEs have no pledgeable history, the expected-loss term is priced from coarse proxies and stays wide and sticky. An MPR cut lowers the funding-cost term, but for a household or SME borrower the risk premium is the larger, binding component — and it does not move when the MPR moves. That is why easing can reach T-bill yields and interbank rates quickly while retail lending rates barely respond. The September 2026 episode is consistent with this reading, though the short-window data are noisy (see the caveat below).

## 3. What the September 2026 cut actually shows — and its limits

Answer 13 (Pioneer) documents the September 2026 decision: the MPC cut the MPR by 350 bp, from **26.50% to 23.00%**, and reset the standing-facilities corridor to **+50/−300 bp**. Two lending-rate series then disagree in direction: search summaries report average maximum lending rates rising from **29.20% (August 2026) to 32.62% (September 2026)**, while the allAfrica report Answer 13 opened shows maximum lending rates falling from **33.78% to 32.58%** between August 2025 and October 2026, with prime rates rising in 8 of 11 sectors. I endorse Answer 13's caution: a 17-day window after the cut is too short to judge pass-through, which is measured over quarters after controlling for risk and loan mix. The September numbers are therefore corroboration of *unevenness*, not a measurement of the pass-through coefficient. The two mechanisms above predict exactly that unevenness: quantity-rationed banks and unpriceable borrowers do not reprice on a policy announcement.

## 4. What would make transmission work better

In the order the breaks occur:

1. **Harmonise the LDR with the CRR — and make the trade-off observable.** Answer 10's fix is the right one: benchmark required lending against *net investable deposits* (deposits × [1 − CRR]) instead of gross deposits, so the two ratios stop jointly exhausting the balance sheet. Add publication of bank-level LDR and CRR compliance, so the penalty-versus-lending choice is visible and the April 2024 lesson — do not loosen the quantity floor while tightening price — is not repeated silently.
2. **Make the risk premium priceable: raise bureau coverage from ~14% toward the OECD's ~67%** (World Bank Doing Business benchmark cited by BusinessDay, 2014). The concrete steps are the ones Answers 3 and 7 name — BVN/NIN-linked reporting, mandatory reporting by microfinance banks, digital lenders and utilities, and scaling the National Collateral Registry for movable assets under the Secured Transactions in Movable Assets Act — but the target should be stated as a coverage number, because coverage is what converts an unpriceable borrower into a priced one.
3. **Cut the CRR tax wedge.** Remunerate reserves held above prudential minimums at a discount to the Standing Deposit Facility rate (Answer 10's interim step). At 45% unremunerated, the effective breakeven cost of loanable deposits roughly doubles at a 12% deposit rate (Answer 10's calculation); no MPR cut can offset a wedge of that size for the marginal borrower.
4. **Make the MPR the marginal price of funds.** A symmetric, consistently enforced corridor around the MPR, an end to arbitrary CRR debits, and strict limits on Ways and Means financing (Answer 7) are the preconditions — but they only bite once mechanisms 1–3 stop overriding the price signal with quantity rationing and unpriceable risk.

## Caveats

- The LDR penalty (additional CRR of 50% of the shortfall) is reported in Omaplex Law Firm's review of the April 2024 circular; I did not open the CBN circular itself.
- The GTCO LDR figure (~24–25%) is Answer 12's, not independently verified by me; I use it only to show that actual lending can sit far below the floor.
- Bureau coverage of ~14% is a 2020 figure (CRC Credit Bureau via MSME Africa Online); the 2024 Findex (6.1% formal borrowing) and 2026 EFInA survey (10% access) are the fresher evidence that the gap persists.
- The September 2026 lending-rate series conflict with each other (see section 3); they should be checked against CBN statistical tables before being used as a pass-through estimate.

## The cut that wasn't 350 basis points — and the floor that now outbids the sovereign

Start with a dated correction, because the arithmetic of the September decision is where the pass-through puzzle actually lives. As of 15 November 2026 there has been no November policy decision: the 308th MPC meeting is scheduled for 23–24 November (Daily Trust, 2026), and the CBN's own decisions register still shows the 307th meeting of 21–22 September as the latest entry (Central Bank of Nigeria [CBN], 2026b). Any statement that the MPR was "held at 23% in November" is describing a meeting that has not happened. The governing stance is the 22 September reset.

That reset was 350bp at the headline and 200bp at the only rate the market actually trades at. The corridor arithmetic, from the CBN's own register:

- Before (306th meeting, July 2026): MPR 26.50%, corridor +50/−450 → standing lending facility 27.00%, standing deposit facility 22.00%, width 500bp.
- After (307th meeting, September 2026): MPR 23.00%, corridor +50/−300 → SLF 23.50%, SDF 20.00%, width 350bp.

So the ceiling fell 350bp and the floor fell 200bp. The corridor was compressed from above, not shifted down. In a system with structural surplus liquidity — banks' balances at the CBN were reported at ₦82.99 trillion in August 2026, down 1.14% (allAfrica, 2026) — the marginal naira is not borrowed at the ceiling and not lent at the MPR. It is parked at the floor. The price that clears Nigerian money is the deposit-facility rate, and it moved by 57% of the advertised impulse (200/350). Every post-September comparison of lending rates against "a 350bp cut" therefore overstates the impulse by roughly 43% before any bank behaviour is invoked.

**The deeper point: the policy rate was adjusted to the market, not the market to the policy rate.** Before September the floor sat 450bp below the MPR, so any headline MPR between roughly 22.5% and 26% would have been non-binding — the market cleared at 22% while the CBN announced 26.5%. That is precisely what the Committee conceded, in its own words: "the observed divergence between the MPR and the prevailing market rates had weakened the effectiveness of monetary policy transmission," and the recalibration "does not constitute a change in the current monetary policy stance" but is "an operational reset" ahead of "the transition to an inflation targeting framework" (CBN, 2026a). A central bank that lowers its target to where the market already sits has not transmitted anything. The observed non-response of lending rates after September is therefore not evidence about the pass-through coefficient at all; it is evidence that no impulse was delivered. Answers that read the episode as a natural experiment on β are reading noise as signal.

## The central bank's own deposit window is now the binding competitor to lending

The standard crowding-out story says government paper pulls banks away from private credit. In Nigeria the ordering is one step worse, and the mechanism is inside the policy framework rather than in fiscal policy. With the floor at 20.00%, a bank can place naira overnight at the central bank at a rate above what the sovereign pays: the government's own paper is quoted at "about 18% to 19%" (Nnamka, 2026). The SDF is not merely risk-free, it is above the risk-free sovereign yield, with no duration, no credit assessment and no risk weight. Fiscal crowding-out has been *underwritten by the monetary authority's floor*.

Measured in real terms against August 2026 headline inflation of 15.39% (CBN, 2026a), the ladder looks like this (Fisher-exact, computed from the stated nominals):

- SDF 20.00% → +4.0% real
- MPR 23.00% → +6.6% real
- SLF 23.50% → +7.0% real
- government paper at 18.5% → +2.7% real
- prime business loan at 30% → +12.7% real
- maximum rate at 46% → +26.5% real
- savings deposit at 8% → −6.4% real

Two things follow. First, the hurdle a lender must clear to make a risky SME loan is a *positive real* 4% available at zero cost, so the relevant test is not "does the loan beat cash" but "does the loan beat 20% nominal after expected loss". A 30% loan carries only a 10pp nominal spread over the SDF; a plausible expected loss on an unsecured Nigerian SME exposure eats most of it, and the rational response is rationing rather than repricing — which is exactly what the loan data show: fewer than one in twenty of roughly 40 million SMEs holds a bank loan, and such firms take about 1% of all credit (Nnamka, 2026).

Second, and this is the part the level-pass-through debate misses: **the broken link is on the deposit side, not the lending side.** The 19.1pp gap between the real prime lending rate (+12.7%) and the real savings rate (−6.4%) is the object that does not respond to policy, and it is a *spread*, not a *level*. A policy rate can pass through completely in levels — every nominal rate falling one-for-one — while that spread is untouched, and it is the spread that decides whether investment is financed. Asymmetric corridors make this mechanical rather than behavioural: when the floor and the ceiling move by different amounts, the intermediation margin is a policy residual.

## Why the aggregate effect is small even if transmission were perfect

Nigeria's bank credit is a thin object. Loans to businesses and households together are about 13% of GDP, against roughly 20% in the rest of Sub-Saharan Africa and near 90% in South Africa (Nnamka, 2026); the CBN's broader "credit to private sector" measure puts the ratio at 21.3% of GDP versus a 33.0% Sub-Saharan average (Strategy&, 2026). The 8pp gap between those two published ratios is itself informative — the broader series includes claims that are not bank loans to firms and households — but take the generous end. A full, textbook 350bp reduction in the rate on the entire stock cuts the private interest bill by 0.035 × 0.213 ≈ 0.75% of GDP; at the 13% measure it is 0.46% of GDP; at a realistic 30% pass-through it is 0.14–0.22% of GDP. The policy rate's real leverage in Nigeria runs through the *government's* interest bill and through the return on banks' ₦83 trillion of CBN balances, not through business lending. That is a composition fact, not a bank-behaviour fact, and no reform of the corridor changes it quickly.

## What would actually move the numbers, in order of arithmetic leverage

1. **Re-price the floor, not the midpoint.** The single highest-leverage change is to put the deposit facility below the sovereign yield rather than 1pp above it — by widening the negative leg of the corridor, or by making remunerated SDF access a quota rather than an open window. Every 100bp taken off the floor is 100bp taken off the risk-free hurdle that every loan must beat, and unlike a CRR change it does not release liquidity into the FX or goods market. The September reset narrowed the corridor but left the floor above government paper; that ordering is the defect.

2. **Sequence CRR cuts against the gross-up, and size them honestly.** The mechanical arithmetic is 1/(1−CRR): at 45% the multiplier is 1.818, at 40% it is 1.667, at 35% it is 1.538. On a 4.2–5.0% deposit cost, each 5pp of CRR relief is worth about 64–76bp of funding cost per lendable naira — larger than the 40–50bp commonly quoted, but still a fraction of the 10pp spread over the SDF. CRR reform is necessary and insufficient; it should be paced to disinflation because it releases liquidity.

3. **Attack the loss-given-default term, which no rate decision touches.** Credit information coverage, movable-collateral perfection and recovery speed change expected loss directly. This is the only lever that moves the 30–46% band without moving the SDF, and it is where the marginal basis point is cheapest per unit of inflation risk.

4. **Rebuild the deposit side, not just the asset side.** The −6.4% real return on savings is why deposit rates do not transmit; competition from money-market funds, agency banking and treasury-bill access for small savers is the channel that would. Deposit-rate pass-through is the precondition for lending-rate pass-through being *sustainable* rather than a margin sacrifice.

5. **Stop reading the September episode as a test.** With a 200bp floor move, an inflation rate still at 15.4%, and a corridor deliberately recalibrated rather than eased, the post-September stability of lending rates is consistent with *complete* transmission of a small impulse. The test to run is the next MPR change, now that the floor sits 300bp — not 450bp — under the MPR and the gap between policy and market has been closed by construction.

## Calibration

High confidence in the corridor arithmetic, the inflation print and the real-rate ladder: they are computed from the CBN's own published decisions and communiqué. Medium confidence that the SDF is the binding marginal rate: it follows from the ₦83 trillion of bank balances at the CBN and from the Committee's own admission of MPR–market divergence, but I could not verify whether remunerated SDF access is capped per bank — if it is, the floor argument holds only up to the cap, and the effective marginal return for a bank with large surplus liquidity would be lower than 20%. Medium confidence on the 13%-versus-21.3% credit-to-GDP gap being definitional; reconciling it requires the CBN's own monetary survey, which I did not consult. The 30–46% lending range and the 8% savings rate are a market survey, not an official series, so treat them as indicative of the order of magnitude rather than as measured averages. I offer no pass-through coefficient: the September decision cannot identify one, and I would not trust an estimate that used it.

## Short answer

As of November 2026, the clearest evidence that the Central Bank of Nigeria's (CBN) policy rate passes through weakly to lending rates is the CBN's own easing cycle: the Monetary Policy Rate (MPR) was cut by 450 basis points in total — from 27.5% in September 2025 to 23.0% on 22 September 2026 — yet average prime lending rates *rose* in 8 of 11 economic sectors between August 2025 and October 2026, and the average maximum lending rate eased only from 33.78% to 32.58% over the same period (CBN published Deposit and Lending Rates schedules, analysed by QNC News, 2 November 2026, https://qncnews.com/2026/11/02/cbn-rate-cuts-fail-to-lower-bank-lending-costs-for-top-borrowers/ ; InfoHub Facts, https://www.infohubfacts.com/finance/business/nigerian-banks-defy-cbn-rate-cuts-raise-lending-rates).

The transmission failure is not mainly about the level of the policy rate. It is about the policy rate not being the marginal price of funds, banks protecting margins asymmetrically, and credit being rationed rather than repriced.

## 1. The MPR was not the price that cleared the market — the deposit-facility floor was

Before the September 2026 reset, the MPR stood at 26.5% while interbank rates were around 22% — the same level as the Standing Deposit Facility (SDF) rate. In other words, the SDF floor, not the MPR, was pricing the money market (Proshare, "Deconstructing CBN's 23% MPR Reset", https://proshare.co/articles/deconstructing-cbns-23-mpr-reset-and-its-sdf-corridor-realignment?menu=Economy&classification=Read&category=Monetary+Policy). The CBN itself framed the 350bp cut to 23.0% as an "operational reset" to realign the MPR with where money was already pricing, explicitly stating that recalibrating the corridor (to +50/-300 basis points, from +50/-450) "did not constitute a change in the current monetary policy stance" (CBN 307th MPC communiqué, 22 September 2026, reported by The Nation, https://www.national.com.ng/2026/11/14/cbn-resets-interest-rate-to-23/).

This matters for transmission: a rate that sits above the market-clearing rate cannot pull lending rates down when it is cut, because banks were never funding at that rate in the first place. The CBN's adoption of the Nigerian Overnight Financing Rate (NOFR) as a transaction-based operational benchmark is part of the same repair — an attempt to anchor the system to an observed market rate rather than an announced one (Proshare, same article). Until the MPR binds on banks' actual marginal funding costs, changes in it are signalling, not pricing.

## 2. The asymmetry is quantified — and it is extreme

The IMF's Selected Issues Paper on Nigeria (Fernandes and Stumphius, SIP/2026/045, June 2026, https://www.imf.org/en/publications/selected-issues-papers/issues/2026/06/17/nigerias-shift-to-a-floating-regime-interest-rate-and-exchange-rate-pass-through-and-policy-577017) estimates that a 100-basis-point *increase* in the MPR raises Treasury-bill and lending rates by roughly 175 to 180 basis points on impact, while an equivalent *cut* lowers them by only about 25 to 30 basis points — a "rockets-and-feathers" pattern the Fund calls statistically significant (reported by BusinessDay, https://businessday.ng/news/article/banks-pass-on-rate-hikes-faster-than-cuts-imf-says/?amp). The same paper finds the interbank call rate now exhibits almost one-for-one pass-through from the MPR, but that "key market rates are not yet firmly anchored to the MPR" — wholesale rates transmit, retail lending rates do not.

The September 2026 episode matches that estimate almost exactly: a 350bp cut produced, within a month, a *rise* in the average maximum lending rate from 29.20% (August) to 32.62% (September) and in the average prime rate from 17.86% to 19.04% (CBN September 2026 Money Market Indicators, reported by Daily News 24, https://dailynews24ng.com/nigerian-banks-cbn-interest-rates-savings-fixed-deposits-2026/).

## 3. Banks passed the cuts to depositors, not to borrowers — the margin evidence

The most telling asymmetry is between the two sides of banks' balance sheets. While prime lending rates rose in 8 of 11 sectors, the average savings deposit rate *fell* from 7.81% in August 2025 to 6.61% in October 2026 (QNC News, 2 November 2026, same link as above). Depositors felt the easing; borrowers did not. Sector detail from the CBN schedules makes the point concrete: average prime rates rose in agriculture, forestry and fishing from 23.44% to 24.77%, in construction from 25.25% to 26.40%, in manufacturing from 23.79% to 24.36%, and in real estate from 25.82% to 26.57% (QNC News / InfoHub Facts, same links as above). The Manufacturers Association of Nigeria's director-general said after the cut that even at a 23% MPR, the prime rate would still be 27–30% (reported by BankiBusiness, https://bankibusiness.com/cbn-loan-interest-rate-after-mpr-cut-23-percent/).

This is margin protection, not a lag: banks reprice deposits down quickly because depositors have weak bargaining power, and keep lending rates up because credit risk and regulatory costs give them cover to do so.

## 4. The 45% cash reserve requirement taxes intermediation — and the CBN kept it

At the same September 2026 meeting that cut the MPR, the MPC retained the Cash Reserve Requirement at 45% for deposit money banks, 16% for merchant banks and 75% for non-Treasury Single Account public-sector deposits (CBN 307th MPC communiqué, via DealMakers BDC, https://www.dealmakersbdc.com/blog/beyond-the-23-what-the-cbns-latest-monetary-policy-decision-could-mean-for-businesses-294906e47573). With nearly half of every naira of deposits sterilised at the CBN unremunerated, banks must recover the cost on the lendable remainder, which widens spreads and dulls the response of lending rates to the policy rate. The IMF paper likewise calls for "a gradual streamlining" of the 45% CRR (reported by Europe Says, https://www.europesays.com/africa/295305/). Cutting the MPR while holding the CRR at 45% is pressing the accelerator with the handbrake on.

## 5. Banks ration credit rather than reprice it — the recapitalisation evidence

Transmission also fails on the quantity margin. Nigeria's bank recapitalisation exercise ended on 31 March 2026 with 33 banks meeting the new requirements and N4.65 trillion raised — yet loans and advances across eight major lenders grew just 2.4% to N55.66 trillion in the nine months to September 2026 (BusinessDay, 12 November 2026, https://businessday.ng/news/article/banks-n55-7trn-loan-book-awaits-recapitalisation-lift/). Banks emerged with far bigger capital buffers and still barely expanded lending. When banks respond to risk by not lending at all, the policy rate cannot reach borrowers through price changes, however large. The dispersion in the CBN's own published lending schedule underlines the point: as of 18 September 2026, prime rates across roughly thirty banks ranged from 3.00% (Guaranty Trust Bank) to 37.07% (Tatum Bank) and maximum rates up to 60% (Stanbic IBTC), a spread of up to 44 percentage points inside a single bank (Growth Intelligence Africa, week ending 16 October 2026, https://www.growthintelafrica.com/intelligence/nigeria/nigeria-2026-10-16). A single policy rate cannot transmit uniformly across a market that fragmented.

## 6. Risk-free sovereign yields compete with private lending

Sovereign paper offers banks a return that competes directly with lending to firms and households: at the 4 November 2026 Treasury-bill auction the one-year bill stopped at 15.80%, and the CBN's own OMO bills sold on 3 November at 17.67%–17.77% — both well below the 23% MPR (GoPexly, 5 November 2026, https://www.gopexly.com/trending/treasury-bill-auction-november-4-2026-rates-unchanged-omo, sourcing FMDA and BusinessDay). When market yields sit 5–7 percentage points below the policy rate, the MPR is not anchoring the yield curve at all, and banks can earn a comfortable spread holding government paper without underwriting private credit risk.

## What would make transmission work better

The fixes follow directly from the mechanisms above, in order of leverage:

1. **Make the MPR bind.** Complete the operational framework the CBN has started: anchor to the transaction-based NOFR, keep the corridor symmetric and narrow enough that the MPR — not the SDF floor — prices the interbank market, and publish the operational target so banks price off it. The September 2026 reset was a step in this direction; its test is whether interbank rates now track the MPR.
2. **Streamline the CRR.** A phased reduction of the 45% requirement for deposit money banks, as the IMF recommends, would lower the regulatory tax on intermediation and narrow the spread banks must charge over funding costs.
3. **Attack the margin asymmetry directly.** The CBN already publishes weekly Deposit and Lending Rates schedules; making those schedules bank-by-bank, timely and prominent — and tying supervisory attention to persistent outliers — would discipline the deposit-down/lending-up pattern documented above.
4. **Fix credit rationing, not just pricing.** Expand collateral registries, enforce contracts faster, and deepen credit reporting so banks price risk instead of refusing it; the recapitalisation gave banks capacity, but only lower information and enforcement costs will convert capacity into loans.
5. **Reduce sovereign competition for bank balance sheets.** Fiscal consolidation that lowers government borrowing would push banks back toward private lending; as long as risk-free paper yields close to lending economics, crowding-out will persist.

## What to watch

The 308th MPC meeting is scheduled for 23–24 November 2026 (CBN MPC calendar, via GoPexly, same link as above). If the Committee holds at 23% while the September cut still has not reached lending rates, that will confirm the problem is transmission, not the level of the rate — and the market test will be the CBN's lending-rate schedules and OMO stop rates in the weeks after, not the communiqué itself.

## Bottom line

Pass-through is weak because the MPR was, until September 2026, a rate above where the market actually cleared; because banks pass hikes through at roughly six times the speed of cuts (IMF: +175–180bp versus −25–30bp per 100bp of MPR); because a 45% CRR taxes every loan; and because banks ration credit rather than reprice it. The September 2026 natural experiment proves the point: a 450bp cumulative cut left prime rates higher in 8 of 11 sectors while deposit rates fell. Transmission will improve only when the MPR binds on marginal funding, the CRR is streamlined, and the credit infrastructure lets banks lend instead of ration — not from further cuts to a rate that does not bind.

This analysis provides a foundational, first-principles examination of the monetary transmission mechanism in Nigeria as of late 2026. Rather than treating interest rate pass-through as a single aggregate elastic function, we trace transmission across five sequential financial friction layers:
1. **The Reserve Tax Wedge (Cash Reserve Ratio Friction)**: How unremunerated, high reserve requirements break the classical link between the central bank policy rate and marginal funding costs.
2. **Sovereign Crowding-Out and Risk-Free Arbitrage**: Why sovereign debt absorption prevents policy rate changes from translating into private balance-sheet expansion.
3. **Banking Market Oligopoly and Deposit Inelasticity**: How structural concentration in low-cost Current and Savings Accounts (CASA) insulates banks' funding costs from policy rate fluctuations.
4. **Institutional Credit-Risk Premia**: How legal enforcement costs, information opacity, and collateral impairment override benchmark rate movements.
5. **Informality and Non-Bank Financial Intermediation**: Why retail and household credit demand bypasses central bank interest rate signals entirely.

### Part I: Causal Mechanisms Behind Weak Monetary Policy Rate (MPR) Pass-Through

In a standard textbook economy, an adjustment in the central bank's policy rate flows sequentially:
$$\Delta \text{Policy Rate} \longrightarrow \Delta \text{Interbank / Money Market Rates} \longrightarrow \Delta \text{Marginal Cost of Funds} \longrightarrow \Delta \text{Retail Deposit \& Lending Rates}$$

In Nigeria, structural and institutional bottlenecks interrupt this causal chain at every node.

#### 1. The Reserve Tax and Discretionary Sterilization Wedge
* **Mechanism**: To curb excess structural liquidity and combat currency pressures, the Central Bank of Nigeria (CBN) relies heavily on a high Cash Reserve Ratio (CRR)—empirically estimated in the range of $40\%$ to $50\%$ of bank deposits—frequently supplemented by discretionary or asymmetric debits. Because cash reserves held at the central bank are unremunerated, they act as an implicit regulatory tax on financial intermediation.
* **Causal Chain**: 
  1. For every unit of deposit mobilized, a bank can only lend out a fraction $(1 - \text{CRR})$.
  2. To cover the zero-return cost on the immobilized reserve portion while targeting a return on equity, the bank must increase the lending margin on the loanable fraction.
  3. Effective lending rate pricing follows the structural floor:
     $$R_{\text{lending}} \approx \frac{R_{\text{cost of funds}} + C_{\text{operating}} + \text{Risk Premium}}{1 - \text{CRR}}$$
  4. When the policy rate rises, the bank’s marginal cost of liabilities increases, but the crushing magnitude of the unremunerated reserve ratio amplifies the spread non-linearly. Conversely, when the policy rate is lowered, banks cannot pass rate cuts to borrowers because their average cost of mobilized deposits remains inflated by the unremunerated reserve drag. As a result, the policy rate ceases to serve as an effective marginal pricing anchor.

#### 2. Risk-Free Sovereign Arbitrage and Crowding-Out
* **Mechanism**: High fiscal deficits and public borrowing needs require continuous domestic debt issuance by the Federal Government of Nigeria (FGN Treasury Bills, FGN Bonds, and Open Market Operations bills).
* **Causal Chain**:
  1. Risk-adjusted yields on short-to-medium-term government paper historically offer high returns (estimated in the range of $18\%$ to $26\%$).
  2. Nigerian deposit money banks face an allocation decision: invest liquid funds in zero-risk-weight sovereign paper, or extend loans to private firms burdened by macroeconomic volatility and foreign exchange risks.
  3. The return on private lending must clear the hurdle rate:
     $$R_{\text{lending}} > R_{\text{sovereign}} + \text{Expected Default Loss} + \text{Capital Charge}$$
  4. Consequently, rate hikes at the policy level simply raise sovereign debt yields, drawing commercial bank liquidity further away from private credit markets. Credit rationing dominates over price adjustments: rather than adjusting private lending volumes smoothly via price elasticity, banks ration private credit to minimize capital-at-risk.

#### 3. Banking Oligopoly and Deposit Rate Rigidity
* **Mechanism**: The Nigerian commercial banking sector is heavily concentrated, with a small tier of dominant banks controlling an estimated $65\%$ to $75\%$ of system-wide deposits.
* **Causal Chain**:
  1. Tier-1 banks hold a dominant share of non-interest-bearing or ultra-low-cost CASA balances from households and corporate operating accounts.
  2. Because retail depositors face high switching costs, weak consumer financial literacy, and limited alternative short-term liquid stores of value, deposit supply is highly interest-inelastic.
  3. When the policy rate moves, commercial banks adjust deposit rates minimally. Because average funding costs remain stable, banks face weak internal liability-side pressure to adjust lending rates for existing borrowers. Policy rate pass-through to deposit rates remains near zero for retail savers, severing the liability side of the transmission mechanism.

#### 4. Institutional Frictions: Information Asymmetry and Contract Invalidation
* **Mechanism**: Pass-through models assume that the default risk premium is an additive constant that allows lending rates to move in lockstep with the risk-free rate ($\Delta R_{\text{lending}} \approx \Delta R_{\text{policy}}$). In Nigeria, the risk premium is endogenous and variable.
* **Causal Chain**:
  1. A rising policy rate worsens debt-service capacity across Nigerian businesses contending with structural inflation, infrastructure bottlenecks, and exchange-rate depreciation.
  2. Lenders anticipate that raising lending rates in tandem with policy hikes causes severe adverse selection and moral hazard.
  3. In addition, weak title registration systems, protracted judicial proceedings for debt recovery (often taking between 3 to 10 years across commercial courts), and imperfect credit registry tracking raise the expected loss given default (LGD).
  4. Lenders respond by freezing credit lines or setting prohibitive maximum lending rates (estimated in the range of $30\%$ to $40\%$) only for distressed rolled-over facilities, while leaving prime corporate rates dictated by bilateral competitive bargaining rather than the policy benchmark.

### Part III: What Would Make Monetary Policy Transmission Work Better?

To establish a functioning interest rate channel where adjustments in the policy rate smoothly determine retail lending rates, structural reforms must target the transmission frictions directly:

#### 1. Transition from Administrative Reserve Quotas to Market-Based Operations
* **Action**: Unify and lower the statutory Cash Reserve Ratio into an estimated target band of $10\%$ to $20\%$, eliminating discretionary ad-hoc debits.
* **Causal Impact**: Reduces the unremunerated reserve tax wedge. By enabling commercial banks to deploy a larger portion of their mobilized liabilities into interest-bearing assets, the structural markup between deposit and lending spreads narrows, restoring the policy rate as the true determinant of marginal cost.

#### 2. Re-anchoring the Policy Corridor via Symmetrical Standing Facilities
* **Action**: Maintain a transparent, symmetric interest rate corridor around the policy rate (e.g., $\pm 200$ to $\pm 300$ basis points for the Standing Lending Facility and Standing Deposit Facility), ensuring the central bank's standing windows clear all interbank trades without volume caps.
* **Causal Impact**: Anchors the interbank overnight rate directly to the policy rate, preventing interbank trading from drifting far below or spiking above official policy targets.

#### 3. Strengthening Legal and Institutional Credit Recovery Infrastructure
* **Action**:
  * Expand the enforcement of the Global Standing Instruction (GSI) mandate to automatically cover non-bank deposit institutions, fintech wallets, and investment holdings across the entire financial system.
  * Establish specialized, expedited commercial debt tribunals to resolve contract enforcement and collateral foreclosure within a defined timeline (e.g., under 180 days).
* **Causal Impact**: Reduces loss given default (LGD) and lowers the structural risk premium, allowing lenders to price credit based on base rates rather than defensive risk markups.

#### 4. Fiscal Consolidation and Sovereign Yield Curve Rationalization
* **Action**: Constrain direct and indirect sovereign borrowing from domestic commercial banks, enforcing strict statutory boundaries on fiscal deficit monetization and capping sovereign bill yields below private investment hurdle rates.
* **Causal Impact**: Eliminates risk-free arbitrage, compelling bank treasury desks to re-engage in corporate and SME underwriting to maintain portfolio yields.

#### 5. Financial Deepening and Digital Collateral Registries
* **Action**: Scale the National Collateral Registry (NCR) for movable assets and integrate centralized digital identities (such as the Bank Verification Number [BVN] and National Identification Number [NIN]) across all micro-lending platforms.
* **Causal Impact**: Eliminates duplicate identity fraud and lowers information verification costs, linking informal and retail credit pricing to systemic liquidity rather than individualized default-risk cushions.

### Uncertainty Calibration and Structural Constraints

* **Fiscal Dominance Variability**: The speed and feasibility of normalising the Cash Reserve Ratio depend directly on fiscal deficit trends. If public financing requirements remain elevated, the central bank may continue using high reserve ratios as an informal domestic liquidity sink, limiting the pace of corridor reform.
* **Informal Economy Bounds**: Approximately $50\%$ to $65\%$ of Nigerian economic output is estimated to occur within the informal cash and unregistered business sector. Because interest rate channels rely on formal balance sheets, monetary transmission will remain structurally constrained until informal transactions migrate into formal, trackable financial channels.

The short answer is that Nigerian banks do transmit the policy rate — but asymmetrically, and mostly upward. The IMF's June 2026 Selected Issues Paper on Nigeria, accompanying its Article IV consultation, measured the asymmetry precisely: a 100-basis-point increase in the MPR raises Treasury-bill and lending rates by roughly 175–180 basis points on impact, while an equivalent 100-basis-point cut lowers them by only about 25–30 basis points. Banks amplify tightening by ~75% and absorb ~75% of easing. That single finding explains why households and firms feel every hike and almost no cut.

**Why the pass-through is so weak on the way down**

1. **Market structure — an oligopoly with pricing power.** Nigeria's five largest banks (Access, UBA, Zenith, First HoldCo, GTCO) hold more than three-quarters of banking-sector assets, which stood at ₦161.3 trillion at end-2025. With so few dominant lenders and thin competition for prime corporate borrowers, there is little competitive pressure to reprice loans down. The same concentration shows up in the data: after the CBN cut the MPR by 450bp over 13 months (27.5% → 27.0% in September 2025 → 26.5% in February 2026 → 23.0% in September 2026), average prime lending rates actually *rose* in 8 of 11 economic sectors between August 2025 and October 2026, according to Financial Vanguard's analysis of the CBN's own rate schedules published 2 November 2026. Agriculture prime rose 23.44% → 24.77%; construction 25.25% → 26.40%. The average maximum lending rate fell only 33.78% → 32.58% — 120bp of relief against a 450bp policy cut.

2. **The funding-cost floor: a 45% cash reserve requirement.** Deposit money banks must park 45% of deposits at the CBN (16% for merchant banks, 75% for non-Treasury Single Account public-sector deposits). That sterilises nearly half of every naira of deposits, so banks' marginal funding cost barely moves when the MPR falls. The day after the September 2026 cut, banks placed ₦7.33 trillion in the CBN's Standing Deposit Facility — a seven-month high — parking liquidity at 20.00% rather than lending it out.

3. **Risk pricing dominates the policy rate.** The MPR is one input; the spread is set by borrower risk, collateral enforcement and operating costs. Private-sector credit is only about 12% of GDP (IMF, 2025), so banks lend to a narrow, screened pool and price the rest out. With headline inflation at 15.39% (August 2026) and a history of double-digit inflation, nominal lending rates carry a large risk and inflation premium that does not compress just because the benchmark moved.

4. **Broken credibility from the 2016–2023 period.** The IMF found transmission "broke down entirely" between 2016 and 2023, when defending the exchange rate repeatedly conflicted with monetary-policy objectives. The June 2023 FX unification restored the channel for market rates — T-bill yields now respond strongly — but lending-rate behaviour still carries the legacy: banks learned to treat CBN signals as reversible, so they reprice up fast (to protect margins) and down slowly (to see if the cut sticks).

5. **The September 2026 reset itself was an admission of disconnect.** The CBN cut 350bp on 22 September 2026 — the largest single move since the MPR was introduced in 2006 — explicitly because the old 26.5% benchmark had become disconnected from market rates: interbank rates were already around 22%. The MPC reset the corridor to +50/−300bp (standing lending facility 23.50%, deposit facility 20.00%) and called it an "operational reset" to restore the MPR as the principal signal. The 308th MPC meeting then held the rate at 23%, pausing to assess impact. Even the CBN concedes the headline rate had stopped being the binding price of money.

**What would make transmission work better**

- **Publish pass-through.** Require banks to disclose, regularly and publicly, what share of each MPR change they transmit to lending rates, by segment. The asymmetry survives partly because it is invisible; a published pass-through ratio creates reputational and competitive pressure.
- **Lower the CRR overhang.** A phased reduction of the 45% CRR would reconnect banks' marginal funding costs to the policy rate; as long as nearly half of deposits are sterilised, the MPR is a signal, not a cost.
- **Deepen competition and credit infrastructure.** Faster collateral enforcement, wider credit-bureau coverage and more mid-tier lenders would compress the risk premium that currently swamps the policy signal — the structural fix behind the 12%-of-GDP credit ratio.

The September 2026 cut is a live test: if prime and maximum lending rates have not converged toward the 23% anchor by the time the 308th MPC's pause ends, the problem is not the level of the rate — it is the structure underneath it. Keeping the 23% anchor credible matters most; another reversal would re-teach banks to wait out cuts.

As of November 2026, why does the Central Bank of Nigeria's policy rate pass through so weakly to lending rates for Nigerian businesses and households, and what would make transmission work better?

Short answer

Nigeria's monetary transmission is weak and, crucially, asymmetric: banks pass on rate rises quickly and even amplify them, but pass on rate cuts slowly and only partly. The International Monetary Fund's June 2026 Selected Issues paper on Nigeria found that a 100-basis-point rise in the Monetary Policy Rate (MPR) lifts Treasury bill and lending rates by roughly 175 to 180 basis points on impact, while an equivalent 100-basis-point cut lowers them by only about 25 to 30 basis points — a "rockets-and-feathers" pattern the IMF called statistically significant. The real-world proof arrived in 2026 itself: between August 2025 and October 2026 the Central Bank of Nigeria (CBN) cut the MPR by 450 basis points, yet average prime lending rates rose in eight of eleven economic sectors over the same period.

The facts as of November 2026

The MPR stood at 23 per cent. The CBN cut it by 350 basis points, from 26.5 per cent to 23 per cent, at its 307th Monetary Policy Committee (MPC) meeting on 22 September 2026 — the largest single reduction since 2006 — after earlier cuts to 27 per cent in September 2025 and 26.5 per cent in February 2026. The Committee then held the rate at 23 per cent at its 308th meeting in November 2026, with the next meeting scheduled for 23–24 November. The CBN described the September move as an "operational reset" to strengthen the MPR as the principal signal for interest rates, and recalibrated the Standing Facilities Corridor to +50 and -300 basis points around the MPR, putting the Standing Lending Facility at 23.5 per cent and the Standing Deposit Facility at 20 per cent. The Cash Reserve Requirement (CRR) was left at 45 per cent for deposit money banks, 16 per cent for merchant banks and 75 per cent for non-Treasury Single Account public-sector deposits. Headline inflation had eased to 15.39 per cent in August 2026 and 14.63 per cent in September, with analysts projecting about 13.59 per cent for October, while real GDP grew 4.43 per cent in the second quarter of 2026.

Yet commercial lending rates barely moved. According to CBN interest-rate schedules analysed by Financial Vanguard and reported in November 2026, average prime lending rates between August 2025 and October 2026 rose in agriculture (23.44 to 24.77 per cent), construction (25.25 to 26.40 per cent), manufacturing (23.79 to 24.36 per cent) and real estate (25.82 to 26.57 per cent), among others. The average maximum lending rate fell only from 33.78 to 32.58 per cent. The Manufacturers Association of Nigeria warned that even at a 23 per cent MPR, prime lending rates would remain around 27 to 30 per cent, against 8 to 12 per cent in Egypt, Morocco and South Africa. Why pass-through is so weak

1. Asymmetric pricing and concentrated market power. The IMF's rockets-and-feathers finding is the core of the story: banks amplify tightening (passing on about 175 per cent of a rise) and absorb easing (passing on only about 25–30 per cent of a cut). Nigeria's five largest banks — Access, UBA, Zenith, First HoldCo and GTCO — hold more than three-quarters of the industry's ₦161.3 trillion in total assets (end-2025), so competitive pressure to pass cuts on to borrowers is limited.

2. The 45 per cent Cash Reserve Requirement acts as a tax on lending. With nearly half of every deposit locked in non-interest-bearing reserves at the CBN, banks must earn their margin on the lendable remainder, widening the spread between the policy rate and the lending rate. The IMF specifically identified the 45 per cent CRR as an area requiring reform. A 2026 study of monetary policy and bank credit in Nigeria (2010–2025) found the MPR had a negative but statistically insignificant effect on private-sector credit growth, while liquidity instruments — above all the CRR — exerted significant influence. Transmission in Nigeria runs mainly through the liquidity channel, not the price channel, so moving the headline rate alone does relatively little.

3. Crowding out by government securities. Banks hold about 22 per cent of their total assets in government securities, which offer an attractive risk-free return with no credit risk, no provisioning and no recovery effort. Credit to the government rose 63 per cent year-on-year to ₦39.4 trillion by September 2026, against 16 per cent growth in private-sector credit to ₦83.9 trillion. When a bank can earn a high, risk-free yield on Treasury bills, the opportunity cost of lending to a risky manufacturer is high. The World Bank warned in September 2026 that banks "can no longer rely solely on government securities for yield" and must redirect capital towards job-creating growth.

4. A large credit-risk premium. Lending rates are the MPR plus a risk premium, and Nigeria's premium is large and sticky. The industry non-performing loan (NPL) ratio rose to 8.03 per cent in January 2026 — about ₦6.04 trillion of troubled loans — after the CBN withdrew pandemic-era regulatory forbearance in mid-2025, well above the CBN's 5 per cent prudential ceiling. S&P Global projected NPLs of 6 to 7 per cent through 2026, with Stage 2 loans at 20 to 22 per cent of the book. Roughly half of bank loans are denominated in foreign currency and about a third are linked to oil and gas, so credit quality is hostage to oil prices and the exchange rate. Banks price this risk into every loan, so a lower MPR shrinks only the risk-free component of the rate, not the premium.

5. A shallow financial system with a huge informal economy. Private-sector credit is only about 12 to 13 per cent of GDP (the IMF's May 2026 assessment put it at about 12 per cent; the African Development Bank's 2026 African Economic Outlook put bank lending to business at 9.4 per cent of GDP), against 38.1 per cent in lower-middle-income economies. Fewer than one in twenty micro, small and medium-sized enterprises can access bank credit, while about nine in ten operate informally, according to the World Bank. Small and medium enterprises receive roughly 1 per cent of total bank credit. Manufacturing credit fell 33.8 per cent, from ₦8.53 trillion in December 2024 to ₦5.65 trillion in August 2026. When most households and small firms never borrow from a bank at all, the interest-rate channel has almost nothing to act on.

6. The policy rate itself had become disconnected from market rates, and credit infrastructure is weak. Before the September 2026 reset, the MPR stood at 26.5 per cent while interbank rates were around 22 per cent; the CBN itself said the benchmark had become misaligned with prevailing market rates, weakening the signal. A 2026 study covering 2002–2024 found the real interest rate had a positive but statistically insignificant effect on the prime lending rate, and the IMF found deposit rates barely react to the MPR in either direction, so banks' funding costs do not fall when the MPR falls. Poor information on borrowers, slow contract enforcement and weak collateral recovery further raise the cost of every loan, and about 55 per cent of bank credit matures in under one year, so banks reprice frequently on the way up but face little pressure to reprice down.

What would make transmission work better

The September 2026 reset shows the CBN already recognises the problem, but a lower MPR alone will not fix it. The evidence points to a package, roughly in order of importance:

First, complete the operational-framework reform. The recalibrated corridor (+50/-300 basis points) and the "reset" are designed to make the MPR anchor the interbank rate, as the IMF recommended. That requires consistent open-market operations and liquidity management so the overnight rate stays close to the MPR. If the interbank rate tracks the MPR, banks' funding costs genuinely fall when the MPR falls, giving them a reason to cut lending rates.

Second, reform the Cash Reserve Requirement. A gradual reduction of the 45 per cent CRR — or remunerating part of it — would directly lower the tax on intermediation, narrow spreads and strengthen the price channel relative to the liquidity channel. This is the single most powerful lever the CBN controls, and the IMF has explicitly flagged it.

Third, reduce fiscal dominance and crowding out. As long as government borrowing grows far faster than private credit and risk-free yields stay high, banks will prefer bills to business loans. Sustained fiscal consolidation is a precondition for the MPR to bite on private lending.

Fourth, attack the risk premium with credit infrastructure. Full enforcement of the Global Standing Instruction framework, the CBN's March 2026 directive denying new credit to obligors with non-performing loans recorded in the Credit Risk Management System or private credit bureaus, deeper credit-bureau coverage, reliable collateral registries and faster debt recovery through the credit tribunals under the Banks and Other Financial Institutions Act 2020 would all lower the cost of lending to good borrowers.

Fifth, deepen competition and transparency. More competition among banks, including from fintechs and non-bank lenders, would compress the margins that let banks absorb rate cuts. Publishing bank-level pass-through — how much of each MPR change each bank transmits to lending rates — would create public accountability for the rockets-and-feathers pattern.

Sixth, deepen the financial system itself. Expanding access to credit for SMEs and households — through development finance, credit guarantees, movable-collateral lending and the formalisation of informal businesses — widens the population the interest-rate channel can reach. Without that, even perfect pass-through would touch only a small share of the economy.

Finally, anchor expectations. Transmission works best when rate changes are seen as durable. The disinflation now under way gives the CBN room to ease, but if banks expect the next move to be a reversal, they will not reprice loans. Clear communication and a steady sequence of decisions — which the November MPC will test on 23–24 November — matter as much as the level of the rate.

## Short answer

As of November 2026, the Central Bank of Nigeria's policy rate passes through weakly to lending rates for a specific, diagnosable reason: **transmission is now two-speed, not uniformly broken.** Since the June 2023 foreign-exchange unification, the wholesale links of the chain work — the interbank call rate now moves almost one-for-one with the Monetary Policy Rate (MPR), and Treasury-bill yields respond strongly. The break is at the last link, between banks' funding costs and the price a business or household actually pays for a loan. The IMF's June 2026 Selected Issues paper on Nigeria (Fernandes and Stumphius, SIP/2026/045) measured the asymmetry precisely: a 100-basis-point rise in the MPR lifts Treasury-bill and lending rates by roughly 175–180 basis points on impact, while an equivalent 100-basis-point cut lowers them by only about 25–30 basis points. Banks amplify tightening and absorb easing — "rockets and feathers".

The consequence is a **ratchet**: each full tightening-then-easing cycle leaves lending rates higher than where the cycle started, even if the policy rate ends exactly where it began. That ratchet, plus the fact that the September 2026 cut was an operational realignment rather than stimulus, is the core of the answer. Fixing transmission therefore means fixing the last link — the reserve-requirement tax, the risk premium, competition, and the deposit channel — not cutting the MPR further and hoping.

One correction to the record matters before the substance. Several earlier answers state that the MPC "held" the rate at 23% at its 308th meeting in November 2026. As of the date this question was asked, 15 November 2026, that meeting had not yet taken place: the CBN's own communiqué from the 307th meeting (21–22 September 2026) schedules the 308th meeting for 23–24 November 2026, and Access Bank's MPC preview of 13 November expected a hold at that meeting. The latest actual decision as of mid-November was therefore the September cut, and the 23–24 November meeting is the first real test of whether the reset is working — not a verdict already delivered.

## The record as of mid-November 2026

The easing cycle ran 27.5% (September 2025) to 27.0%, then 26.5% (February 2026), then a 350-basis-point cut to 23.0% on 22 September 2026 at the 307th MPC meeting — the largest single reduction since the MPR was introduced in 2006. The Standing Facilities Corridor was recalibrated to +50/−300 basis points around the MPR (Standing Lending Facility 23.5%, Standing Deposit Facility 20.0%). The Cash Reserve Requirement was left unchanged at 45% for deposit money banks, 16% for merchant banks, and 75% for non-Treasury Single Account public-sector deposits. Headline inflation had eased to 15.39% in August 2026 and 14.63% in September, down from 34.8% in November 2024, and real GDP grew 4.43% in the second quarter of 2026.

Against that 450-basis-point cumulative cut, lending rates barely moved — and for the best borrowers they moved the wrong way. Financial Vanguard's analysis of the CBN's own published deposit and lending rate schedules, reported in November 2026, found average prime lending rates rose in eight of eleven sectors between August 2025 and October 2026: agriculture 23.44% to 24.77%, construction 25.25% to 26.40%, manufacturing 23.79% to 24.36%, real estate 25.82% to 26.57%. The average maximum lending rate fell only from 33.78% to 32.58%. Meanwhile banks cut what they pay savers promptly: average savings deposit rates fell from 7.81% to 6.61% and time-deposit rates from 14.52% to 12.28% over the same window.

Two cautions belong with those numbers. First, the September cut came only 17 days before the October rate observation, so part of the apparent non-response is lag, not refusal — Nnamdi Nwizu of Comercio Partners made exactly this point, and it is a fair one. Second, the CBN's own framing matters: Director Hakama Sidi Ali said in November 2026 that the September move was "intended to improve the effectiveness of the policy rate as the principal signal", an operational realignment rather than a loosening. Judging the cut as failed stimulus misreads its purpose; the right test is whether market rates now sit inside the new corridor and track the MPR, which is what the 23–24 November meeting will assess.

## The new diagnosis: transmission is two-speed

The IMF paper's most important finding is not the asymmetry alone; it is that **transmission has strengthened since the FX unification, but unevenly**. Before June 2023, defending the exchange rate repeatedly conflicted with monetary-policy objectives, and the IMF found transmission had "broken down entirely" between 2016 and 2023. After unification, market rates respond strongly to the MPR — the interbank call rate exhibits almost one-for-one pass-through — but lending rates do not. The operating framework now works; the banking system does not transmit it.

That distinction changes the remedy. If the MPR were still disconnected from money markets, the fix would be operating-framework reform. The September 2026 reset did much of that work already. What remains is a set of wedges between banks' marginal funding cost and the all-in price of a loan, and those wedges are large relative to the policy rate itself. A loan rate can be decomposed as the funding cost, plus the reserve-requirement tax, plus the expected-loss charge, plus operating and capital costs, plus markup. When the MPR falls, only the first term falls — and in Nigeria it barely falls at all.

## The ratchet: what one full cycle costs borrowers

The IMF coefficients imply a quantified, compounding cost that earlier answers have not stated. Take a full cycle: the CBN raises the MPR by 100 basis points, then later cuts it by 100 basis points, ending exactly where it started. Lending rates rise by about 175–180 basis points on the way up and fall by only about 25–30 basis points on the way down. **The net effect is that lending rates end roughly 1.5 percentage points higher than before the cycle, with the policy rate unchanged.** Run that cycle twice and the wedge is about 3 percentage points — a permanent upward drift in the cost of credit that has nothing to do with the level of the MPR and everything to do with the asymmetry of bank pricing.

This is not a theoretical curiosity; it matches the 2025–2026 record. A 450-basis-point cumulative cut produced roughly 120 basis points of relief in the average maximum lending rate and none at all in prime rates for most sectors. If the asymmetry coefficients held mechanically, a 450-basis-point cut should have delivered about 110–135 basis points of lending-rate relief — which is close to what the maximum rate actually did. The prime-rate rises are the anomaly, and they point to the wedges widening at the same time as the policy rate fell: risk premia, funding-cost floors, and repricing behaviour moving against borrowers even as the benchmark eased.

## Why the last link breaks

**1. The 45% Cash Reserve Requirement is a tax on lending that the MPR cut did not touch.** With nearly half of every deposit locked in non-interest-bearing reserves at the CBN, banks must earn their margin on the lendable remainder. The September decision cut the price of money while leaving the quantity tax untouched — an unresolved contradiction that the CBN itself has not reconciled. The IMF's June 2026 paper and its earlier assessments both flag the CRR as an area requiring reform. The arithmetic is stark: at a 45% CRR, each naira of deposits yields only 55 kobo of lendable funds, so the effective funding cost per lendable naira is roughly 1.8 times the deposit rate. A cut in the MPR that does not move deposit rates — and the evidence is that deposit rates barely react to the MPR in either direction — therefore does almost nothing to the marginal cost of a loan.

**2. Market power lets banks absorb cuts.** Nigeria's five largest banks — Access, UBA, Zenith, First HoldCo and GTCO — hold more than three-quarters of the industry's ₦161.3 trillion in total assets (end-2025). With so few dominant lenders and thin competition for prime corporate borrowers, there is little pressure to reprice loans down. The asymmetry is the observable signature of that power: banks reprice up fast to protect margins and down slowly to see whether the cut sticks. This is also a credibility legacy — banks learned during 2016–2023 to treat CBN signals as reversible, so they wait out easing.

**3. Crowding out by government securities.** Banks hold about 22% of their total assets in government securities, which offer a high risk-free return with no credit risk, no provisioning and no recovery effort. Credit to the government rose 63% year-on-year to ₦39.4 trillion by September 2026, against 16% growth in private-sector credit to ₦83.9 trillion. When a bank can earn a high, risk-free yield on Treasury bills, the opportunity cost of lending to a risky manufacturer is high — and a lower MPR does not change that comparison, because the bill yield is itself anchored by the government's borrowing needs rather than by the policy rate.

**4. A large, sticky risk premium.** Lending rates are the policy rate plus a risk premium, and Nigeria's premium is large. The industry non-performing loan ratio rose to about 8% in January 2026 — roughly ₦6 trillion of troubled loans — after the CBN withdrew pandemic-era regulatory forbearance in mid-2025, well above the CBN's 5% prudential ceiling, with S&P Global projecting 6–7% through 2026 and Stage 2 loans at 20–22% of the book. Roughly half of bank loans are denominated in foreign currency and about a third are linked to oil and gas, so credit quality is hostage to oil prices and the exchange rate. Add weak credit information, slow contract enforcement and poor collateral recovery, and the premium becomes a floor that no MPR cut can reach. Manufacturing credit fell 33.8%, from ₦8.53 trillion in December 2024 to ₦5.65 trillion in August 2026, even as banks were recapitalised — capital was never the binding constraint; expected loss was.

**5. The deposit channel is broken in both directions, and households lose twice.** Savings deposit rates near 5–7% against a 23% MPR show depositors do not share in tightening, and the prompt fall in deposit rates when the MPR is cut shows they bear easing immediately. Households therefore lose on both sides of the cycle: their savings earn far below the policy rate when rates are high, and are cut further when rates fall, while their borrowing costs barely move. This is the household half of the question, and it is sharper than the business half: for a household with a salary loan or a small business loan priced near the maximum rate of about 32.6%, the MPR is nearly irrelevant to the price they pay.

**6. A shallow system limits the channel's reach.** Private-sector credit is only about 12% of GDP (IMF, 2026), against 38.1% in lower-middle-income economies, and bank lending to business is about 9.4% of GDP (African Development Bank, 2026). Fewer than one in twenty micro, small and medium-sized enterprises can access bank credit, while about nine in ten operate informally. Small and medium enterprises receive roughly 1% of total bank credit. Even perfect pass-through would touch only a small share of the economy — the interest-rate channel is narrow as well as weak.

**7. The reactivated exchange-rate channel cuts the other way.** The IMF paper's second finding deserves more weight than it has received: after the June 2023 unification, exchange-rate pass-through became positive and economically meaningful, particularly for external financial shocks such as US monetary tightening. That means easing now transmits through the naira as well as through interest rates — a rate cut that weakens the currency raises import prices and feeds back into inflation, which is itself a reason for banks to keep lending rates high. The MPC cannot treat the interest-rate channel in isolation; every cut is simultaneously a currency decision, and the exchange-rate channel may currently be the stronger of the two.

## What would make transmission work better

The package follows from the diagnosis, in rough order of importance — and each item has an observable test, so the 23–24 November meeting and the months after it can be judged on evidence rather than intentions.

**First, put the CRR on a published glide path.** A phased reduction of the 45% CRR toward emerging-market norms (10–15%), or remuneration of part of it, directly lowers the tax on intermediation. The credible, dated timetable matters more than the speed: banks price the expected future tax into today's lending rates, so an announced glide path compresses spreads immediately while an unannounced intention does not. The test: the effective funding-cost multiplier on lendable deposits falls, and the gap between the MPR and the marginal cost of funds narrows.

**Second, make the September reset operational and judge it on overnight rates.** The test of the framework change is whether the overnight interbank rate trades consistently within the new +50/−300 corridor around the 23% MPR, and whether the Nigerian Overnight Financing Rate tracks the MPR. The CBN should publish the daily deviation of the overnight rate from the MPR, and the MPC should treat persistent deviation as an implementation failure. If the operating target does not hold, no downstream reform can work, because banks' marginal funding cost will still not be the MPR.

**Third, publish bank-level pass-through.** The CBN already publishes weekly deposit and lending rate schedules; it should publish, bank by bank and segment by segment, what share of each MPR change each bank transmits to new-loan rates. The asymmetry survives partly because it is invisible. A published pass-through ratio creates reputational and competitive pressure, and it gives the MPC a gauge — new-loan rates and approval volumes, not the stock average lending rate — by which to judge its own decisions.

**Fourth, narrow the Standing Deposit Facility parking incentive.** The day after the September cut, banks placed ₦7.33 trillion in the SDF — a seven-month high — parking liquidity at 20.00% rather than lending it out. Banks should not earn more, risk-free, for parking liquidity than the sovereign pays to borrow it; the SDF floor is a subsidy for not lending, and it directly competes with every private loan.

**Fifth, attack the risk premium with credit infrastructure, and convert recapitalised balance sheets into lending with risk-sharing.** The ₦4.65 trillion recapitalisation completed in March 2026 produced only about 2.4% loan-book growth, because capital was not the constraint. Partial credit guarantees with strict loss-sharing, extended to the MSME and agriculture portfolios where prime rates rose most, would address the actual constraint — expected loss — while keeping banks' first-loss exposure so underwriting discipline survives. Alongside that: full enforcement of the Global Standing Instruction framework, the CBN's March 2026 directive denying new credit to obligors with non-performing loans in the Credit Risk Management System or private credit bureaus, deeper credit-bureau coverage, reliable collateral registries, and faster debt recovery through the credit tribunals under the Banks and Other Financial Institutions Act 2020.

**Sixth, reduce fiscal dominance.** As long as government borrowing grows far faster than private credit and risk-free yields stay high, banks will prefer bills to business loans. Sustained fiscal consolidation is a precondition for the MPR to bite on private lending — and the September 2026 memorandum of understanding between the CBN and the Ministry of Finance will be tested by the 2027 election cycle, when fiscal pressures typically intensify.

**Seventh, deepen competition and the deposit channel.** More competition among banks, including from fintechs and non-bank lenders, would compress the margins that let banks absorb rate cuts. Measures that increase deposit competition — easier account switching, transparent comparison of deposit rates — would force banks' cost of funds to track the MPR, which is the precondition for lending rates to track it too. And deepening the system itself — credit guarantees, movable-collateral lending, formalisation of informal businesses — widens the population the interest-rate channel can reach.

**Finally, anchor expectations where households actually live: food and the exchange rate.** Food inflation (about 19.6%) exceeds headline inflation (14.63%) by five percentage points, so monetary tightening alone cannot anchor household expectations. Coordinated action on food supply chains, storage and transport — outside the CBN's remit but decisive for its credibility — is a precondition for the policy rate to be read as a real signal by households. And because the exchange-rate channel is now live, the MPC must communicate how it weighs currency effects against lending-rate effects with each decision; a cut that is read as a weaker naira will be priced into lending rates before it reaches borrowers.

## How to judge success

Track the chain link by link — policy rate to overnight rate to marginal funding cost to all-in new-loan rates — alongside approvals, disbursements, collateral requirements and maturities, separating tightening from easing. Three numbers decide whether the September reset worked: whether the overnight rate stays inside the corridor; whether the average maximum lending rate converges toward the 23% anchor over the next two quarters rather than drifting up; and whether the prime-to-maximum spread narrows, which is the gap households and small businesses actually experience. If the 23–24 November meeting holds at 23% and those gauges do not move by the first quarter of 2027, the problem is confirmed as structural, not a matter of lags — and the CRR glide path, not another MPR cut, is the decision that matters.

## Caveats

The IMF asymmetry coefficients are estimated over 2007–2025 and describe average responses, not a mechanical rule for any single decision; the 17-day lag after the September cut means the October rate observation understates eventual pass-through. The sectoral prime-rate figures come from Financial Vanguard's analysis of CBN schedules as reported in the Nigerian press, not from a CBN release I could independently verify. The NPL and credit-stock figures are as reported in late-2026 press and agency coverage of CBN data. And the ratchet arithmetic assumes the asymmetry coefficients apply symmetrically across cycles; in practice the wedge will vary with the cycle, the corridor, and the CRR path — the direction of the effect is robust, its exact size is not.
